raw.title: Sir Ian McKellen leads tributes to 'beloved actor' Sir Patrick Stewart after his death at 86
raw.summary: The actor died in Los Angeles following a "a brief and poignant journey" with Alzheimer's Disease and Lewy Body Dementia.
paragraphs: Sir Ian McKellen leads tributes to 'beloved actor' Sir Patrick Stewart after his death at 86
Sir Ian McKellen has led tributes to Sir Patrick Stewart following his death at the age of 86, calling him "the most respected and beloved actor of his generation".

Tributes to the renowned British actor have poured in since his death at his Los Angeles home after "a brief and poignant journey" with Alzheimer's disease and Lewy Body Dementia was announced on Thursday.
"He wore his heart on his sleeve, which made him a man to rely on, to admire and, in my case, love," Sir Ian, Sir Patrick's X-Men co-star, said.
Famous for his role as Captain Jean-Luc Picard in Star Trek, Sir Patrick was a versatile actor who won multiple awards, balancing Hollywood roles and a career in classical theatre.
- Sir Patrick Stewart: Actor who moved effortlessly between Star Trek and Shakespeare
- 'RSC was where Sir Patrick Stewart felt at home'
William Shatner, who also helmed the USS Enterprise in Star Trek, said Sir Patrick brought "intelligence, grace and a deep sense of humanity to everything he did".
"Captain Picard stood for the best of us and so did the man who played him. I was filled with affection and admiration for him and his work," Shatner added.
Stewart depicted Picard in more than 170 episodes of the hit sci-fi TV series between 1987 and 1994, as well as in four feature films. He returned to the role for Star Trek: Picard in 2020.
George Takei, who played Hikaru Sulu in Star Trek, said the actor "inspired a whole next generation of star-gazers who looked longingly ahead to a brighter future for all humanity".
Sir Patrick would later be celebrated for his portrayal of Professor Charles Xavier - most commonly known as Professor X - in the X-Men film franchise.
Hugh Jackman, who starred alongside him in the franchise, called him a "tremendous friend and man", saying: "We lost one of the greats of stage and screen today."
Sir Ian, a longtime friend of his X-Men co-star, who officiated his wedding in 2013, said Sir Patrick was "defined by being born and bred in Yorkshire".
"You could hear it in his accented voice and in the stern honesty with which he told you what he thought and felt. Yorkshiremen have no truck with half-truths or avoidance of big issues."
Sir Ian recalled first meeting Sir Patrick as young actors in the Royal Shakespeare Company (RSC) and how he had expressed caution over him taking on the Star Trek role.
"He took the risk and thank goodness for us all that he did," said Sir Ian, who appeared with Sir Patrick in a 2009 theatre production of Waiting for Godot.

He added that while the US had become Sir Patrick's "adopted home", he "never forsook his origins" growing up in Yorkshire, and said "the proudest achievement of the most respected and beloved actor of his generation on either side of the Atlantic, was his appointment as chancellor of Huddersfield University".

Sir Ian noted that Sir Patrick's final film appearance will be as Professor X in the upcoming Avengers: Doomsday film. Marvel Studios described him as "a singular talent, a generous collaborator and a true gentleman".

The Academy dubbed his voice "unmistakable", adding: "Whether commanding the bridge of the Enterprise or guiding a generation of young mutants, Sir Patrick Stewart brought a tenderness to his characters that made us feel we knew them."

Sir Patrick died on Wednesday "in the loving care of his wife", a statement from his family said. "We will forever cherish the peaceful ease and reflection on his face, an enduring reminder of his invincible grace," it added.
The veteran actor is survived by his wife, Sunny Ozell, as well as by his two adult children from his first marriage, Daniel and Sophie Stewart.

Born in the town of Mirfield in 1940, Sir Patrick's love of drama began at school where he was introduced to Shakespeare and his first public performance was in a local church production of Cinderella.
He threw himself enthusiastically into the flourishing local theatre. "I used to recite Shakespeare from memory," he said. "I just learned all these big speeches."
When Sir Patrick was knighted by Queen Elizabeth II in 2010, he said he owed "literally everything" to his former English teacher who first encouraged him to perform.
His first foray into professional acting was when he joined the RSC in 1966, going on to play King John, Oberon in A Midsummer Night's Dream and Henry IV.

The RSC described him as a "colossus of both stage and screen", remembering him as "one of the finest classical Shakespearean actors of his generation" whose contribution to the company was "beyond measure".
Dame Harriet Walter, who first met Sir Patrick in his theatre days more than 40 years ago, said his passing was like a "huge giant tree has fallen in the forest".

"He had fire in his eyes and you were absolutely in the room with him," the Succession actress told BBC Newsnight. "I've never heard a bad word against him. And I think the world's going to be very poor without him."
Theatres in London's West End will dim their lights for two minutes on 3 November in his honour.
Hannah Essex, co-chief of the Society of London Theatre and UK Theatre, called him "one of the greatest stage actors this country has ever seen".

As well as having roles in films such as Safe House, Robin Hood: Men in Tights and the original Dune, Sir Patrick continued to appear on TV throughout his career, making guest appearances on Frasier, Futurama and the Simpsons.

US actor and animator Seth MacFarlane, who grew up as a fan of Sir Patrick, said he was "gifted the privilege of becoming a colleague and friend" as they worked together on Family Guy, American Dad! and Ted.
MacFarlane described him as a "rare actor who could take any bit of dialogue and elevate it, making a good writer sound great and a great writer sound masterful".
Comedian Ricky Gervais, whose BBC programme Extras Sir Patrick guest starred in, described him as a "legend".
Sharing a video of the pair giggling in a set of bloopers for the series, Gervais said: "I still can't believe he agreed to do this scene. And he didn't even mind when I ruined every take."
Sir Patrick was a lifelong supporter of English Football League club Huddersfield Town, which called him a "titan of his craft".
"Fiercely proud of his Yorkshire roots, Sir Patrick was a Terrier in every sense, and we're proud to have counted him as one of our own," the club added.
Alzheimer's is the most common type of dementia, while Lewy Body Dementia is another common form caused by abnormal protein deposits, which cause a loss of cognitive function.

The Alzheimer's Society CEO Michelle Dyson said Sir Patrick was an "extraordinarily talented and much-loved actor, admired by millions around the world", adding: "His death is a heartbreaking reminder of the devastating impact dementia has on people and families across the globe."

The actor became a campaigner on domestic violence in later life, including becoming an ambassador for domestic abuse charity Refuge in 2007, after witnessing his mother suffer violence at the hands of his father.
Hetti Barkworth-Nanton, Refuge's board chair, said it had been a privilege to "watch his endless devotion" to the cause, adding that he "broke down barriers and taboos on the subject".
Andy Burnham considered Sir Patrick to be "one of the very best" who "never forgot his working-class Yorkshire roots".

"He brought joy to millions," the prime minister's spokesman said on his behalf. "He always stood up for what he believed in, including through his campaigning to help those affected by domestic violence.

raw.title: Hundreds of millions at risk from Chinese shopping app malware
raw.summary: While many apps collect vast troves of user data, sometimes without explicit consent, experts say Chinese e-commerce giant Pinduoduo has taken violations of privacy and data security to the next level.
paragraphs: It is one of China’s most popular shopping apps, selling clothing, groceries and just about everything else under the sun to more than 750 million users a month.
But according to cybersecurity researchers, it can also bypass users’ cell phone security to monitor activities on other apps, check notifications, read private messages and change settings.
While many apps collect vast troves of user data, sometimes without explicit consent, experts say e-commerce giant Pinduoduo has taken violations of privacy and data security to the next level.

In a detailed investigation, CNN spoke to half a dozen cybersecurity teams from Asia, Europe and the United States — as well as multiple former and current Pinduoduo employees — after receiving a tipoff.

Multiple experts identified the presence of malware on the Pinduoduo app that exploited vulnerabilities in Android operating systems. Company insiders said the exploits were utilized to spy on users and competitors, allegedly to boost sales.

“We haven’t seen a mainstream app like this trying to escalate their privileges to gain access to things that they’re not supposed to gain access to,” said Mikko Hyppönen, chief research officer at WithSecure, a Finnish cybersecurity firm.
“This is highly unusual, and it is pretty damning for Pinduoduo.”
Malware, short for malicious software, refers to any software developed to steal data or interfere with computer systems and mobile devices.
Evidence of sophisticated malware in the Pinduoduo app comes amid intense scrutiny of Chinese-developed apps like TikTok over concerns about data security.

Some American lawmakers are pushing for a national ban on the popular short-video app, whose CEO Shou Chew was grilled by Congress for five hours last week about its relations with the Chinese government.

The revelations are also likely to draw more attention to Pinduoduo’s international sister app, Temu, which is topping US download charts and fast expanding in other Western markets. Both are owned by Nasdaq-listed PDD, a multinational company with roots in China.
While Temu has not been implicated, Pinduoduo’s alleged actions risk casting a shadow over its sister app’s global expansion.

There is no evidence that Pinduoduo has handed data to the Chinese government. But as Beijing enjoys significant leverage over businesses under its jurisdiction, there are concerns from US lawmakers that any company operating in China could be forced to cooperate with a broad range of security activities.
The findings follow Google’s suspension of Pinduoduo from its Play Store in March, citing malware identified in versions of the app.
An ensuing report from Bloomberg said a Russian cybersecurity firm had also identified potential malware in the app.
Pinduoduo has previously rejected “the speculation and accusation that Pinduoduo app is malicious.”
CNN has contacted PDD multiple times over email and phone for comment, but has not received a response.
Pinduoduo, which boasts a user base that accounts for three quarters of China’s online population and a market value three times that of eBay (EBAY), wasn’t always an online shopping behemoth.
Founded in 2015 in Shanghai by Colin Huang, a former Google employee, the startup was fighting to establish itself in a market long dominated by e-commerce stalwarts Alibaba (BABA) and JD.com (JD).
It succeeded by offering steep discounts on friends-and-family group buying orders and focusing on lower-income rural areas.

Pinduoduo posted triple digit growth in monthly users until the end of 2018, the year it listed in New York. By the middle of 2020, though, the increase in monthly users had slowed to around 50% and would continue to decline, according to its earnings reports.

It was in 2020, according to a current Pinduoduo employee, that the company set up a team of about 100 engineers and product managers to dig for vulnerabilities in Android phones, develop ways to exploit them — and turn that into profit.

According to the source, who requested anonymity for fear of reprisals, the company only targeted users in rural areas and smaller towns initially, while avoiding users in megacities such as Beijing and Shanghai.
“The goal was to reduce the risk of being exposed,” they said.
By collecting expansive data on user activities, the company was able to create a comprehensive portrait of users’ habits, interests and preferences, according to the source.
This allowed it to improve its machine learning model to offer more personalized push notifications and ads, attracting users to open the app and place orders, they said.
The team was disbanded in early March, the source added, after questions about their activities came to light.
PDD didn’t reply to CNN’s repeated requests for comment on the team.

Approached by CNN, researchers from Tel Aviv-based cyber firm Check Point Research, Delaware-based app security startup Oversecured and Hyppönen’s WithSecure conducted independent analysis of the 6.49.0 version of the app, released on Chinese app stores in late February.

Google Play is not available in China, and Android users in the country download their apps from local stores. In March, when Google suspended Pinduoduo, it said it had found malware in off-Play versions of the app.

The researchers found code designed to achieve “privilege escalation”: a type of cyberattack that exploits a vulnerable operating system to gain a higher level of access to data than it’s supposed to have, according to experts.
“Our team has reverse engineered that code and we can confirm that it tries to escalate rights, tries to gain access to things normal apps wouldn’t be able to do on Android phones,” said Hyppönen.

The app was able to continue running in the background and prevent itself from being uninstalled, which allowed it to boost its monthly active user rates, Hyppönen said. It also had the ability to spy on competitors by tracking activity on other shopping apps and getting information from them, he added.
Check Point Research additionally identified ways in which the app was able to evade scrutiny.
The app deployed a method that allowed it to push updates without an app store review process meant to detect malicious applications, the researchers said.
They also identified in some plug-ins the intent to obscure potentially malicious components by hiding them under legitimate file names, such as Google’s.
“Such a technique is widely used by malware developers that inject malicious code into applications that have legitimate functionality,” they said.
In China, about three quarters of smartphone users are on the Android system. Apple (AAPL)’s iPhone has 25% market share, according to Daniel Ives of Wedbush Securities.
Sergey Toshin, the founder of Oversecured, said Pinduoduo’s malware specifically targeted different Android-based operating systems, including those used by Samsung, Huawei, Xiaomi and Oppo.
CNN has reached out to these companies for comment.
Toshin described Pinduoduo as “the most dangerous malware” ever found among mainstream apps.
“I’ve never seen anything like this before. It’s like, super expansive,” he said.
Most phone manufacturers globally customize the core Android software, the Android Open Source Project (AOSP), to add unique features and applications to their own devices.

Toshin found Pinduoduo to have exploited about 50 Android system vulnerabilities. Most of the exploits were tailor made for customized parts known as the original equipment manufacturer (OEM) code, which tends to be audited less often than AOSP and is therefore more prone to vulnerabilities, he said.
Pinduoduo also exploited a number of AOSP vulnerabilities, including one which was flagged by Toshin to Google in February 2022. Google fixed the bug this March, he said.

According to Toshin, the exploits allowed Pinduoduo access to users’ locations, contacts, calendars, notifications and photo albums without their consent. They were also able to change system settings and access users’ social network accounts and chats, he said.

Of the six teams CNN spoke to for this story, three did not conduct full examinations. But their primary reviews showed that Pinduoduo asked for a large number of permissions beyond the normal functions of a shopping app.

They included “potentially invasive permissions” such as “set wallpaper” and “download without notification,” said René Mayrhofer, head of the Institute of Networks and Security at the Johannes Kepler University Linz in Austria.

Suspicions about malware in Pinduoduo’s app were first raised in late February in a report by a Chinese cybersecurity firm called Dark Navy. Even though the analysis didn’t directly name the shopping giant, the report spread quickly among other researchers, who did name the company. Some of the analysts followed up with their own reports confirming the original findings.
Soon after, on March 5, Pinduoduo issued a new update of its app, version 6.50.0, which removed the exploits, according to two experts who CNN spoke to.
Two days after the update, Pinduoduo disbanded the team of engineers and product managers who had developed the exploits, according to the Pinduoduo source.

The next day, team members found themselves locked out of Pinduoduo’s bespoke workplace communication app, Knock, and lost access to files on the company’s internal network. Engineers also found their access to big data, data sheets and the log system revoked, the source said.

Most of the team were transferred to work at Temu. They were assigned to different departments at the subsidiary, with some working on marketing or developing push notifications, according to the source.
A core group of about 20 cybersecurity engineers who specialize in finding and exploiting vulnerabilities remain at Pinduoduo, they said.
Toshin of Oversecured, who looked into the update, said although the exploits were removed, the underlying code was still there and could be reactivated to carry out attacks.
Pinduoduo has been able to grow its user base against a backdrop of the Chinese government’s regulatory clampdown on Big Tech that began in late 2020.
That year, the Ministry of Industry and Information Technology launched a sweeping crackdown on apps that illegally collect and use personal data.
In 2021, Beijing passed its first comprehensive data privacy legislation.

The Personal Information Protection Law stipulates that no party should illegally collect, process or transmit personal information. They’re also banned from exploiting internet-related security vulnerabilities or engaging in actions that endanger cybersecurity.
Pinduoduo’s apparent malware would be a violation of those laws, tech policy experts say, and should have been detected by the regulator.

“This would be embarrassing for the Ministry of Industry and Information Technology, because this is their job,” said Kendra Schaefer, a tech policy expert at Trivium China, a consultancy. “They’re supposed to check Pinduoduo, and the fact that they didn’t find (anything) is embarrassing for the regulator.”

The ministry has regularly published lists to name and shame apps found to have undermined user privacy or other rights. It also publishes a separate list of apps that are removed from app stores for failing to comply with regulations.
Pinduoduo did not appear on any of the lists.
CNN has reached out to the Ministry of Industry and Information Technology and the Cyberspace Administration of China for comment.
On Chinese social media, some cybersecurity experts questioned why regulators haven’t taken any action.

“Probably none of our regulators can understand coding and programming, nor do they understand technology. You can’t even understand the malicious code when it’s shoved right in front of your face,” a cybersecurity expert with 1.8 million followers wrote last week in a viral post on Weibo, a Twitter-like platform.
CNN’s Kristie Lu Stout and Sean Lyngaas contributed reporting.

raw.title: Ex-football chief admits offences linked to woman's drugging and rape by husband
raw.summary: Karl Lindsay resigned from non-league Taunton Town Football Club in Somerset before he was charged.
paragraphs: Ex-football chief admits offences linked to woman's drugging and rape by husband
A former football club chief executive has pleaded guilty to offences relating to the drugging and raping of a woman by her husband and others.
Karl Lindsay, 56, who resigned from non-league Taunton Town Football Club in Somerset before he was charged, has admitted the offences, which happened between 2015 and 2025.

Manchester Minshull Street Crown Court heard Lindsay's offending related to the rape of the woman by her husband and others in the Stockport area of Greater Manchester, and the administration of substances to stupefy her for the purpose of sexual acts.
The woman's husband, who is in his 60s and cannot be named to protect his wife's anonymity, has already admitted 62 offences against his wife, including rape.
The woman at the centre of the case was in court with one of her relatives and watched Lindsay intently as he entered his guilty pleas.

Three other men, Keith Fotheringham, 59, from Dundee, Scotland, Sean Peers, 38, from Stockport, and Graham Brougham, 74, from Northwich, have already admitted sexually abusing her at previous hearings.
The trial of nine other defendants accused of sexual offences against the woman has been scheduled to start on Monday after a series of delays.
The men are all alleged to have committed offences between 2015 and 2025.
- David Graves, 59, from Ilkeston, Derbyshire
Lindsay was told he would be sentenced at the conclusion of that trial.

raw.title: Arteta warns Dowman 'we are not in Disneyland' after red card
raw.summary: Mikel Arteta says "we are not in Disneyland" and that he will hold Max Dowman to the same standards as other first-team players after the teenager's red card against Fleetwood.
paragraphs: Arteta warns Dowman 'we are not in Disneyland' after red card
Arsenal manager Mikel Arteta has told Max Dowman "we are not in Disneyland" and that he intends to hold the teenager to the same standards as other first-team players.

Dowman, 16, was sent off in the 85th minute of Arsenal's penalty shoot-out loss to Fleetwood Town in the Carabao Cup on Tuesday after reacting to a heavy challenge by Harrison Neal and will serve a three-match ban.

A visibly annoyed Arteta spoke to Dowman as the teenager left the pitch, and on Friday spoke about the incident for the first time, saying he warned the attacker before the game about dealing with provocation.

"I haven't seen the reaction to my reaction, whether it is positive or negative. But you need to understand the context and the relationship that I have with him and what we discussed just before we went out," Arteta said of his words to Dowman.

"But, I don't know. You can have another reaction. If you see the reaction of my father and my mother with me some days you might say 'I don't like the reaction'. For me, it was the best reaction to be who I am."

Arteta revealed that he had spoken to Dowman on Thursday and said there were "no issues at all" between the pair. However, he added that he needs to be "very straight" with Dowman and clear of the standards expected.
Dowman was sent off for the England U19s earlier this month where he was also on the end of heavy challenges in a match with the United States.
Of that red card, Arteta said: "They are his age. They are 16 – the same. What is the reaction? That is the level and that is the reaction.
"And whether it is right or wrong, that is the reaction."
Arteta also spoke of the impact the red card had on the team, saying: "And the reaction when I don't win, you want to know what my reaction is? I am [angry] big time.
"So, we need to be ready for that. This is the environment and this is the reality, otherwise we are in Disneyland. We are not in Disneyland, we are in the Premier League and this level.
"We look after him so much that you cannot imagine.
"But at the same time we are going to demand from him, like everybody else, because he needs to earn the right to play. Because the other boys, what are they going to tell me? You need to be fair."

The Gunners did appeal against the red card but the Football Association (FA) upheld the decision. Of that, Arteta said he was "very disappointed", adding "we are lucky today that he (Dowman) hasn't had a broken foot."

raw.title: The acting legend defined by Yorkshire who 'loved it to the end'
raw.summary: Tributes have been paid to the legendary Star Trek actor Sir Patrick Stewart, who was born in Mirfield.
paragraphs: Sir Patrick Stewart remembered as 'Mirfield's finest'
Sir Patrick Stewart once said he had to drop his Yorkshire accent for Hollywood, but he never forgot his roots.

The Mirfield-born actor, best known for his roles in Star Trek and the X-Men films, died at the age of 86 at his home in Los Angeles on Wednesday after suffering with Alzheimer's Disease and Lewy Body Dementia.
His death has prompted an outpouring of love from the community he proudly called home, along with his beloved Huddersfield Town - the club he followed from childhood.
Stewart's friend and fellow legendary actor Sir Ian McKellen said Stewart "never forsook his origins".
He added: "Before everything else, Patrick was defined by being born and bred in Yorkshire, the proud county in the north of England which he loved to the end."
Referencing a trait often associated with people from the region McKellen said Stewart "told you what he thought and felt".
Prime Minister Andy Burnham said he was "very sad" to hear about Stewart's death, describing him as "one of the very best" who "never forgot his working-class Yorkshire roots".
In a TV interview with fellow Yorkshireman Michael Parkinson, Stewart said "we did toy" with using his regional accent when playing Captain Jean-Luc Picard in the Star Trek franchise.
But he added: "It was incomprehensible to the producers."
In 2004 he became chancellor of the University of Huddersfield - a role he filled until 2015. A year later the university's drama building was named after him.
Speaking at the time, he said: "I'm thrilled. It still makes me a little self conscious to think there's a building named after me."
Bob Cryan, the Vice Chancellor of the university, said Stewart was "very proud" of being chancellor and his success never changed him.
"It's something he took very personally," he said.

"He saw it as a way of paying back to Yorkshire because he was very proud of the fact that he was given a scholarship from what was then the West Riding of Yorkshire, but he felt he had never paid back."
Born in Mirfield in 1940, Stewart attended Crowlees Church of England Junior and Infant School before moving onto Mirfield Secondary Modern School.
His mother Gladys was a textile worker. She was active in amateur dramatics and encouraged her three sons to take part.
His father was a former Sergeant Major in the Parachute Regiment, whose experience during the wartime evacuation of Dunkirk had badly affected his mental health.
Stewart's love of drama came at school when one of his teachers introduced him to Shakespeare and encouraged him to perform.
His first public performance was in a local church production of Cinderella.
He left school at 15 and eventually got a job as a reporter and obituary writer on the Dewsbury Reporter.
He later won a scholarship to the Bristol Old Vic Theatre School launching a career that would take him from Yorkshire to the world stage.

Although he became one of Britain's most celebrated actors through roles including in Star Trek and Professor Charles Xavier in the X-Men film series, Stewart spoke of his pride in being from West Yorkshire.
Spen Valley MP Kim Leadbeater described Stewart as "Mirfield's finest".
Posting on X, the Labour MP described him as "an outstanding talent and someone who came across as a thoroughly decent and lovely".
Leadbeater said she had met the actor at Huddersfield Town football matches and corresponded with him several times, adding: "He was incredibly kind and he will be greatly missed."
A lifelong Huddersfield Town supporter, Stewart attended games when his schedule allowed and celebrated the Terriers' promotion to the Premier League at Wembley in 2017.

The club's chief operating officer David Threlfall-Sykes said: "Obviously it was Sir Patrick Stewart walking around so people would get star-struck, but he would get star-struck by seeing the players and the manager because they were his heroes.
"It was a weird dichotomy but it just shows how much this place meant to him, just like it does to everyone that comes here every weekend to fill the ground. He was no different in that respect."
For many, it was the combination of worldwide fame and his down-to-earth Yorkshire roots that made him such a star across the world.
Reflecting on his sense of humour, Cryan, of the University of Huddersfield, said: "He had a great sense of fun.
"I remember saying to him we were hosting a dinner for staff at the university to say thank you for all their hard work and we decided he and I were going to be waiters.
"You can imagine peoples' faces when Patrick served them their meal."

The statement announcing Stewart's death, which was shared on his Instagram account, ended with a quote from his memoirs: "Like me, Jean-Luc has lived an unusual life that has taken him far beyond the bounds of normal human experience.
"But he is also someone who remains true to his earthbound roots, for they are what gave him his identity. In the end, he feels the call of home, as do I."
Additional reporting by Tom Ingall and David Spereall

raw.title: «Είδαμε τον δράστη στις κάμερες ασφαλείας»: Μαρτυρία στο CNN Greece για τον εμπρηστή της Γλυφάδας
raw.summary: Τις δραματικές στιγμές που εκτυλίχθηκαν τα ξημερώματα στην πολυκατοικία της Γλυφάδας, μετά την εμπρηστική επίθεση σε διαμέρισμα, περιγράφει στο CNN Greece συγγενικό πρόσωπο της 36χρονης πρώην συντρόφου του 46χρονου υπαξιωματικού...Περισσότερα...
paragraphs: «Είδαμε τον δράστη στις κάμερες ασφαλείας»: Μαρτυρία στο CNN Greece για τον εμπρηστή της Γλυφάδας

Τις δραματικές στιγμές που εκτυλίχθηκαν τα ξημερώματα στην πολυκατοικία της Γλυφάδας, μετά την εμπρηστική επίθεση σε διαμέρισμα, περιγράφει στο CNN Greece συγγενικό πρόσωπο της 36χρονης πρώην συντρόφου του 46χρονου υπαξιωματικού του Πολεμικού Ναυτικού.

Η γυναίκα βρισκόταν στην πολυκατοικία την ώρα του περιστατικού και ήταν εκείνη που άνοιξε την πόρτα του διαμερίσματος, το οποίο είχε ήδη παραδοθεί στις φλόγες και τελικά καταστράφηκε ολοσχερώς. Σύμφωνα με όσα περιγράφει, όλα ξεκίνησαν όταν ακούστηκε μία έκρηξη, προκαλώντας αναστάτωση στους ενοίκους.
Αμέσως, μαζί με τους υπόλοιπους ανθρώπους που βρίσκονταν στην πολυκατοικία, επιχείρησαν να περιορίσουν τη φωτιά χρησιμοποιώντας πυροσβεστήρες, μέχρι να έρθει η Πυροσβεστική.

«Στις 02:10 ακούστηκε μια έκρηξη και βγήκαν όλοι οι ένοικοι της πολυκατοικίας. Μου χτύπησαν την πόρτα γιατί το διαμέρισμα που πήρε φωτιά είναι συγγενικού μου προσώπου και είχα τα κλειδιά και έπρεπε να ανοίξω. Το άτομο που κατοικεί στο σπίτι έλειπε. Άνοιξα την πόρτα και προσπαθούσαμε να σβήσουμε τη φωτιά με όλους τους πυροσβεστήρες που υπάρχαν. Ευτυχώς ήρθε γρήγορα η πυροσβεστική και έσβησε τη φωτιά.»

Όπως ανέφερε, κανείς από τους ενοίκους δεν αντιλήφθηκε εκείνη τη στιγμή την παρουσία του δράστη, ούτε τον είδε να απομακρύνεται μετά την εκδήλωση της φωτιάς. Σύμφωνα με την ίδια, αντιλήφθηκαν ότι ο δράστης είναι ο 46χρονος πρώην σύντροφος της 36χρονης, όταν είδαν το υλικό από τις κάμερες ασφαλείας.
«Κανείς δεν κατάλαβε κάτι. Από την κάμερα τα βρήκαμε όλα μετά.»

raw.title: Yorkshire Water boss resigns after firm downgraded
raw.summary: Nicola Shaw, who has led the company since 2022, will step down in January, it is announced.
paragraphs: Yorkshire Water boss resigns after firm downgraded
Yorkshire Water's chief executive has announced she is to step down, just 24 hours after the company was given the lowest possible environmental rating by the Environment Agency.
Nicola Shaw, who has led the firm since 2022, will leave the role on 1 January to be replaced by Nicola Medalova, a chartered environmental health officer who previously worked for the National Grid.
In a statement on Friday, Shaw said it had been a "privilege" to lead the company but that it was the "right time" to leave her post.
Shaw has faced criticism in recent years, including for taking £1.9m in undisclosed payments between 2023 and 2026, while the company has come under scrutiny for its performance.
The payments were made by Yorkshire Water's parent company, Kelda Holdings, for what the firm said was "investor engagement" and "financial oversight".
On Thursday, the Environment Agency gave the firm one star out of four - its lowest possible rating - meaning Yorkshire Water was classed as a "poorly performing company".
The EA said Yorkshire Water was responsible for 260 pollution incidents in 2025, which was its highest total since 2011.
In 2024, Ofwat announced it was fining the company £47m for historic sewage leaks.
In her statement, Shaw said: "It has been a privilege to lead Yorkshire Water and serve the people of Yorkshire.

"Although there remains a huge amount of work to do, I am extremely proud of what our colleagues have achieved, putting the business on a stronger footing for delivery across all aspects of its work."

Yorkshire Water said Medalova, who is a former non-executive director of the company's board, would join the firm on Monday as part of a transition period before assuming the chief executive officer role full time in the new year.
She said: "I am delighted to be joining Yorkshire Water and grateful to the board for the opportunity to lead the business through its next chapter.

"Yorkshire Water faces huge challenges but also great opportunities for continued improvement and I look forward to working with Nicola Shaw, the leadership team and colleagues across the business as I get up to speed."

In December last year Shaw said "not being transparent" about receiving £1.3m in shareholder-funded payments across two instalments had been a "mistake", but had insisted those amounts were "not for me to decide".
She received a further £660,000 earlier this year. Ofwat said the payments were not performance-related.
The previously undisclosed payments had come to light the previous August when the government banned Yorkshire Water and five other water companies from paying "unfair" bonuses to bosses.
Tom Gordon, Liberal Democrat MP for Harrogate and Knaresborough, said Shaw should have stepped down "much earlier".
"Good riddance. Nicola Shaw oversaw abysmal management of our precious natural resources, trashing our rivers while receiving an eye-watering salary," he said.
"Her replacement needs to understand that residents are at their wits' end, paying ever-rising bills for polluted rivers and threats of hosepipe bans while someone at the top rakes in millions."
Meanwhile, Judith Cummins, Labour MP for Bradford South, said Yorkshire Water needed "more than a change of leadership" but a "complete change of direction".
"A new face at the top cannot wash away years of Yorkshire Water failing to put customers first," she said.

"Nicola Shaw's time as Yorkshire Water boss saw customers frustrated by poor service, skyrocketing bills, record pollution incidents, and a plummet from 'good' to the worst possible one-star environment rating.
"There must be a wholesale shift in culture that finally prioritises customers. Only then can the company begin to restore public trust."
Robbie Moore, Conservative MP for Keighley and Ilkley, said Shaw's resignation "could not have come quick enough".
He added: "I have therefore already requested an urgent meeting with the new CEO Designate Nicola Medalova to understand how she plans to improve Yorkshire Water's performance at speed.
Chris Stewart at York campaign group Ouse It Lose It said the new CEO's priority had to be looking at "failures in the system".
"There's been a continual decline in the operation of this business," he said.

Stewart said he was not surprised by Shaw's resignation but it was a "shocking indictment of the way the company has been performing, while making loud noises about how much they're putting into improving".
Naomi Tilley, campaigns manager at protest group Surfers Against Sewage, said "systematic change" was needed to fix the company.
"Regardless of who the CEO is, there's sewage entering the sea and the water companies are failing. Yorkshire Water is not an outlier," said Tilley.
"The whole system and every water company is failing in different ways and we are seeing that the system is broken and we need fundamental change.
"While these companies are set up for a profit, we're never going to see pollution curbed and stopped."
Additional reporting by David Rhodes and Grace Wood

paragraphs: Θεσσαλονίκη: Φυλάκιση δέκα μηνών με αναστολή σε γυναίκα που χτύπησε τον γάτο του γείτονά της

Ένοχη κρίθηκε από το δικαστήριο γυναίκα που καταγγέλθηκε από τον γείτονά της ότι χτύπησε με κοντάρι σκούπας τον γάτο του στη Θεσσαλονίκη, με αποτέλεσμα να τον τραυματίσει και να χρειαστεί χειρουργική επέμβαση.
Το Μονομελές Πλημμελειοδικείο την καταδίκασε σε συνολική φυλάκιση 10 μηνών, με 3ετή αναστολή.

Σύμφωνα με την καταγγελία, το περιστατικό συνέβη τον Οκτώβριο του 2024, ενώ, από το χτύπημα ο γάτος υπέστη συντριπτικό κάταγμα στη δεξιά πίσω κνήμη και χρειάστηκε να υποβληθεί σε χειρουργική επέμβαση, με τοποθέτηση μεταλλικής πλάκας για την αποκατάσταση του τραυματισμού του.

Το Δικαστήριο έκρινε ένοχη την γυναίκα, με αναγνώριση ελαφρυντικού πρότερου σύννομου βίου, για κακοποίηση ζώου συντροφιάς, φθορά ξένης ιδιοκτησίας (συνδεόμενη με τα έξοδα επέμβασης και νοσηλείας του γάτου), όπως επίσης για εξύβριση και απειλή, πράξεις που, σύμφωνα με την καταγγελία, συνδέονται με φράσεις που απηύθυνε η γυναίκα στον ιδιοκτήτη, μετά το περιστατικό.
Στην απολογία της, η κατηγορούμενη αρνήθηκε οποιαδήποτε σχέση με τον τραυματισμό του γάτου.

raw.title: Driver guilty of hitting cyclist and dragging him to death under car
raw.summary: Simon Richardson is convicted of murdering head teacher Michael Mullins and will be sentenced on Monday.
paragraphs: Driver guilty of dragging head teacher to his death
Warning: This article contains distressing content
A man has been found guilty of murdering a head teacher who was dragged to his death for more than a mile while trapped under the wheels of a car.

Simon Richardson crashed into 56-year-old Michael Mullins, who was cycling home from his job at Stretford Grammar School on the evening of 20 April in the village of Warburton in Trafford, Greater Manchester.

Prosecutors claimed Richardson, 35, fled the scene of the crash before stopping to try to dislodge the injured but still-living cyclist and then driving on with Mr Mullins still lodged underneath the vehicle.
Richardson was also convicted of dangerous driving and will return to Manchester Minshull Street Crown Court to be sentenced on Monday.
There were shouts of "Yes!" from the court's public gallery as the guilty murder verdict was announced.
The judge, Mrs Justice Brunner KC, told Richardson that there was only one sentence for murder, namely life imprisonment.
In a statement released after the verdicts had been returned, Mr Mullins' family described him as "an anchor", "the perfect dad" and "our everything".
"My past, present and future have been brutally and callously torn apart," said his widow.
"My memories of being with Michael through the rough and the smooth are now permanently tainted with sadness."
Mr Mullins' son described his late father as "the type of Dad that would show up to everything".
He said: "Our last exchange of words together before he dropped me at the station was him reminding me of how proud he was of me."
Mr Mullins' daughter added: "I made a promise in those first days that I would live the rest of my life for my Dad and give myself the life he had started to see me grow into and wanted for me.
"I am here telling you all that my Dad was and always will be our everything."
The court heard Richardson, of no fixed address, had driven through "give way" markings at a junction in Warburton before colliding with the father-of-two, who went under the Volvo XC90.
Richardson then drove off before stopping in a country lane and twice getting out of the vehicle in attempts to pull Mr Mullins free, the jury was told.
He then mounted the grass verge in his Volvo and finally dislodged him before reversing over Mr Mullins, causing "crushing" chest injuries.

Richardson's cousin Gabrielle Debotte, who was a passenger in the front seat of the car, previously told the court that both of them had heard "moaning" shortly after the collision in Paddock Lane and that he had gone on to say: "He is under the car."
The prosecution claimed Mr Mullins' injuries were caused by "dragging and crushing" rather than the impact of the crash itself.
Prosecutor Phil Barnes KC told jurors: "Simon Richardson knew he was there and he inevitably knew what the consequences of driving on would be, and he did it anyway.

"For a split second after the collision, for a brief moment he possibly thought about doing the right thing and getting out and taking ownership of what he had just done and help the man he had just run down.
"But Simon Richardson did not get out. He did not do the right thing. He chose to drive away.
"The obvious reason is because he wanted to escape the consequences of what he had just done."
A motorcyclist followed a trail of blood and discovered Mr Mullins alone and barely breathing as he lay on a grass verge in a secluded country lane in Lymm, Cheshire.
The head teacher was pronounced dead at the scene shortly afterwards by emergency services.
Richardson was arrested the next day following a police chase.
He denied murder as he claimed he did not realise Mr Mullins was underneath his car and said he did not get out of his vehicle in a bid to free him.
But jurors did not believe him and found him guilty of murder.
Mrs Justice Brunner KC thanked members of the jury and acknowledged their job "cannot have been easy".
She discharged the jurors from taking jury service again for 10 years and told them: "This was, I know, an upsetting case and there was evidence which you may have found distressing."

raw.title: Six dead after helicopter crashes in northern Indian state
raw.summary: The aircraft reportedly took off from the Hindu pilgrimage site of Badrinath on Friday afternoon before losing contact.
paragraphs: Six dead after helicopter crashes in northern Indian state
Five pilgrims and a pilot have died after their helicopter crashed in the northern Indian state of Uttarakhand, officials say.
The aircraft reportedly took off from the Hindu pilgrimage site of Badrinath on Friday afternoon before losing contact.
The cause of the crash is not yet known but there had been reports of heavy rain and poor visibility in the region.
Uttarakhand, a Himalayan state which borders China and Nepal, is home to some of Hinduism's holiest shrines and attracts millions of pilgrims every year.

Badrinath is one of four sacred sites on the Char Dham pilgrimage circuit, alongside Kedarnath, Gangotri and Yamunotri. Many devotees travel through steep Himalayan valleys to reach the temples, which are open for only part of the year because of harsh winter conditions.
Uttarakhand's Chief Minister Pushkar Singh Dhami said the helicopter came down near a village close to Joshimath in Chamoli district.
The local civil aviation authority later confirmed to Indian media that six bodies had been located.
Helicopter services have become increasingly popular among pilgrims seeking to avoid difficult mountain journeys, but their safety has come under scrutiny following a series of accidents.
Before Friday's crash, India's weather department had issued an orange alert for the area, warning of thunderstorms, hail and strong winds.
In June 2025, seven people were killed when a helicopter carrying pilgrims crashed near Kedarnath. Another seven died in a crash on the same pilgrimage route in October 2022.
Several other helicopter accidents were reported during the 2025 pilgrimage season, prompting aviation authorities to tighten safety checks and restrict some operations.

raw.title: Israeli opposition accuses Netanyahu of trying to 'delegitimise' election
raw.summary: The PM's Likud party has alleged foreign interference and said Arab-led parties "stole" the election after his coalition lost its majority.
paragraphs: Israeli opposition accuses Netanyahu of trying to 'delegitimise' election

The main Israeli opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot and Arab-led party leaders have denounced Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu for alleging foreign interference following the election which saw his coalition lose its majority.
Netanyahu's Likud accused Israel's Arab-led parties of "stealing" the election. Home security agency Shin Bet is investigating whether they received illegal funding from Qatar and Turkey.
Qatar's foreign ministry denied the "ridiculous and dangerous" allegations and accused Israeli politicians of conducting a disinformation campaign against Doha.
Final results confirmed that neither Netanyahu's bloc nor the Jewish opposition had won a majority in parliament.
The two Arab party lists - The Joint List and the Ra'am - defied expectations to win a record 19 seats in the 120-seat Knesset following a surge in turnout among Arab voters.
That positions them as potential kingmakers, with Netanyahu's bloc winning 53 seats and his rival Gadi Eisenkot's bloc securing 48.

On Thursday Likud alleged that voters had been "bribed" to vote for Arab parties, after the head of the Central Elections Committee (CEC) asked the Shin Bet security service to investigate "serious suspicions" of foreign interference.
Both Arab parties strongly rejected the claim, with the Arab-majority Joint List alliance saying it was baseless.

The row is being seen by Netanyahu's critics as an attempt to delegitimise the Arab parties, thereby making it politically impossible for Eisenkot to join forces with them - which is currently his bloc's only route to power.

Israeli media reported that the CEC had been presented with a claim that Qatar had provided funding aimed at increasing voter turnout in Arab communities. Qatar's Foreign Ministry "categorically" denied the claims.
Netanyahu and his Likud Party framed the allegations as a "political earthquake" and an "an attack on democracy", aimed at removing their right-wing government.

But the Shin Bet later clarified that their investigation did not implicate an entire community who had voted legally, while acting CEC Director General Dean Livne said there was "no basis for allegations of systematic violations of election integrity."

Eisenkot, who was briefed on the investigation, said "it is too early to determine what happened, or if anything happened at all," and accused Netanyahu of running "an orchestrated and organized campaign to delegitimize the election results".

Balad chairman Sami Abu Shehadeh, who is part of the Joint List, dismissed the allegation, saying: "The losing side is constructing a racist blood libel and calling on the security agencies to use force in order to overturn the election results."

Netanyahu's attacks on Arab voters and parties have been ongoing for days. He spent much of election day posting on social media that high Arab turnout is an "emergency" and a "matter of life or death" for the Israeli right. He also shared AI-generated images of Arab voters at polling stations, in an attempt to encourage right-wingers to get out and vote.
Arab Israelis, many of whom refer to themselves as Palestinian citizens of Israel, make up about one fifth of the country.

For years, many boycotted Israeli elections, saying voting would legitimise a system that they say treats them as second-class citizens. But their turnout on Tuesday was inspired by a desire to oust the most right-wing governing coalition in Israel's history, led by Netanyahu.

The final results offer only three plausible options for a government to be formed: a national unity government involving Netanyahu and Eisenkot, a right-wing coalition involving Netanyahu and defectors from Eisenkot's bloc, or an Eisenkot-led government supported by the Arab parties.
Eisenkot and every member of his bloc bar one has previously refused to enter government with Arab parties, but speculation has swirled in recent days that an agreement could yet be reached.

A snap poll conducted by Hebrew University showed that the most popular option for voters from every party in the opposition bloc was for Eisenkot to form a minority government with Ra'am, and supported from outside by the Joint List.

raw.title: Spain transport minister says he won't resign over high-speed rail disaster
raw.summary: Óscar Puente has been facing calls to resign after two high-speed trains collided earlier in the week, killing at least 69 people.
paragraphs: Spain transport minister says he won't resign over high-speed rail disaster
Spain's transport minister says he won't resign over the high-speed rail collision that has left at least 69 people dead.
Óscar Puente told a news conference in Madrid he had "nothing to hide" while repeating the government's vow to get to the bottom of the disaster, saying many questions needed to be answered.
"My duty right now is not to talk about whether I should remain in my position, but to resolve the problem," Puente said.

The transport minister has been facing calls to step down in the aftermath of the tragedy, including from political rivals, a trade union and demonstrators who protested outside the transport ministry on Wednesday night.

Dozens were killed and many more injured when a state-operated Renfe high-speed train smashed into the back of another stationary train operated by the Iryo company near the town of Urda, in the central Toledo province, on Wednesday morning.

A preliminary report released by transport investigators late on Thursday found the Renfe train was travelling between 160km/h (99.4mph) and 200km/h when the collision occurred, causing its front carriage to become embedded in the tail of the stationary train.

Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez said earlier on Friday that public trust in Spain's high-speed rail network had been broken and repeated it was "unacceptable" that there had been two similar tragedies within a year.
In January a collision on the same Madrid-Seville route killed 46 people in Adamuz in southern Spain.
Wednesday's tragedy was one of the worst rail disasters in Europe's modern history, and Spain's worst crash since 2013.
Puente said on Wednesday a computer failure at about 08:30 that morning led to the initial halt of six moving trains, including the two trains that subsequently collided.
Leaked audio recordings published in Spanish media revealed conversations between train drivers and a control centre just minutes before the crash.

Three audio recordings between Madrid's control centre and two train drivers appear to show that one high-speed train was given clearance to move even though another train had stalled on the track, about 25km (15 miles) ahead.
Puente had said that the decision to instruct the trains to move again, without any speed restrictions, was "inexplicable".

The leaking of the audio recordings has been criticised by some Spanish politicians, with Alberto Ibáñez, a member of Congress for the left-wing Sumar platform, writing on X that they were "despicable".

Meanwhile, Irene Montero - the prime ministerial candidate for the left-wing Podemos party - said responsibility for the crash should not be placed on one worker, adding that train drivers and experts have been warning against the liberalisation of the railway sector for years.
On Friday Puente said he was "not going to use any worker as a shield".
But he said "many questions" arose as a result of the tragedy and he wanted to look at them "one by one".
"If the investigation shows there is human error we will act in consequence of that," he said.
The conservative People's Party joined calls for Puente's resignation after trade union CSIF called for the same earlier this week.
But Puente said on Friday he would not budge from his position.
"The easy thing for me would be to leave, but neither that fits with my character nor is it what the Prime Minister has asked me to do," he said.
"I feel immense pain and immense sadness for the victims and their relatives... I cannot let this pain paralyse me though. We have to find solutions to this problem."
The country is observing three days of mourning, as the families of victims and the survivors of the crash struggle to comprehend how it could have happened.
A 24-year-old athlete and a former government minister are among the victims of Wednesday's disaster, but many families are still waiting for information from authorities about their loved ones.
Esther San Emeterio, whose 54-year-old brother Pepe is still missing, told reporters in Toledo, near Urda, that officials were forcing families to wait in "uncertainty".
"We went to bed crying, outraged and full of shame," she said. "We are desperate and I want all of Spain to know. How can they keep us like this?"
Additional reporting by Sergi Forcada Freixas

raw.title: Pope Leo XIV becomes first pontiff to vote in a US election
raw.summary: The Chicago-born pontiff, who has a tense relationship with Trump, mailed in a ballot for the midterm elections that will decide control of the US Congress.
paragraphs: Pope Leo XIV becomes first pontiff to vote in a US election
Pope Leo XIV has submitted his mail-in ballot in Illinois, for the midterm elections, becoming the first-ever pope to vote in a US election.
"The Holy Father expresses his belief in the right and the duty of citizens to participate in democratic processes," the Holy See Press Office said in a statement.
The Chicago-born pontiff is the first US citizen to hold the Vatican's highest seat, after his selection in May 2025.
Since then, he has clashed with the Trump administration over various issues, including immigration enforcement and the US-Israel war with Iran.
"Pope Leo XIV has exercised his right to vote as a United States citizen, whenever he was eligible to do so," the press office said, including during his years in Peru.
The US midterm elections will determine which political party controls Congress and have a significant impact on the final years of Donald Trump's presidency.
Elections will be held nationwide on 3 November, but early voting has begun in most states.
According to NBC News, the Pope requested his mail-in ballot from the Will County Clerk's Office on 3 October.
Less than two weeks later, the Vatican announced he had surgery to remove a lower lobe of his right lung after he was diagnosed with lung cancer.
The Vatican confirmed last week that the Pope, aged 71, will travel as planned to Uruguay, Argentina, and Peru in early November.
Tensions escalated between the Pope and the US president in April, after the Pope called for peace in the wake of US-Israeli strikes on Iran.
"I don't think he's doing a very good job," Trump said about the Pope afterwards.
"We don't like a Pope that's going to say that it's OK to have a nuclear weapon," he continued. "I'm not a big fan of Pope Leo."
Pope Leo followed with his own remarks later, saying: "The mission of the Church is to preach the Gospel, to preach peace," according to Reuters.
"If someone wants to criticise me for preaching the Gospel... I hope simply to be listened to because of the value of God's words."
In the final few days before the midterms, Republican and Democratic officials alike are sprinting across the country to boost their party's chances of success.

Polls suggest Democrats are the favourite to gain control of the lower chamber of Congress, called the House of Representatives, and are poised to win seats in Republican-leaning areas that overwhelmingly voted for Trump in the 2024 presidential election.
Democrats also appear to have a chance to win additional seats in the Senate, the upper chamber of Congress.
The gloomy outlook for Trump's Republican party has seen the president hold several rallies in states where Republican victories are typically all but guaranteed.

paragraphs: Ινδία: Συνετρίβη ελικόπτερο στα Ιμαλάϊα - Νεκροί οι πέντε επιβάτες και ο πιλότος
Ελικόπτερο συνετρίβη σήμερα (30/10) την κοιλάδα Χοσιμάθ στα Ιμαλάια, με αποτέλεσμα τον θάνατο των πέντε επιβατών και του πιλότου, ανακοίνωσαν οι αρχές.
Το ελικόπτερο είχε αναχωρήσει από το Μπαντρινάθ, στο βόρειο κρατίδιο Ουταρανχάλ.
«Αυτή τη στιγμή καταβάλλονται προσπάθειες για τη μεταφορά των πτωμάτων από το δυσπρόσιτο σημείο της συντριβής στον πλησιέστερο δρόμο», ανέφερε η αστυνομία του κρατιδίου σε ανακοίνωσή της.
Οι αρχές δεν διευκρίνισαν τα αίται της συντριβής.
Η Ινδική Μετεωρολογική Υπηρεσία είχε προβλέψει βροχές σε όλο το κρατίδιο για σήμερα, δύο ημέρες αφότου ο κυκλώνας Αρνάμπ έπληξε τη νοτιοανατολική ακτή της Ινδίας.
Η Ουταρανχάλ είναι τόπος πολλών ινδουιστικών τόπων προσκυνήματος, συμπεριλαμβανομένου του Μπαντρινάθ, όπου ένας ιερός ναός αφιερωμένος στον θεό Βισνού προσελκύει εκατομμύρια προσκυνητές κάθε χρόνο.
Οι εταιρείες ναυλωμένων ελικοπτέρων εξυπηρετούν εύπορους προσκυνητές που επιθυμούν να επισκεφθούν ορεινά ιερά αποφεύγοντας τις επίπονες πεζοπορίες.

Λαμβάνοντας υπόψη τις ιδιαίτερες συνθήκες που έχουν διαμορφωθεί στην αγορά καυσίμων, η HELLENiQ ENERGY ανακοινώνει ότι παρατείνει μέχρι και τις 15 Νοεμβρίου την ειδική έκτακτη έκπτωση για το πετρέλαιο θέρμανσης και το πετρέλαιο κίνησης.

Παράλληλα, παραμένει σε ισχύ η έκτακτη έκπτωση των 4 λεπτών ανά λίτρο, δηλαδή μείωση τιμής 5 λεπτά με ΦΠΑ, για το Πετρέλαιο κίνησης.
Η έκτακτη έκπτωση θα εμφανίζεται σε ξεχωριστό πεδίο στα τιμολόγια που εκδίδονται και αφορά αποκλειστικά τα καύσιμα που προορίζονται για κατανάλωση στην εσωτερική αγορά.

raw.summary: The renowned British actor died after "a brief and poignant journey" with Alzheimer's disease and Lewy Body Dementia, his spokesperson says.
paragraphs: Sir Patrick Stewart: The life of an iconic actor

Iconic Star Trek actor Sir Patrick Stewart has died, aged 86. Stewart died at his home in Los Angeles on 28 October after suffering with Alzheimer's Disease and Lewy Body Dementia, according to a statement shared on his social media.
“His sonorous voice and singular talent will forever be synonymous with indelible performances in every genre,” the statement reads.
In a career that spanned seven decades, Sir Patrick won multiple Emmys and Golden Globes, a star on the Hollywood Walk of Fame and a knighthood from Queen Elizabeth II.

raw.title: Alaska Senate candidate denies knowing about alleged plot to put two Dan Sullivans on ballot
raw.summary: Dan S Sullivan, the incumbent Republican senator running for re-election, and allies have accused the Democrats of trying to confuse voters by recruiting Dan J Sullivan to also stand in the race.
paragraphs: Alaska Senate candidate denies knowing about alleged plot to put two Dan Sullivans on ballot
Democratic Senate candidate Mary Peltola has denied she knew anything about an alleged "scheme" that led to two men named Dan Sullivan standing in the Alaska Senate race.

The denial comes as the Trump administration continues to escalate a criminal investigation into the matter, according to US media. The Republican governor of the state ordered an official inquiry earlier this week.
Dan S Sullivan, the incumbent Republican senator running for re-election, and allies have accused the Democrats of trying to confuse voters.
The Alaska race is considered by analysts to be one of the tightest of the upcoming US midterm elections, which will decide which party controls Congress.

"I just want to clear the air," Peltola said while speaking to voters on Thursday. "I knew nothing about any other candidate on the ballot except for me and the incumbent. That is all I have ever known about. I am not interested in tricking voters."

Both Dan Sullivans have been running for the open Senate seat for some time. Still, controversy erupted earlier this week when The New York Times, external reported that Peltola's team worked with people who tried to recruit spoiler candidates in the Senate race.

The Times's report alleged that people connected to Peltola's campaign, as well as senior aides at the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee (DSCC), worked to try to recruit Dan J Sullivan, a retired teacher who lives in a remote fishing village, to stand in the Senate race.

The paper said it had seen text messages and interviewed 12 people who participated in or were told of the plan, or were would-be candidates who the team tried to recruit. The BBC has not independently verified the reporting.
The Peltola campaign has denied those reports and Sullivan has denied any links to the campaign.
But those denials have not stopped the US Department of Justice and Republicans from attacking Peltola.

The justice department has begun issuing subpoenas targeting Democratic officials allegedly connected to the effort to recruit Dan J Sullivan to be on the Alaska ballot, according to CBS News, the BBC's US news partner.
No charges have been filed as of Friday morning.

The Trump administration filed a federal lawsuit last week aimed at preventing the certification of the result if the Trump-backed Sullivan loses, arguing that the presence of both of them on the ballot could confuse voters.

On Wednesday, the justice department amended its lawsuit to include the reporting by the Times, citing significant sections of the story as well as Governor Mike Dunleavy's announcement of an investigation.

The legal action comes days before voters across the US head to the polls. This race in Alaska is among the closest-watched in the country, as it could be the deciding factor in who controls the Senate.
The non-partisan Cook Political Report currently classifies the race as a toss-up.
As the final weekend of campaigning approaches, President Donald Trump will appear at back-to-back rallies in Kansas and Iowa on Sunday.
The in-person appearances were previously cancelled, but a source familiar with planning told the BBC that they were rescheduled to accommodate remote appearances by Trump at tele-rallies.
