raw.summary: Αρνείται να παραιτηθεί από τη θέση του υπουργού Μεταφορών ο Όσκαρ Πουέντε, παρά το δεύτερο σιδηροδρομικό δυστύχημα που σημειώθηκε στην Ισπανία επί των ημερών του.Περισσότερα...
paragraphs: Αρνείται να παραιτηθεί ο Ισπανός υπουργός Μεταφορών μετά το νέο πολύνεκρο σιδηροδρομικό ατύχημα
Αρνείται να παραιτηθεί από τη θέση του υπουργού Μεταφορών ο Όσκαρ Πουέντε, παρά το δεύτερο σιδηροδρομικό δυστύχημα που σημειώθηκε στην Ισπανία επί των ημερών του.

«Το καθήκον μου αυτή τη στιγμή δεν είναι να επικεντρωθώ στη συζήτηση για το αν θα παραμείνω στη θέση μου, αλλά στην επίλυση του προβλήματος, στον ακριβή προσδιορισμό του τι συνέβη και στην παροχή σαφών εξηγήσεων», δήλωσε σήμερα, Παρασκευή 30 Οκτωβρίου ο Πουέντε σε συνέντευξη Τύπου.

Βουλευτές όλων των κομμάτων και τα συνδικάτα των εργαζομένων στους σιδηρόδρομους ασκούν κριτική στον υπουργό Μεταφορών επειδή απέδωσε το δυστύχημα σε ανθρώπινο λάθος, αντί να αναλάβει την πολιτική ευθύνη.

Τα δύο δυστυχήματα αναζωπύρωσαν τη συζήτηση για την ασφάλεια και τη συντήρηση του ισπανικού σιδηροδρομικού δικτύου υψηλής ταχύτητας, του μεγαλύτερου σε έκταση στην Ευρώπη, σε μια περίοδο κατά την οποία η χώρα εισέρχεται σε προεκλογική τροχιά, ενόψει των εκλογών που έχει προκηρύξει για τις 29 Νοεμβρίου ο αριστερός πρωθυπουργός, Πέδρο Σάντσες.

raw.title: Trump pleads not guilty to 34 felony counts
raw.summary: Former President Donald Trump has been indicted by a Manhattan grand jury, marking the first time in US history that a current or former president has faced criminal charges.
paragraphs: Watch Trump arrive in New York for his arraignment

Former President Donald Trump arrived in New York City Monday, a day before he is expected to turn himself in to law enforcement and face more than 30 criminal charges in a Manhattan court following last week’s historic grand jury indictment.
Trump’s legal team said the former president will voluntarily surrender and will look to challenge “every potential issue” once the indictment is unsealed.

Trump, who has vowed to continue his 2024 bid, is the first current or former president in US history who has faced criminal charges. The district attorney’s office has been investigating Trump’s alleged role in a hush money payment scheme involving adult film star Stormy Daniels that dates to the 2016 presidential election.
Trump arraignment has "unparalleled public interest," but it won't be broadcast, judge says

Acting New York Supreme Court Judge Juan Merchan wrote his Monday night order that the media’s request to broadcast the arraignment of former President Donald Trump was understandable, but that the news organizations’ interests in providing the broadest possible access to the proceedings must be weighed against “competing interests.”
In rejecting the request to broadcast the arraignment live on television, Merchan still wrote about the historical significance of the proceeding in stark terms.
Judge will only briefly allow photos in the courtroom before Trump arraignment begins

News outlets will not be allowed to broadcast former President Donald Trump’s arraignment on Tuesday in a New York state court, a judge said Monday night, but he will allow some photographers to take pictures in the courtroom before the proceedings formally begin.

Acting New York Supreme Court Judge Juan Merchan rejected the request by several media organizations, including CNN, for permission to broadcast the historic proceedings. Trump’s arraignment — like most arraignments in the Manhattan courthouse — is a public proceeding, but news cameras are not usually allowed to broadcast from inside the courtroom.
However, the judge is allowing five pool photographers to take still photos at the beginning of the proceedings “until such time as they are directed to vacate the jury box by court personnel.”

Earlier on Monday, Trump’s lawyers urged the judge to reject the media’s request for live cameras in the courtroom. The Manhattan District Attorney’s office told the judge they didn’t have a position.

The media outlets that tried to get cameras into the courtroom argued that “the gravity of this proceeding … and, consequently, the need for the broadest possible public access, cannot be overstated.”
The arraignment is also expected to bring the unsealing of the criminal charges against Trump, which have not yet been seen by his lawyers or the public.

The indictment stems from Manhattan District Attorney Alvin Bragg’s investigation into hush-money payments, made during the 2016 presidential campaign, to women who claimed they had extramarital affairs with Trump, which he denies.
Trump denies all wrongdoing and his lawyers said last week that they’ll fight to get the charges dropped.
Tuesday is the first test for Trump to navigate a legal and political strategy

Donald Trump is not planning to speak publicly in New York on Tuesday, aides say, if he follows advice from members of his legal team who have urged the former President to refrain from the vitriol he’s been directing toward the prosecutor and judge presiding over the case.

But that restraint does not extend to Florida, aides said, where he is planning to deliver a full-throated defense of his New York case as well as other investigations he is facing during a prime time address from Mar-a-Lago on Tuesday night.
It’s the first test to see whether Trump can navigate two vasty different approaches to his legal case and his political campaign, which are now inextricably linked.
Trump is "ready to go in and do what he needs to do tomorrow," attorney says
Alina Habba, lawyer for former President Donald Trump, gives an interview outside of Trump Tower on March 21 in New York City.

Alina Habba, who represents Donald Trump in several civil matters, spent time with the former president in New York today and said, “He’s in good spirits. Honestly, he’s as he normally would be. He’s ready to go in and do what he needs to do tomorrow.”
Habba — appearing on on Fox News’ “Jesse Watters” — was asked about the “game plan” for Trump’s appearance in court in Manhattan Tuesday and said, “It’s all mapped out.”
She added, “Barring any surprises, I think that it should be smooth. We’re trying to coordinate and cooperate with everybody to make sure that there are no problems.”

On whether Trump can get a fair trial in Manhattan, Habba said, “No, no. I think it’s very difficult. I’d like to have faith in this state, but I’ve been practicing for him now for a couple years and gone to court in New York for a few years, and I can tell you, it’s not the same as representing anybody else.”
The former president met with attorneys at Trump Tower on the eve of his arraignment
From left to right: Susan Necheles, Todd Blanche and Joe Tacopina.
Former President Donald Trump met with his attorneys Susan Necheles and Joe Tacopina at Trump Tower after arriving in New York City Monday, a source familiar with the meeting told CNN.
It is unclear if the newest addition to Trump’s New York legal team, Todd Blanche, attended the meeting.
Photos: Trump arrives in New York City a day before his expected arraignment
Former President Donald Trump has landed in New York’s La Guardia Airport ahead of his expected Tuesday arraignment in a Manhattan courthouse.
History was made Thursday when he was indicted by a New York grand jury. It’s the first time that a current or former US president has been criminally charged.

The Manhattan district attorney’s office has been investigating Trump’s alleged role in a hush money payment scheme and cover-up involving adult film star Stormy Daniels that dates to the 2016 presidential campaign.
Trump’s attorney said he plans to file “substantial” legal challenges. The former president has repeatedly denied wrongdoing in the matter and accused Democrats of targeting him politically.
Former President Donald Trump waves to supporters upon arriving at Trump Tower in New York on Monday, April 3. Trump is in New York for an expected arraignment on Tuesday.
Trump's plane lands at LaGuardia Airport in New York on Monday, April 3.

Dan Ray waves an American flag as a plane carrying former President Donald Trump takes off from the Palm Beach International Airport in Florida on Monday, April 3. Trump was heading to New York for an expected arraignment on Tuesday.
A television news reporter from Spain is seen outside Trump Tower in New York on Monday, April 3.
Trump supporters cheer as his motorcade passes by in West Palm Beach, Florida, on Monday, April 3.
Former president poised to huddle with advisers at Trump Tower
A supporter of former President Donald Trump holds a "Trump Won" sign outside of Trump Tower in New York on Monday, April 3.

A small group of supporters chanted as former President Donald Trump arrived at his namesake tower on Monday afternoon, with a handful of people waving banners with messages like “Trump won” and “Arrest Biden.”
While Trump couldn’t see his admirers as he entered a side door on 56th Street, his arrival came with more fanfare and security than at any other time in his post presidency.

Now that he is inside the building — where he launched his presidential bid nearly eight years ago — Trump is expected to meet with lawyers and political advisers on the eve of his arraignment, an aide told CNN.
Trump’s mood was described by an adviser as “defiant and focused,” as he watched expansive television coverage while flying back to his native New York City from Florida.
Special counsel has secured evidence of how Trump handled classified records at Mar-a-Lago, sources say

Special counsel prosecutors have secured evidence including daily notes, texts, emails and photographs and are focused on cataloging how Donald Trump handled classified records around the Mar-a-Lago resort and those who may have witnessed the former president with them, according to multiple sources familiar with the investigation.
The new details come amid signs the Justice Department is taking steps that are typically near the end of an investigation.

The recent investigative activity before a federal grand jury in Washington, DC, also includes subpoenaing witnesses in March and April who had previously spoken to investigators, the sources said. While the FBI interviewed many aides and workers at Mar-a-Lago nearly a year ago voluntarily, grand jury appearances are transcribed and under oath — an indication the prosecutors are locking in witness testimony.

The focus of both the mishandling of records and obstruction of justice probes has remained on the actions of the former president, the sources say. That includes prosecutors pursuing evidence of Trump’s intent to keep classified records after he left the White House, plus his knowledge that the records remained in his possession after the Justice Department demanded their return last May.
Witnesses are being questioned about what they saw in Trump’s private residential and work areas within the club, some of the sources said.
Former President Donald Trump arrives at Trump Tower ahead of his expected arraignment Tuesday.
Former President Donald Trump has arrived at his midtown Manhattan property Trump Tower.
He will stay at Trump Tower tonight and is expected to depart New York immediately after Tuesday’s arraignment to head back to Florida — where he plans to deliver remarks at his Mar-a-lago home.
Law enforcement officers stand guard near Trump Tower.
Biden says he has faith in the legal system ahead of Trump arraignment
President Joe Biden told CNN’s Betsy Klein he isn’t worried about unrest due to former President Donald Trump’s criminal indictment in New York.
“No, I have faith in the New York Police Department,” Biden said on Monday during a tour of a power generation facility in Fridley, Minnesota.
Asked if he had faith in the legal system, Biden replied: “Yes.”
Trump has tried to avoid his day in court for a long time, CNN's Gloria Borger says
As former President Donald Trump walked down from his plane at La Guardia Airport on the eve of his arraignment, CNN’s Gloria Borger noted the unique situation he’s in.

Trump is “one of the most famous people in the world, and he is a former president, presidential candidate, and now he’s a defendant. We haven’t seen that. It’s hard to kind of process that,” Borger said to CNN’s Dana Bash.
Borger also highlighted how Trump’s day in court is something he’s avoided for decades and that it will be a grievance he uses to rile up his supporters.
CNN’s Audie Cornish noted how Trump ending up in court seemed unavoidable given the “sheer number of investigations against him.”
Judge says he expects to issue decision Monday night on broadcasting Trump arraignment
Acting New York Supreme Court Judge Juan Merchan said he’ll likely issue a decision tonight on whether media outlets can broadcast former President Donald Trump’s arraignment on Tuesday.
CNN is part of the media coalition that asked the judge for permission to broadcast the hearing.
More on this: Trump’s attorneys said in their letter to Merchan that he is required under court rules to take into account potential security concerns.

“As Your Honor is well-aware, this case presents extraordinary security concerns (including Secret Service-related concerns) and we submit that any video or photography of the proceedings will only heighten these serious concerns,” they wrote.
The Manhattan District Attorney’s office also responded Monday to the news outlets’ request and said that it was deferring to the judge to make a decision on how best to manage his courtroom.
Here is what we know about Trump's next steps in New York today — and how tomorrow's arraignment will unfold
Then-President Donald Trump listens during a meeting in the Cabinet Room of the White House in 2020.

Donald Trump — the first former president in history to face criminal charges — has arrived in New York for an expected arraignment on Tuesday after being indicted last week by a Manhattan grand jury.

The former president will stay at Trump Tower tonight, according to a source familiar with his plans. But even before Trump’s appearance, his presence will be felt in the Manhattan courthouse Tuesday, as all trials and most other court activity is being halted before he is slated to arrive.
The Secret Service is scheduled to accompany Trump in the early afternoon to the district attorney’s office, which is in the same building as the courthouse.

Trump will be booked by the investigators, which includes taking his fingerprints. Ordinarily, a mug shot would be taken. But sources familiar with the preparations were uncertain as to whether there would be a mugshot – because Trump’s appearance is widely known and authorities were concerned about the improper leaking of the photo, which would be a violation of state law.

Typically, after defendants are arrested, they are booked and held in cells near the courtroom before they are arraigned. But that won’t happen with Trump. Once the former president is finished being processed, he’ll be taken through a back set of hallways and elevators to the floor where the courtroom is located. He’ll then come out to a public hallway to walk into the courtroom.
Trump is not expected to be handcuffed, as he will be surrounded by armed federal agents for his protection.

By the afternoon, Trump is expected to be brought to the courtroom, where the indictment will be unsealed and he will formally face the charges. After he is arraigned, Trump will almost certainly be released on his own recognizance. It is possible, though perhaps unlikely, that conditions could be set on his travel.

Ordinarily, a defendant who is released would walk out the front doors, but Secret Service will want to limit the time and space where Trump is in public. So instead, once the court hearing is over, Trump is expected to walk again through the public hallway and into the back corridors to the district attorney’s office, back to where his motorcade will be waiting.
Then he’ll head to the airport so he can get back to Mar-a-Lago, where he’s scheduled an event that evening to speak publicly.

CNN’s John Miller, Jeremy Herb, Katelyn Polantz, Tierney Sneed, Sydney Kashiwagi, Kristen Holmes, Holmes Lybrand, Hannah Rabinowitz, Paula Reid, Alayna Treene, Gregory Clary and Devan Cole contributed reporting to this post.
NOW: Trump lands in New York ahead of Tuesday's historic arraignment
Former President Donald Trump arrives in New York on Monday.
The former president touched down shortly after 3:25 p.m. ET.

Trump faces more than 30 counts related to business fraud, CNN has reported, but the indictment remains under seal. He is the first current or former president to face criminal charges in American history.
He will spend Monday night at the Trump Tower, according to a source familiar with his plans.

The Secret Service is scheduled to accompany Trump in the early afternoon Tuesday to the district attorney’s office, which is in the same building as the courthouse, where he is expected to be arraigned.
The former president is expected to return to Florida shortly after his court appearance and has scheduled an event that evening to speak publicly.
Former President Donald Trump's plane taxis on the runway at LaGuardia Airport, Monday, April 3, in New York.
Trump opposes news outlets' request to broadcast arraignment as Manhattan DA defers to judge
Members of the media are seen positioned outside Trump Tower in New York on Monday.
Lawyers for former President Donald Trump told a New York judge on Monday that they oppose the request by media outlets to broadcast Trump’s arraignment on Tuesday.
Trump’s attorneys said in their letter to Acting New York Supreme Court Judge Juan Merchan that he is required under court rules to take into account potential security concerns.
Among the Trump lawyers signing the new letter was Todd Blanche, who, CNN reported, recently joined the former president’s legal team.
Meanwhile, the Manhattan District Attorney’s office also responded Monday to the news outlets’ request, and said that it was deferring to the judge to decide how best to manage his court room.

However, the district attorney’s office wrote that it would “be a defensible exercise of the Court’s discretion to exclude or restrict videography, photography, and radio coverage of the arraignment in the interest of avoiding potential prejudice to the defendant, maintaining an orderly proceeding, assuring the safety of the participants in the proceeding, or for other reasons within the Court’s broad authority to manage and control these proceedings.”
But the prosecutors also noted that there “does not appear to be a categorical prohibition on cameras during an arraignment” under existing New York statutes and case law.

While the district attorney’s office stopped short of opposing the request, its lawyer pointed out to Merchan that a similar request for audio-video broadcasting was made for the 2021 arraignment in the tax fraud case against Trump Organization and its CFO Allen Weisselberg.
The judge responded to that 2021 request by “allowing a limited number of still photographs to be taken prior to the commencement of proceedings,” the prosecutors noted Monday.
CNN is one of the outlets requesting camera access for Tuesday’s arraignment.
Trump hires new lead counsel for Manhattan district attorney case
From CNN's Kaitlan Collins, Alayna Treene, Kara Scannel and Kirsten Holmes
Former President Donald Trump has hired a new attorney to serve as lead counsel in his defense against charges brought by the Manhattan district attorney’s office, multiple sources tell CNN.

Trump has hired Todd Blanche, who was most recently a partner at law firm Cadwalader, Wickersham & Taft. Blanche has previously represented Trump campaign manager Paul Manafort and Igor Fruman, a former associate of Rudy Giuliani who was also a key figure in Trump’s first impeachment trial. Politico was first to report the news of Blanche’s hiring.

Blanche’s hiring has been seen by some inside Trump’s orbit as a sidelining of Tacopina, who up until this point has been one of the most forward-facing attorney’s dealing with Trump’s defense. However, a senior adviser to Trump pushed back on that characterization and said the addition of Blanche was intended to add more legal firepower to Trump’s defense.

When pressed by CNN’s Kaitlan Collins on Friday if Tacopina was the right lawyer in New York to take Trump to trial, another lawyer representing the former president, Tim Parlatore, pointed to a potential conflict of interest.

“I know that Joe has certain potential conflict issues, given his prior contacts, with Stormy Daniels. So, who’s the right attorney, to take it to trial, is something that the client will have to decide. Ultimately, the decision of who to stand next to, before a jury, is a decision that only the client can make,” Parlatore said.
Asked by CNN’s Paula Reid if he is still on the case and whether he will be in court tomorrow, Tacopina said: “Yes of course ! And I will be the lead trial lawyer when the bell rings!”
CNN’s Paula Reid contributed reporting to this post.
No indication that DC protests will become dangerous, Senate Homeland Security chair says
Senate Homeland Security Chairman Gary Peters said he has not seen any indication that protests in Washington, DC, over former President Donald Trump’s indictment will become dangerous.

Peters, who is also a member of Senate Democrat leadership, said it is unclear what effect the indictment will have on the Senate. “We don’t know what’s gonna transpire tomorrow, let alone what’s going to happen in the few weeks and months. I think we’d have to take a look at what the indictment is all about.”
NOW: Trump leaves Florida for New York ahead of tomorrow's arraignment

Foi president Donald Trump takes off from Palm Beach International Airport in West Palm Beach, Florida, on April 3, 2023. - Former US President Donald Trump is to be booked, fingerprinted, and will have a mugshot taken at a Manhattan courthouse on the afternoon of April 4, 2023, before appearing before a judge as the first ever American president to face criminal charges. (Photo by CHANDAN KHANNA / AFP) (Photo by CHANDAN KHANNA/AFP via Getty Images)
Former President Donald Trump has departed Florida and is en route to New York to face criminal charges.
His personalized Boeing 757 took off from the Palm Beach International Airport this afternoon at about 12:59 p.m. ET ahead of his Tuesday appearance in a Manhattan courtroom to be arraigned.

Trump, the first current or former president to face criminal charges in American history, is expected to land at New York’s LaGuardia airport around 3 p.m. ET, according to a source familiar with his plans. He will stay at Trump Tower tonight, the source told CNN.

Trump faces more than 30 counts related to business fraud, according to two sources familiar with the case. A New York grand jury handed down the sealed indictment late last week. The charges have yet to be made public.

The former president is not expected to stay in New York City for very long. Immediately after his Tuesday court appearance, Trump plans to return to Florida, the source said, where he has scheduled an event to speak publicly.
Track Trump’s plane from Florida to New York here.
Former President Donald Trump waves from a vehicle as he leaves his Mar-a-Lago home on Monday.
CNN’s Alta D. Spells and Jack Forrest contributed reporting to this post.
New York City mayor to Marjorie Taylor Greene: "While you're in town, be on your best behavior"
New York City Mayor Eric Adams pauses during a briefing on Monday about security preparations ahead of former President Donald Trump's arrival in New York.

New York City Mayor Eric Adams warned GOP Rep. Marjorie Taylor Greene to “be on your best behavior” after the Republican firebrand said she will travel to the city to protest former President Donald Trump’s indictment.
Adams made the statement at a press conference as New York security officials detailed plans ahead of Trump’s arrival in Manhattan for his arraignment scheduled on Tuesday.

“As always, we will not allow violence or vandalism of any kind. And if one is caught participating in any act of violence, they will be arrested and held accountable. No matter who you are,” he added.

paragraphs: The Ukrainian military has reported little change to the front lines but heavy fire from Russian forces at various parts of the front line in the Donetsk region.
The General Staff said that more than 45 enemy attacks had been repelled over the past day, with the focus on Lyman, Bakhmut, Avdiivka and Mariinka.
It said there were 17 air strikes and more than 20 strikes by multiple launch rocket systems.
“In the Bakhmut direction, the enemy is trying to take full control over the city of Bakhmut and continues to storm it,” the General Staff said.
West of the city, Ukrainian defense forces repelled about 20 enemy attacks, according to the General Staff.

Oleksandr Syrskyi, commander of Ukrainian Land Forces, posted on Telegram that in Bakhmut he had met with “soldiers and commanders who destroyed the myth of invincibility of the Wagner fighters and Russian paratroopers.”
Syrskyi referenced the possibility of a future counter-offensive, saying that “the forward movement of our entire army depends on what every soldier is doing right now on their section of the front.”

Some of the most intense fighting is to the northwest and west of the city of Donetsk – as the Russians continue months-long efforts to dislodge Ukrainian defenses in Avdiivka and Mariinka. The General Staff said that some 20 assaults had been repelled.

“There are also some operational successes of our military in the Donetsk area. Our military have taken some positions. They have taken a more strategic and favourable position,” said Oleksii Dmytrashkivskyi, spokesperson for the military in that zone.
He also noted that Russian special forces had been introduced in the area.
“The enemy is trying to attack our positions between Avdiivka and Marinka. These attempts do not stop. It should be noted that the enemy has suffered quite significant losses,” Dmytrashkivskyi said.
He also claimed that the Russians “don’t have the same amount of equipment and, as they themselves say, they are on a ‘diet’ of ammunition for assaults.”
Social media video showed both sides engaged in heavy fire in the Avdiivka area, which the Russians have surrounded on three sides.
Denis Pushilin, the leader of the self-declared Donetsk People’s Republic, claimed that Russian forces were still advancing in the Avdiivka direction.

“It is still premature to speak of encirclement, but the situation is being created, if not critical, then extremely difficult for the enemy… After clearing Kamianka, our units are moving further. There are difficulties both with the terrain, which must also be overcome, and there are also similarities with weather conditions. But these difficulties are mutual — both for the enemy and for us,” Pushilin said.

raw.title: Ceasefire allows evacuation from devastated Russian-occupied Oleshky
raw.summary: But several hundred people are understood to have decided to stay in the frontline town, despite the lack of gas, electricity and running water.
paragraphs: Ceasefire allows evacuation from devastated Russian-occupied Oleshky

Hundreds of residents of the devastated Russian-occupied city of Oleshky have been evacuated, Russian and Ukrainian authorities have said, following a humanitarian ceasefire brokered by US First Lady Melania Trump.
"Everything unfolded without any incidents, and both sides noted the high level of organisation," Russia's human rights ombudsman Yana Lantratova said.
Ukrainian authorities confirmed the evacuees were on their way to southern Russia, from where they will travel on to Ukraine through Belarus.
Melania Trump said that "all elements of the convoy, including the safe passageway in and out of Oleshky, was established through mutual agreement between Russian and Ukrainian leaders".

A ceasefire - the longest and most widespread since the start of Russia's invasion of Ukraine in 2022 - has been in force in the entire frontline region of Kherson since Tuesday, allowing for the road out of Oleshky to be demined.

Residents who wished to leave had a four-hour window to do so on Friday. A convoy of 25 buses was brought in to allow up to 750 people to leave the town until 14:00 (12:00 GMT), along with ambulances for people with limited mobility.
Several hundred people are understood to have decided to stay, despite the widespread devastation and the lack of gas, electricity and running water.
"Everyone who wishes to leave Oleshky will be given the opportunity to do so safely," Ukraine's human rights ombudsman Dmytro Lubinets said on Friday morning.
"At the same time, those who decide to remain will be able to stay and will receive all the necessary humanitarian assistance."
Ukrainian territory lies 5km (3.1miles) from Oleshky, but the evacuees will first have to travel into Russian-occupied territory and then to the southern Russian city of Anapa.
They will board a Russian government plane to Gomel in Belarus, and then drive across the border into Ukraine's Chernihiv region.
Others are expected to choose to stay in Russian-occupied territory.
Lubinets and his Russian counterpart Yana Lantratova travelled to Oleshky together on Friday, setting off from Armiansk, in the Russian-occupied Crimean peninsula.

Lubinets is the first Ukrainian official since the start of the war to visit Russian-occupied parts of Ukraine. He will also become the first to visit Russia when he escorts the evacuees back into Ukraine on Saturday.
The Oleshky ceasefire has required close cooperation with Lantratova, which Lubinets said he carried out in the interests of saving lives.

But some in Ukraine have recoiled at the sight of him standing beside a representative of the Russian occupying power which has killed so many of the city's residents and made life unbearable for the rest.

Both Lubinets and Lantratova posted videos from Oleshky on their social media channels, saying people were given the chance to form two groups depending on whether they wanted to be taken to Russian-controlled territory or to Ukraine.

In one video, Lubinets can be seen meeting tearful locals. "The problem is that a lot of people are staying," he can be heard saying. "I was told that it was their own choice, we will do everything possible for the humanitarian aid to arrive."
Russia said on Thursday that it had prepared "dozens of tonnes" of aid for the residents who do not wish to leave, including food, medicine, hygiene products and fuel for generators.
An Oleshky resident told the BBC she had decided against leaving because "they wouldn't take my animals, so that's it."
Olena, who now lives in Kyiv, said her grandmother and wider family in Oleshky were also staying behind.
"The older generation does not want to leave," she told the BBC. "I've barely managed to persuade my father - and only because I've just had a baby, who he would never see otherwise."
Olena's grandmother's sister died in Oleshky last winter.
"She lost her legs after stepping on a landmine, covered in snow... People took her to the hospital in a garden wheelbarrow," Olena said.
"That's how locals transport all wounded and dead people in Oleshky to the hospital and the hospital's morgue: in garden wheelbarrows."

The ceasefire is due to be in force until the end of Sunday 1 November. It has provided the first few days of peace in the Kherson region since the start of Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.

Residents of Kherson told the BBC they were "overjoyed" by the ceasefire. However, they are concerned the truce has given Russia time to build up its military presence on the banks of the Dnipro river, which could result in a renewed assault once the ceasefire expires.
On Friday, the Kremlin made it clear that the success of the Oleshky ceasefire should not be interpreted as willingness to extend the truce to the rest of Ukraine.

A handful of foreign journalists have been invited to witness the evacuation of the town, which Moscow is expected to present as a humanitarian mission conducted with mercy to protect the people of Oleshky.
Many Ukrainians suspect Russia's real intention is to earn credit with the White House, and to provide US President Donald Trump with a boost ahead of next week's midterm elections.

raw.summary: Τέλος στη δράση εγκληματικής οργάνωσης τα μέλη της οποίας διέπρατταν διακεκριμένες κλοπές και απάτες προσποιούμενοι τους υπαλλήλους εταιρίας παροχής ηλεκτρικής ενέργειας αποσπώντας χρυσαφικά και χρηματικά ποσά σε περιοχές της Αττικής...Περισσότερα...
paragraphs: Άρπαζαν χρήματα και τιμαλφή στην Αττική με πρόσχημα διαρροή ηλεκτρικού ρεύματος - Τέσσερις συλλήψεις

Τέλος στη δράση εγκληματικής οργάνωσης τα μέλη της οποίας διέπρατταν διακεκριμένες κλοπές και απάτες προσποιούμενοι τους υπαλλήλους εταιρίας παροχής ηλεκτρικής ενέργειας αποσπώντας χρυσαφικά και χρηματικά ποσά σε περιοχές της Αττικής έβαλαν οι Αρχές.

Για την υπόθεση συνελήφθησαν από αστυνομικούς του Τμήματος Δίωξης και Εξιχνίασης Εγκλημάτων Ν. Φιλαδέλφειας – Ν. Χαλκηδόνας, το απόγευμα της Τετάρτης (28/10), τέσσερα μέλη της εγκληματικής οργάνωσης, ηλικίας 20, 32, 38 και 39 ετών.

Σε βάρος τους σχηματίστηκε δικογραφία για σύσταση και συμμετοχή σε εγκληματική οργάνωση που διέπραττε διακεκριμένες κλοπές, ληστεία και απάτες, κατά συναυτουργία, κατ’ εξακολούθηση και κατ’ επάγγελμα και για νομιμοποίηση εσόδων από εγκληματικές δραστηριότητες.

Από την ενδελεχή προανακριτική έρευνα του Τμήματος Δίωξης και Εξιχνίασης Εγκλημάτων Ν. Φιλαδέλφειας – Ν. Χαλκηδόνας και κατόπιν συνδυαστικής αξιολόγησης δεδομένων και στοιχείων, προέκυψε ότι οι κατηγορούμενοι τουλάχιστον από το Σεπτέμβριο του τρέχοντος έτους είχαν συστήσει και ενταχθεί σε εγκληματική οργάνωση με σκοπό την τέλεση διακεκριμένων κλοπών και απατών.
Τα μέλη της εγκληματικής ομάδας, έχοντας ως «ορμητήριο» οικία στην περιοχή της Δυτικής Αττικής, την είχαν μετατρέψει σε τηλεφωνικό κέντρο, με σκοπό την εξαπάτηση πολιτών.

Ως προς την μεθοδολογία της δράσης τους, τα μέλη της εγκληματικής οργάνωσης πραγματοποιούσαν αρχικά τηλεφωνικές κλήσεις, χρησιμοποιώντας επιχειρησιακούς αριθμούς τηλεφωνικών συνδέσεων καταχωρημένους σε ανύπαρκτα πρόσωπα (ghost phones) και προσποιούμενοι υπαλλήλους εταιρίας παροχής ηλεκτρικής ενέργειας, με διάφορα προσχήματα, όπως δήθεν διαρροή ηλεκτρικού ρεύματος, έπειθαν τα θύματα να συγκεντρώσουν κοσμήματα και χρηματικά ποσά.

Στη συνέχεια, τους καθοδηγούσαν να τα τοποθετήσουν σε προκαθορισμένο σημείο εντός της οικίας και να μεταβούν σε διαφορετικό χώρο, αφήνοντας παράλληλα την κεντρική είσοδο ανοιχτή, ώστε οι δράστες να προσεγγίζουν στις οικίες και να αφαιρούν τα αντικείμενα.
Στη συνέχεια, οι συνεργοί τους προσέγγιζαν πεζή τις οικίες, εισέρχονταν σε αυτές και αφαιρούσαν τα κλοπιμαία.

Σημειώνεται ότι κατά τη διάπραξη των αξιόποινων πράξεων, λάμβαναν ιδιαίτερα μέτρα ασφαλείας, αποκρύπτοντας τα χαρακτηριστικά τους ενώ για τις μετακινήσεις τους χρησιμοποιούσαν ως «επιχειρησιακό» όχημα, αυτοκίνητο ιδιοκτησίας του 39χρονου.

Από τη μέχρι στιγμής προανακριτική έρευνα έχουν εξιχνιαστεί περίπτωση ληστείας και 15 περιπτώσεις κλοπών σε διάφορες περιοχές της Αττικής με το παράνομο περιουσιακό όφελος να ανέρχεται σε χρηματικό ποσό άνω των 227.000 ευρώ.
Οι συλληφθέντες οδηγήθηκαν στον αρμόδιο Εισαγγελέα.

raw.title: Burnham's Number 10 North goes on multi-million pound hiring spree
raw.summary: The new government office in Manchester has launched 50 job adverts for roles including a "rewiring the state deputy director".
paragraphs: Burnham's Number 10 North goes on multi-million pound hiring spree
Andy Burnham's Number 10 North has gone on a multi-million pound hiring spree with dozens of new jobs being advertised.
The office in Manchester, set up by the prime minister in July, has launched 50 external job adverts, including a "rewiring the state deputy director".
It is the latest sign of how pivotal the government outpost - designed as a sister office to London's Downing Street - may prove to Burnham's aim to devolve power across the country.
Government sources say the roles will be paid for out of existing budgets.
The new recruits "will work with mayors and councils to identify barriers holding places back", but the Conservatives have described the office as a "gimmick".
There will be no redundancies elsewehere in the civil service as a result of the hiring spree, the BBC has been told, with some jobs expected to be relocated and other vacant roles closed.
The new roles, all based in Manchester, cover areas including strategy, communications, engagement, private office and policy.
BBC News has calculated they total up to £2.8m for basic salaries alone, excluding employer pension contributions in the civil service of 28.97%.
No10 North now has 120 members of staff, nearly half of the 280 staff who work in No10 London.

Among the highest paid of the roles are a "rewiring the state deputy director", with a salary band of £86,000 to £117,000, who will "lead the Rewiring the State Unit... shaping the government's approach to devolution across departments".
The government said it was launching a recruitment campaign for staff who would "bring fresh perspectives and knowledge of the places they serve, moving decisions closer to the people they affect".
No10 North "is driving the most significant transfer of power out of Westminster in a generation," the government added in a statement.
Some apprenticeships and secondments are also being advertised.

It comes as the government confirmed on Friday that No10 North would move from its current temporary home in Heron House, on Manchester's Albert Square, to a new government office on First Street in spring 2027.
No10 North will share the city centre building with other government departments spanning business, education, local government and the Cabinet Office.
Burnham made opening No10 North one of his first acts as prime minister, describing it as "the nerve-centre of a rewired Britain" that would help bring growth to more areas of Britain.

No10 North's deputy director Duncan Parish said in a speech last week that officials faced "institutional challenges" with delivering on these aims and called for a "mindset shift" across the UK's central government.

Conservative Party deputy leader Alex Burghart said: "He [Burnham] promised to streamline the civil service, but now he is hiring extra staff and, once again, won't say where the money is coming from.
"Manchesterism is just more bureaucracy at taxpayers' expense."

Meanwhile, Tory shadow cabinet minister Mike Wood has said there is "so little transparency" around No10 North after ministers told him they could not reveal figures on headcounts and office attendance.
According to the new job adverts, the Office for the Prime Minister - with exceptions for certain roles - expects No10 staff to be in the office a minimum of 60% of the time.

Since opening, No10 North has hosted summits of regional mayors, at least two of which have been partly held as video calls on Microsoft Teams. At one of these meetings, ministers unveiled controversial powers for mayors in England to charge new fees on visitors' overnight stays.
It has also hosted an education summit of school leaders and Irish Taoiseach Micheál Martin met Burnham for the first time as PM at No10 North in September.

Την προσεχή Τρίτη 3 Νοεμβρίου, ανοίγει ξανά το Γυμνάσιο Βασιλικών στην Θέρμη Θεσσαλονίκης, το οποίο είχε κλείσει μετά τον τραυματισμό μαθητή από πτώση σοβάδων.
Το σχολικό συγκρότημα ήταν κλειστό τρεις εβδομάδες για να γίνουν εργασίες αποκατάστασης.

Σύμφωνα με ανακοίνωση του Δήμου Θέρμης, «για προληπτικούς λόγους η διοίκηση του Δήμου αποφάσισε να προχωρήσει στο ξήλωμα του επιχρίσματος στις οροφές σε όλες τις αίθουσες και τους διαδρόμους του πρώτου ορόφου καθώς και σε ορισμένα σημεία του ισογείου προκειμένου να αποκλειστεί κάθε ενδεχόμενο επανάληψης ανάλογου συμβάντος».

Σύμφωνα με τον Δήμο, σήμερα πραγματοποιήθηκε νέα αυτοψία στο σχολείο και διαπιστώθηκε ότι οι εργασίες θα ολοκληρωθούν μέσα στο Σαββατοκύριακό ενώ παράλληλα, συνεργεία έχουν ξεκινήσει να καθαρίζουν τις αίθουσες του πρώτου ορόφου του σχολείου όπου έχουν ολοκληρωθεί οι εργασίες.
«Η καθαριότητα στο σύνολο του σχολικού συγκροτήματος θα ολοκληρωθεί τη Δευτέρα. Για το λόγο αυτό το Γυμνάσιο θα επαναλειτουργήσει την Τρίτη 3 Νοεμβρίου», γνωστοποιεί ο Δήμος Θέρμης.

raw.title: US inmate Christa Pike says she woke up 'confused and in pain' after failed execution
raw.summary: It is Pike's first public statement since she survived an execution attempt by lethal injection in September.
paragraphs: US inmate Christa Pike says she woke up 'confused and in pain' after failed execution
US death row inmate Christa Pike has released her first public statement since her botched execution in September.
"There hasn't been a moment since that night when I haven't been in pain," she said in the statement.
"My body hurts. My arms hurt. My hands hurt. My throat hurts. I still struggle to speak. And the pain isn't just physical. There is pain in my mind and in my soul."
Pike, 50, was discharged from hospital at the end of last month after surviving two lethal injections of the drug pentobarbital, which left her in a critical condition.
She has since been sent back to the prison where she has spent the last 30 years for murdering Colleen Slemmer in 1995.
Pike is thought to be the only person to have survived an execution attempt by lethal injection.
- I've seen nearly 500 executions - but never one like Christa Pike's
- What happened in Christa Pike's failed US execution, and how did she survive?
"I am recovering, and I know that I am getting stronger," she said in her statement on Friday. "But healing is not the same as being okay."
Her lawyers previously said she had suffered from pneumonia following the attempted execution, had significant swelling on her arms and was also unable to swallow.
Pike was 18 when she and her then-boyfriend, Tadaryl Shipp, beat, tortured and killed 19-year-old Slemmer, whom they had met at a job training camp for low-income young people.
Shipp was spared the death penalty because he was not legally an adult when the crime was committed. He remains in prison.
Pike's botched execution captivated and shocked the world last month and shocked Pike, too.
"I had not contemplated life beyond that night, and I'm deeply hurt by the incompetence that has put so many people in this terrible position," she said in her statement.
Slemmer's mother, May Martinez, was among those pushing for Pike to be put to death and attended the botched execution, later calling it a "mess".
She told a local ABC News affiliate in Florida, where she lives, that she thinks the state owes her an apology.
The Tennessee Department of Correction is yet to say why the execution did not go as planned, though it has defended the method it used.
It declined comment on Pike's statement when contacted by the BBC.
Tennessee Governor Bill Lee paused all executions for the remainder of the year and ordered an independent review to "determine exactly what occurred".
Lee was asked by reporters this week about a potential second execution attempt of Pike, saying: "I suspect her sentence will be the same as before unless determined otherwise by the courts."
Pike was the first woman scheduled to be executed in the state of Tennessee in over 200 years.
Her lawyers have spent decades appealing her case. In the days leading up to her scheduled execution, both the US Supreme Court and Lee declined to block the execution.

raw.title: P&R urged to speed up review of relocation grants
raw.summary: Forward Guernsey believes the allowance is putting pressure on rental prices.
paragraphs: P&R urged to speed up review of relocation grants
Guernsey's top political committee is being urged to prioritise a review of relocation allowances amid concerns it is putting pressure on rental prices.
Policy and Resources (P&R) said in June last year, external the review was "on track" to be finished by the end of September 2025.
Deputy Tom Rylatt, from Forward Guernsey, said the review should "be a priority for P&R" and the delay was disappointing.
P&R President Lindsay de Sausmarez said "several stages of work on the review have been completed" and the committee was due to consider it again shortly.
She blamed the delay on how busy the committee had been recently including delivering reforms to the island's tax system and a budget for 2027.
A recent report from the Scutiny Management Committee, external linked the relocation allowances to the current high price of renting a home in Guernsey.

The current policy, external entitles people relocating to Guernsey for jobs with the States of Guernsey to a £5,000 grant (£6,600 for Alderney) alongside help with rental costs for up to four years, storage costs and, in some cases, support with an unsold home's mortgage.
In the last decade rents have risen by 65% to on average £2,138 per month, according to the States of Guernsey, external.
A freedom of information request earlier this year revealed more than £5m was spent by the States on relocation packages in 2025, the most since the support was introduced.
Deputy Rylatt said: "It is disappointing that the review has still not been completed, having originally been due in September 2025.

"With housing costs continuing to place enormous pressure on islanders, it needs to be a priority for P&R that we understand the impact these packages may be having, particularly on the rental market.
"I hope the committee will now bring this work to a conclusion and set out what changes, if any, it intends to make."
Those buying a home in Guernsey can also qualify for a £8,750 house purchase grant, while short-term recruits could receive smaller payments towards travel and moving costs.
Scrutiny Management Committee President Andy Sloan said the current policy was "excessive" and believes "such a subsidy is likely to have an upward impact on local market rents".
In June 2025 P&R said the review of these grants would look at different options for relocation support, including possible alternatives, using workforce data and financial analysis.
It said any changes would need to balance potential savings against the need to recruit and retain staff in essential public services such as health, education, social care and law enforcement.
Officials said the review was unlikely to be made public as it was looking at an internal policy but any changes would be clearly communicated by P&R.

raw.title: Russell Brand accusers 'haunted' for years by alleged crimes, court hears
raw.summary: The women involved in the case had "nothing to gain" apart from "some closure", the prosecutor says.
paragraphs: Russell Brand accusers 'haunted' for years by alleged crimes, court hears
Some of the women in Russell Brand's rape and sexual assault case have been "haunted" for years by what they allege he did to them, jurors have been told.
In her closing speech at London's Southwark Crown Court on Friday, prosecutor Reil Karmy-Jones KC said the women had "nothing to gain" from coming forward apart from "some closure".
Speaking for the defence, Polly Dyer told jurors Brand had pleaded guilty and been fined over possession of cannabis in 1995, but had no other "convictions, cautions, reprimands or warnings".
Brand, 51, is on trial facing seven charges; three counts of rape, three charges of sexual assault and one allegation of attempted indecent assault. He denies the charges.
Karmy-Jones KC told the court that this case brings together six different women, none of whom knows each other.
She said that while all the alleged victims have since moved on with their lives, due to this trial they have been forced to "relive what has happened to them".
None of the women involved has "sought the limelight" or "any kind of publicity", she said, adding there was "no benefit to them from perhaps some closure."
Referring to Brand's accuser's evidence the prosecutor said "how many said he was nice and then there was a like a personality change…
"His eyes changed, he snapped, from charming to frightening to nasty," Karmy-Jones KC said.
She added that the complainant's evidence had been that "he didn't listen when I said no, he didn't stop, he didn't care, pulling pushing… thrusting".
"In the rape cases, he kept on going until he achieved his ultimate aim."
The prosecutor also dismissed the idea that a documentary had caused the women to "re-invent" what actually happened.
"There is no magic force in this documentary", she added.
"What in fact happened was these women have realised they are not alone and have bravely come before you to tell the truth."
She added: "Truth they have lived with, which in some cases has haunted them for years."
She told the jury: "The experience of people raped may be something that looms a little bit larger in your mind rather than the intricacies of the outfit.
"The defendant couldn't really remember anything when he was interviewed, in stark contrast to now when he suddenly seems to remember all sorts of details about the week."
You can follow the trial day by day on the BBC podcast Russell Brand on Trial - available on BBC Sounds, YouTube, iPlayer, or wherever you get your BBC podcasts
Addressing Brand's presented change in character, Karmy-Jones KC told the court "He may now be a completely different person to the man he was between 1999 and 2009."
She added: "He may well look back and not find some of his jokes funny".
"He may now treat women with kindness and consent".
Brand's wife Laura gave evidence yesterday, when she told the court her husband was a "kind and a wonderful father".
Karmy-Jones KC called her Russell Brand's "undoubtedly lovely wife", who "bravely" gave evidence.
However, she also noted that she was not with him at the time many of the alleged acts are said to have taken place.
"The reality is she wasn't there then, for the first five counts, she wasn't with him, nor was she with him for the final two counts."
In the final set of agreed facts in his trial, the court heard from Dyer about Brand's fine after he "pleaded guilty to one charge of possessing cannabis on 20 April 1995".
"He received a fine. He has no other convictions, cautions, reprimands or warnings", she said.

- Εξασφάλιση νέων ναυλώσεων για δύο πλοία μεταφοράς υγροποιημένου φυσικού αερίου LNG/C και για τέσσερα πλοία μεταφοράς αερίων, συμπεριλαμβανομένης μονοετούς χρονοναύλωσης με ναύλο συνδεδεμένο με δείκτη για ένα από τα έξι υπό ναυπήγηση LNG/C καθώς και μονοετούς χρονοναύλωσης για το MG/C Aridaios
- Επίτευξη μέσου ημερήσιου ναύλου ύψους $83.862 για τον στόλο LNG/C και $40.987 για τον στόλο μεταφοράς αερίων κατά το τρίτο τρίμηνο του 2026
- Ανακοίνωση μερίσματος ύψους $0,15 ανά μετοχή για το τρίτο τρίμηνο του 2026

Ο κ. Γεράσιμος Καλογηράτος, Διευθύνων Σύμβουλος της CCEC, σχολίασε: «Το τρίτο τρίμηνο του 2026 χαρακτηρίστηκε από τη συνεχιζόμενη αβεβαιότητα στη Μέση Ανατολή, με τις διελεύσεις πλοίων μεταφοράς LNG από τα Στενά του Ορμούζ να πραγματοποιούνται μόνο σποραδικά.

Παρότι η αυξανόμενη δυναμικότητα υγροποίησης φυσικού αερίου της Βόρειας Αμερικής μετρίασε εν μέρει τις επιπτώσεις, η συνακόλουθη μείωση των ποσοτήτων LNG από τη Μέση Ανατολή ενέτεινε τη στενότητα προσφοράς στην αγορά LNG της λεκάνης του Ατλαντικού, με τα ευρωπαϊκά αποθέματα ενόψει χειμώνα να βρίσκονται σε πολυετή χαμηλά και τους αγοραστές από την Ασία να ανταγωνίζονται για φορτία από τις ΗΠΑ. Ταυτόχρονα, οι αυξημένες παραδόσεις νεότευκτων πλοίων και η μεγαλύτερη διαθεσιμότητα πλοίων οδήγησαν σε υποχώρηση των ναύλων μεταφοράς LNG στην αγορά spot σε σχέση με τα επίπεδα του πρώτου εξαμήνου του έτους.

Η στρατηγική μας, που εστιάζει στην απασχόληση πλοίων τελευταίας γενιάς σε μακροχρόνιες ναυλώσεις με υψηλής ποιότητας αντισυμβαλλομένους, έχει θωρακίσει τη CCEC έναντι αυτής της βραχυπρόθεσμης μεταβλητότητας.

Από την αρχή του έτους μέχρι σήμερα, έχουμε παραλάβει οκτώ πλοία (τρία LNG/C, δύο MG/C και τρία HMG/C), ενώ ακόμη οκτώ είναι προγραμματισμένα να παραδοθούν μέσα στο 2027, σηματοδοτώντας την επιτάχυνση της ανάπτυξης της ναυτιλιακής πλατφόρμας της CCEC.

Ο εν ενεργεία στόλος μας αποτελείται πλέον από 15 LNG/C τελευταίας γενιάς, τρία HMG/C, δύο MG/C και ένα πλοίο μεταφοράς εμπορευματοκιβωτίων κατηγορίας Neo-Panamax, ενώ βρίσκονται υπό παραγγελία ακόμη έξι LNG/C, τέσσερα MG/C, ένα HMG/C και ένα πλοίο ανεφοδιασμού υγροποιημένου φυσικού αερίου («LNGB/V»).

Η CCEC είναι η μεγαλύτερη εισηγμένη στις ΗΠΑ ναυτιλιακή εταιρεία μεταφοράς LNG, με βάση το μέγεθος του στόλου της, με σημαντική και αυξανόμενη παρουσία στην αγορά υγραερίου (LPG), υποστηριζόμενη από συμβασιοποιημένη ανάπτυξη του στόλου της έως το 2029. Η μέση διάρκεια της περιόδου των ναυλώσεών μας ανέρχεται σε 6,4 έτη για τον στόλο LNG/C και σε 0,7 έτη για τον στόλο μεταφοράς LPG/πολλαπλών αερίων.

Τα συμβασιοποιημένα έσοδά μας ανέρχονται σε περίπου $2,8 δισ. και, εφόσον ασκηθούν όλα τα δικαιώματα προαίρεσης των ναυλωτών μας, αυξάνονται σε περίπου $4,2 δισ., παρέχοντας υψηλή ορατότητα ως προς τις μελλοντικές ταμειακές ροές.

Κοιτώντας μπροστά, αναμένουμε ότι η ναυλαγορά μεταφοράς LNG θα παραμείνει ευμετάβλητη, δεδομένης της γεωπολιτικής αβεβαιότητας που επηρεάζει επί του παρόντος τους μεταφερόμενους όγκους LNG, την προσφορά πλοίων και τις ευκαιρίες εξισορροπητικής εμπορίας (arbitrage) εμπορευμάτων.

Ωστόσο, παραμένουμε αισιόδοξοι για τα μακροπρόθεσμα θεμελιώδη μεγέθη της αγοράς. Οι νέες μονάδες υγροποίησης που αναμένεται να τεθούν σε λειτουργία έως το τέλος της δεκαετίας, σε συνδυασμό με την αυξημένη επιδίωξη διασφάλισης της ενεργειακής ασφάλειας, εκτιμάται ότι θα στηρίξουν τη ζήτηση για LNG.

Επιπρόσθετα, η ανάγκη αντικατάστασης παλαιότερων, λιγότερο αποδοτικών πλοίων αναμένεται να ενισχύσει τη ζήτηση για σύγχρονα πλοία μεταφοράς LNG. Τα θεμελιώδη αυτά μεγέθη θέτουν τη CCEC σε ισχυρή θέση ώστε να δημιουργεί μακροπρόθεσμη αξία για τους μετόχους μας.»

raw.title: US tech stocks see sharp falls over AI cost fears
raw.summary: Shares in Intel continue to fall while the tech-heavy Nasdaq opens at its lowest level in more than two months.
paragraphs: US tech stocks see sharp falls over AI cost fears
US stocks have continued to slide as concerns continue to intensify over the increasing costs of the artificial intelligence (AI) build out.

Shares in Intel continued their overnight slide into early trading on Friday, falling as much as 30% after the chip maker warned of a weaker computer market even as it plans to increase spending on AI.
Amazon shares fell as far as 6% before recovering after its reported earnings on Thursday evening fell short of investors' expectations.
The tech-heavy Nasdaq stock exchange opened on Friday at its lowest level in more than two months, down 2.5%, as other tech stocks including Reddit and Roblox continued to fall.
The losses follow the value of Google owner Alphabet plunging by more than $500bn on Thursday after it revealed its own AI summaries were affecting its core search advertising revenue.
Alphabet stock continued to fall in early trading, down 1% after Thursday's massive slide.
The bigger losses on Friday were elsewhere, with Intel on track to lose more than $130bn in value after its earnings update rattled investors.
On Thursday, Intel's finance chief David Zinsner said the firm did not expect to bring in more cash than it spent this year, and forecast lower-than-expected revenue for its fourth quarter.
"Looking ahead, we see the PC slowdown continuing at least through the first half of next year," he said in the chip maker's third quarter earnings report.
In the earnings call, he said the firm had significantly ramped up investment in equipment in the third quarter and expected that to be "even more significant" in the following three months.
Amazon on Thursday revealed the company was also spending more cash that it was making, and that spending had increased six-fold over the span of three months.
Shares in Amazon recovered slightly from the overnight fall but were still down about 1.6% in Friday trading.
Reddit stock was down by 26%, after the social media platform revealed weaker-than-expected daily user figures and warned that Google's growing AI-driven search was hurting referral traffic.
Stock in online game platform Roblox also fell, down by nearly 20%, as its daily active user numbers dropped.
Several major tech firms have reported earnings this week, including Microsoft, and analysts said there were questions about the payout from the huge investments in AI.
Chris Low, from investment management firm FHN Financial, said the bulk of what was happening in the stock market was in reaction to some of the biggest tech players such as Amazon and Google.
He told Reuters the companies were "showing some pretty significant growing pains as they aggressively pursue the AI build-out".
"The thinking is that these signs suggest that the entire sector is going to slow down."

raw.title: Syrians struggle with soaring prices as crisis challenges post-Assad recovery
raw.summary: End of subsidies and rising prices drive discontent, testing support for Ahmed al-Sharaa's government.
paragraphs: Syrians struggle with soaring prices as crisis challenges post-Assad recovery

Last month, protests erupted in squares and streets across Syria. People burned tyres, blocked roads and chanted slogans, angry at the government's decision to raise fuel prices again. It was the largest show of discontent yet since President Ahmed al-Sharaa came to power two years ago.

Speaking on a Syrian TV channel, a man said he still supported the authorities but that his situation had deteriorated to the point where he could no longer afford to buy bread. "Honestly," another said, "we have begun to fear what kind of new decision each morning will bring".

The increase was the latest in a series of measures people blame for a growing cost-of-living crisis. For many Syrians, life, financially, has worsened since rebels led by Sharaa ousted President Bashar al-Assad, ending five decades of his family's brutal rule and more than 13 years of a devastating civil war.
Catapulted to the presidency, Sharaa has, since then, led Syria's transition and efforts to revive a broken economy after a long period of mismanagement, isolation and conflict.

There was never any doubt about how challenging this would be. But as they celebrated Assad's overthrow and their new freedoms, Syrians, perhaps unrealistically, hoped things would quickly improve. That, however, has not materialised, and the handling of the economy has frustrated many here.

From essential bills to basic items, the cost of virtually everything has gone up. And many saw a further and unexpected rise in fuel prices as a sign of a government out of touch with its country. "We don't want roundabouts. Every day they build a new roundabout. People stood by you and are still with you," another protester said, addressing Sharaa, "but this will [make] things explode".
Days later, amid calls for further demonstrations, the increase was revoked.

In a suburb of Damascus, I joined Fatima Saleh Eid at an open-air market for her weekly shop. At 50, she works as a cleaner to help support her family. "We've suffered a lot," she said. Her husband had recently been hired by a ceramic factory after a year unemployed. He is among the lucky ones, as many are struggling to find work. In some streets, men gather in the hope of meeting someone offering a day job; often, they wait in vain.

Since coming to power, the government has slashed long-held subsidies as part of an austerity drive. The price of bread, a Syrian staple, has increased tenfold. Fuel prices are now in line with the international average, which has put pressure on farmers and made transportation more expensive, while the cost of electricity has gone up several hundred per cent for some.
The authorities, in response, have adjusted public sector wages, including pensions; unsurprisingly, the effect of the additional pay for people has been lost as prices keep rising.
"We eat more sparingly now. We can't afford chicken anymore nor meat. We only eat vegetables but even [that is] expensive," Fatima said. "Inshallah [God willing] things will get cheaper."

As she spoke, around a dozen people, of all ages, gathered around us. Nobody disagreed. One elderly man also said he had stopped eating meat. Another, in his 20s, told me his family were no longer able to pay the medicine for his father, who had a heart condition. One young woman said she and her four children could only afford to have a proper meal every two days.
- Assad regime planned US journalist's kidnap for weeks, BBC finds
- The phone book that led us to Assad's spy chief in hiding
Marwan Bashour, a 68-year-old pensioner, said his monthly pay was around $90 (£70), which is the public sector minimum wage. "It's not enough at all," he said.

The United Nations Development Programme said 90% of Syrians were in poverty last year. Marwan told me how he made ends meet. "Sometimes I borrow money, sometimes I sell things from my house," he said, "like an old pot or plates that we never used, gifts that were given to us. I've even had to sell furniture".

There have been other pressures too. Like many Syrians, Marwan used to rely on help from aid agencies. But, for him, that has stopped, as organisations have been forced to cut back services because of funding cuts. Syria has also not been immune to the impact of the US-Iran war. The government said the fuel increase that led to the protests was, in part, due to the pressure on energy markets because of the conflict.

I met another pensioner, Nabil al-Remhein, who is 63. None of his four adult children could find work. "We're now having only one meal a day. It's tragic," he said. His face looked tired. "It isn't only me. It's the entire population. We're all hungry... We're suffocating under rising costs."

Nabil took me to his house, in a poor area of narrow alleys and modest buildings. There, I met his wife. She was doing her chores in the dark. "I'm afraid of the electricity bill," Nabil said. "We've cut back on lighting up the house and we [also] turn off the fridge for about five hours a day". Still, their latest bill was about a third of the family's income. He has not paid it.

Dr Haid Haid, a Syrian columnist and consulting fellow at the London-based think tank Chatham House, said a "significant portion of the population" was worse off than before Assad's fall. The economic crisis, he told me, was "one of the most dangerous issues" for the government, and that some of it was of its own making.

"Part of [the crisis] is related to the lack of [financial] resources and the legacy left by the former regime," he said. "But it's also the direct impact of the new policies that are moving [Syria] towards a liberal and free-market sort of economy, which don't take into account the impact on people".
A spokesman for the Syrian economy and industry ministry told me no-one was available for an interview.

Sharaa has, of course, scored some important gains. International sanctions imposed in the Assad-era have been lifted, and the US has removed the country from its list of state sponsors of terrorism. Security remains volatile and a source of concern, but the country feels more stable.

And the president continues to consolidate his power and, earlier this year, retook the resource-rich north-east from a Kurdish-led militia. (The Druze still control areas in the south, where they want to create an autonomous state; Israel occupies parts of the south-west.)

But real economic recovery is yet to happen. Large parts of Syria remain in ruins after a war that killed half a million people and displaced half of the population. Unable to afford rent, many families live in partially destroyed buildings. The World Bank says reconstruction costs are estimated at $216bn and, without foreign help and investment, it will be impossible for Syrians to rebuild.

Samir Aita, a Syrian economist who heads the Circle of Arab Economists, a Paris-based independent think-tank, said the crisis was a "combination of policies with the [government] not managing expectations and creating unrealistic hopes". When I asked him about how he felt about the future, he said: "It's unsustainable. If they don't change, I fear chaos."

Exhausted after years of conflict, Syrians, left with almost no choice, remain hopeful. Abu Mahmoud, a cab driver, told me: "They inherited the country bankrupt, so people need to be patient. Things don't happen overnight."
Additional reporting by Lana Antaki, Samantha Granville and Neha Sharma

raw.title: How a passenger's confession helped convict her cousin of murder
raw.summary: Simon Richardson hit cyclist Michael Mullins with his car and dragged him along for over a mile.
paragraphs: How a passenger's confession helped convict her cousin of murder
Warning: This article contains distressing content
One afternoon in April, a children's nursery worker approached her manager in a what she described as an hysterical state.
Gabrielle Debotte said she had something serious to tell Nicola Goddard, adding: "You're going to hate me and I'm going to lose my job."

What the 27-year-old said next proved a turning point in the investigation into the death of popular head teacher Michael Mullins, who had been struck by a car the previous day and dragged under its wheels for more than a mile.
Debotte told the astonished Goddard she not only knew who was responsible for hitting the 56-year-old as he cycled home from work, but she witnessed what happened from the passenger seat.
That night, having initially been treated as a suspect, she sat in the interview suite at Stretford Police Station and named her cousin, 35-year-old former mechanic Simon Richardson, as the driver.
Thanks in part to the evidence provided by Debotte, Richardson was found guilty of murder after a two-week trial at Manchester's Minshull Street Crown Court.
The contrasts between the lives of the killer and his victim were stark.
Less than a month before he struck the head teacher, Richardson was freed from prison.

He had served 47 days on remand awaiting sentence for stalking, harassment, threats to damage property and assaulting an emergency worker, and was freed on 26 March after being sentenced to a non-custodial community order.
In the following weeks, he was "sofa-surfing" between various addresses - including the home Debotte shared with her father in Altrincham, Greater Manchester.
In contrast, the head teacher had spent the past 17 years leading Stretford Grammar School, where he was known as a man of "unshakeable principles and a compassionate leader".
To his family, he was a beloved husband, father and grandfather, who "truly excelled" in his "role as grandad".
He was a lover of sport and remained physically fit, regularly cycling the 19 miles between the school and his home in Northwich, Cheshire.
At 17:35 BST on 20 April, he changed into his cycling clothes, put on his helmet and set off as normal.
Detectives would later be able to plot his journey via his Apple watch, which monitored his speed, location and heart rate.

Not far from the cyclist's starting point, a black Volvo XC90 was already catching the attention of other drivers as it sped "erratically" along the semi-rural roads on the outskirts of Trafford and north-east Cheshire.
It was being driven by Richardson, who had agreed to give his cousin a lift from Altrincham to a beauty salon in Lymm to pick up some weight-loss jabs.
In court, Debotte told jurors Richardson had been driving very fast and when she told him to slow down, his only response was to "smirk" and claim he was "a professional driver".
At 18:07, the car reached a junction in Warburton, Trafford, which connected Dunham Road with Paddock Lane.
According to Debotte and other witnesses, the Volvo ignored stop signs and road markings on Dunham Road as it attempted to turn left.
Debotte told the court she shouted "bike" three times, but Richardson made no attempt to slow down or brake before the Volvo smashed into the left side of the cyclist.
Witnesses saw the head teacher being thrown into the air while his bike, phone, part of his helmet and a wireless earphone were scattered across the road.
Witness Leon Dalziel-Bush, who saw the crash from his own vehicle, said the Volvo was going at such speed that "by the time I processed what had happened, it had gone".
Dalziel-Bush and others got out to help, but after searching in ditches and grass verges, they realised the cyclist was nowhere to be seen.
Richardson, who according to Debotte, stopped for a "split-second" before accelerating away, was already guilty of very serious criminal offences.
What happened over the next four minutes or so, prosecutors argued in court, made him a murderer.
The prosecution case hinged on whether it could prove Richardson was aware the cyclist was trapped and suffering increasingly appalling injuries just inches from his feet.
Phil Barnes KC, prosecuting, told the jury that many of them would know what it feels like to drive "with a flat tyre, or with wheels that are slightly out of balance or misaligned".
"Now imagine driving your car, at north of 60mph, with a fully grown human being wedged in the suspension and steering assembly of one of your wheels," he said.

Barnes had suggested it "must have been obvious" to Richardson that the 56-year-old was there, but "he carried on regardless", knowing his actions "were in all likelihood killing the man beneath his feet".
But, thanks to Debotte's workplace revelation, the case was built on much more than that simple premise.
When she gave her statement to police, she described a scene of absolute shock and panic in the car, complete with "screaming and crying".
"I had never seen anything like that in my life," she said, adding: "I still have visions of it."
She also recalled how "moaning" could clearly be heard from beneath the Volvo as it sped away and that Richardson blurted out: "He's under the car."
Detectives would be able to prove, via watch and phone data, that his car had stopped on Wet Gate Lane in Lymm a short time after the collision.
The data showed the car had remained stationary on the rural country lane for about 90 seconds, as the cyclist was still clinging to life.
Debotte's account of those moments was absolutely crucial to proving Richardson was guilty of more than causing death by dangerous driving and failing to stop.
She said as she sat "frozen" in the passenger seat, he got out, walked around the front of the vehicle and tried to pull the head teacher free.
When the first attempt failed, he returned to the driver's seat and moved the steering wheel to try and free the wheels.
Debotte said Richardson got out again and crouched down to make another attempt to pull his victim free.
After failing again, he started the engine and drove further along Wet Gate Lane.
CCTV from a nearby farm showed the car swerving from side-to-side before the cyclist was finally thrown clear on to a grass verge.

From the position he was found, prosecutors were also able to say that the car must have driven over his body when it reversed and turned back towards the main road, all but ensuring his injuries were fatal.
The court was shown distressing evidence in support of Debotte's account, including images of a sharp-angled tyre mark left in a pool of blood where the car had stopped.
The jury heard the mark could only have been made by the wheels being turned while the car was stationary.

Nobody was around when the 56-year-old was thrown from the vehicle and left to his fate, but a few minutes later, motorcylist Andrew Beasant-Roberts found him after following a trail of blood from close to the crash site just over a mile away.
Beasant-Roberts made a 999 call and tried to perform CPR, but it was too late.
Detectives later found CCTV footage which showed Richardson and Debotte at Lymm Service Station minutes later, filling the car with petrol.
The pair then finished the errand they initially set out to do and picked up Debotte's jabs from the salon in Lymm.
She was dropped off at her Altrincham home at 18:45, where she stayed until she left for work again the following morning.
After dropping her off, Richardson quickly arranged to swap the Volvo for a silver Ford Transit work van with an associate.
He returned to Debotte's house in the van with a friend and the pair came and went from the house throughout the night.

Debotte said the men had been "laughing and joking" while listening to music and drinking her father's alcohol, but Richardson also lost his temper when she asked them to leave, punching a hole in plasterwork and kicking a chair.
She said there were no direct threats, but Richards outlined an account for her to give to police if they came knocking, which she wrote down in a note-taking app on her phone.
It included instructions to say she had lent Richardson her bank card on the day before and had not seen him again until late on the day of the crash.
However, Debotte said she already "knew she was going to talk to the police" and would be telling the truth.

In court, Debotte accepted she "absolutely" could have done more to alert the police to what had happened earlier, but her decision to seek them out before anyone else knew she had been in the vehicle allowed them to treat her as a witness.
Based on her description of the van, Greater Manchester Police officers found it the following day in Failsworth.
Despite knowing he was being tailed by a trained pursuit driver, Richardson tried to flee, first speeding through narrow residential streets and then making a final futile attempt to escape on foot.
He has never given a public account of his actions on 20 April.
The court heard he declined to answer police questions and on 22 October, at the conclusion of the prosecution case, the jury were told he would not be giving evidence in his own defence.
Jaime Hamilton KC, defending, explained while questioning witnesses that Richardson denied he knew the cyclist was under the car and denied he had got out of the vehicle on Wet Gate Lane.

However, the evidence and the testimony of Debotte meant the jury were sure he was guilty of more than a serious driving offence and fully convinced he had made the conscious decision to drag a helpless and well-respected family man to a most horrific death.

raw.title: Police Scotland carrying out 'active inquiries' into Andrew and Epstein Balmoral visits
raw.summary: The force said it had received information and stressed its inquiries were at "an early stage".
paragraphs: Police Scotland carrying out 'active inquiries' into Andrew and Epstein Balmoral visits
Police Scotland is making inquiries into the activities of Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor, Jeffrey Epstein and Ghislane Maxwell during their time at Balmoral Castle.
The Daily Express reported, external that the inquiry relates to allegations that women were trafficked to the royal residence in Aberdeenshire.

Sex offender Epstein - who died in 2019 - and Maxwell, who was jailed in 2022 for sex trafficking, are understood to have visited the castle with Mountbatten-Windsor, who has previously denied any wrongdoing.
Police Scotland said inquiries were at "a very early stage" and that it would be inappropriate to comment further.
Representatives of Mountbatten-Windsor have been contacted for comment.
The Royal family traditionally spend summer at Balmoral, where Queen Elizabeth II died in 2022.
Asked about the Express report, a Police Scotland spokesperson said: "We have received information and active inquiries are ongoing but these are at a very early stage.
"All inquiries are evidence led, with the needs of victim survivors at the heart of those inquiries.
"We would never confirm details of ongoing inquiries and it would be inappropriate to comment further."
In February, the force said it wanted to "speak to anyone with information" about Epstein's private jet using Edinburgh Airport.
At the time officers said they had not received any reports or complaints in relating to the trip.
- Epstein's UK flights had alleged British abuse victims on board - BBC investigation
- Email by 'A' from 'Balmoral' asked Ghislaine Maxwell for 'inappropriate friends', Epstein files show
- Prince Andrew hosted Epstein, Maxwell and Weinstein at Royal Lodge
Flight logs show Mountbatten-Windsor and Maxwell flew from Luton to Edinburgh on Epstein's private jet with two other passengers on 1 September 2006.
An image believed to show disgraced financier Epstein and former socialite Maxwell at Balmoral was also released by US prosecutors during her sex trafficking trial.
It is thought to have been taken in 1999, when Mountbatten-Windsor reportedly invited the couple to stay at the castle.
Epstein and Maxwell were reportedly regular guests at royal residences in the late 1990s and early 2000s.
Last year, the so-called Epstein Files were released by the US Department of Justice.
Among them was an email from someone named 'A' to Maxwell which said they were at Balmoral and asked for "new inappropriate friends".
The message, sent to Maxwell on 16 August 2001, begins: "I am up here at Balmoral Summer Camp for the Royal Family."
Later in the email, the sender asks: "How's LA? Have you found me some new inappropriate friends?" before signing off "see ya A xxx".
Jeffrey Epstein was 66 when he died by suicide in 2019 in a US prison while awaiting trial for sex trafficking charges.
Maxwell, 60, was jailed for 20 years in 2022 for her role in procuring girls for Epstein.
Last October it was confirmed Andrew had been stripped of his "prince" title and would be leaving his Windsor mansion, Royal Lodge.
In February he was arrested on suspicion of misconduct in public office, in the wake of information that emerged from the Epstein files in the US, and later released.
Earlier this month it emerged he was taking legal action against Thames Valley Police over search warrants issued before his arrest.
Mountbatten-Windsor has consistently denied any wrongdoing linked to his association with Epstein.
Asked about the latest reports, Scottish First Minister John Swinney said: "I understand the seriousness of the points that have been made and the concern that has been expressed.
"This is an operational matter for Police Scotland to fully and comprehensively investigate and I'm very confident that's exactly what Police Scotland will do."
Prime Minister Andy Burnham said he did not want to comment on the police inquiries, which "should properly be independent".
