raw.title: Britain's first £100m man facing defining moment
raw.summary: Is it 'now or never' for Jack Grealish after he was dropped by Everton for a breach of club discipline, asks chief football writer Phil McNulty?
paragraphs: Britain's first £100m man facing defining moment

When Jack Grealish breezed back into Everton in his white Lamborghini one hour before the end of this summer's transfer deadline, the excitement among supporters and the player himself was clearly evident.

Grealish's previous spell on loan from Manchester City had been cut short by a serious foot injury, but the 31-year-old had produced enough moments of excitement to make his return to the Finch Farm training base a rare moment of joy amid a miserable summer in the transfer market.

When Grealish finally left in the early hours - with the deal done, every autograph signed and every selfie posed for - it was a sort of homecoming for an everyman personality Everton fans had come to regard as one of their own.

This was a move with a lot riding on it - for Everton manager David Moyes, who had been left with only 18 senior players after a botched transfer window, and especially for Grealish, whose exile from City at the start of the final year of his contract confirmed his banishment.
Now, Grealish's future and Everton's faith in him, has reached a defining moment.
Grealish's exclusion from Everton's squad before the Carabao Cup tie at home to Newcastle was publicly described as "a breach of club discipline".

Specifically, it was a failure to turn up for training on Monday, leaving the talented maverick - who was Britain's first £100m footballer when he signed for City from Aston Villa in summer 2021 - facing another rebuild in his career.
Everton's decision to go public before the game with the reasons for Grealish's absence emphasised the seriousness of his transgression.
The fall-out means this now looks increasingly like Grealish's 'now or never' moment, because failure at Everton will surely mark a downward spiral from the top echelons of the Premier League.

Everton do not regard this week's misdemeanour as marking the proverbial 'Last Chance Saloon' for Grealish. Moyes does not have enough players at his disposal to make rapid outcasts of potential game-changers.
But it increases the pressure on the former England forward to win back the faith of fans who love his obvious enjoyment of life and the magic he has shown he can produce.
Moyes will hope it is a harsh lesson learned, because Everton now have even more to play for, given Wembley has suddenly come into view in the Carabao Cup.

BBC Sport believes there have been occasional time-keeping issues with Grealish in the past, but nothing on this scale from a personality regarded as a hard trainer who, in general, keeps himself in good condition.

Grealish has held talks with those in authority at Everton, where it is sure to have been made crystal clear there must be no repeat, certainly not under a strict disciplinarian such as Moyes, and he must now attempt to be rehabilitated back into the squad.
The inevitable decision to punish Grealish, taken at a high level within the club but with input and full support from Moyes, leaves him at the crossroads.

That is especially the case because Everton gave arguably their best performance of the season to beat Newcastle United 3-1 and set up a quarter-final at League Two Fleetwood Town, conquerors of Premier League champions Arsenal in the last round.
And it was done with the more dynamic style of 20-year-old Tyrique George playing on the left flank, which Grealish might have been expected to occupy.
Moyes was guarded after the game and instead preferred to focus on a vital victory.
"You probably know I'm not going to give any details. It's a club decision and I support it. It's something I don't want to speak too much about," he said.
"The one thing about Everton is that they have got real good values. All the players stand behind it and accept the values, on the pitch and off the pitch, and I think the players did a good job.
"It is a small squad, but we are doing our best to keep challenging. We are not accepting any excuses for anything and I think the players are doing a great job. There was a humility about us."
The words were not specifically aimed at Grealish, but they might as well have been from a manager who will have been bitterly disappointed and angry about his transgression.

Moyes and Grealish formed a close relationship from virtually their first moment of contact in August 2025, the latter saying: "As soon as I spoke to the manager, I knew there was only one place that I wanted to go and that was Everton."

And Grealish, a key figure when Manchester City won the Treble of Premier League, FA Cup and Champions League in 2023, played his part until sustaining a foot fracture that ended his season in Everton's 1-0 win at his former club Aston Villa in January.
Grealish's happiness with life at Everton was illustrated when he decided against returning to City, continuing his rehabilitation at Finch Farm rather than going back to Etihad Stadium.

Everton weighed up a second loan deal to bring Grealish back carefully, with his injury, finances and - to a certain extent - his character all entering the equation before Moyes decided to move again for a player who insisted Merseyside was the only place he wanted to be.
Moyes was also juggling very limited options as owners The Friedkin Group appeared to back away from serious squad strengthening as they prepared to put the club up for sale.

Grealish's form this season has been underwhelming, failing to score or create an assist in eight appearances - two of those at City before returning to Everton - while his tendency to slow play down is at odds with the usual tempo Moyes requires from his team.

Moyes' fury will have increased because Grealish, who missed Saturday's loss at Arsenal through "illness", is part of a paper-thin squad that simply cannot carry passengers or have players ruling themselves out through needless ill-discipline.

There will be frustration too, as Grealish is a hugely popular within Everton's dressing room as well as with staff in every area of the club. He has been described as "a lad with a heart of gold, kind and charming, who actually loves being here".
This was illustrated when he recently made a £10,000 donation to a GoFundMe page for Everton fan Leon Skapars, 36, a father of three who has been diagnosed with cancer.

The family are raising money in a search for treatment options, and Skapars' wife Crystal said: "In that moment, Jack gave our whole family something we desperately needed, hope. What he has done for our family is something we will never forget. It makes us feel incredibly emotional."
Grealish also appeared to present awards at the Daily Mirror's 'Pride Of Britain' event recently, saying: "Footballers are classed as heroes - but these are the real heroes."
On Friday, Manchester City boss Enzo Maresca refused to discuss Grealish's actions at Everton, but did praise his character.
Maresca said: "It's not correct to talk about Jack in this moment, first of all because he is an Everton player and secondly because I don't have all the information.
"I still think he is a good guy and has a big heart."
In April, Grealish extended his role as principal ambassador to Special Olympics Great Britain for a further three years, having first joined in 2022.

Grealish marked the occasion by hosting five of the 10 Special Olympics GB athletes who completed the London Marathon at Everton's Hill Dickinson Stadium, surprising the athletes with a VIP experience, a stadium tour and spending time with them pitchside.
Those at Everton also regard Grealish as one of the first to engage with their community programme at Finch Farm, as well as meeting with the Everton in the Community Down Syndrome team.
Grealish often talks about the inspiration he takes from his sister Hollie, who has cerebral palsy.
He has, however, hit the headlines in less welcome circumstances over the years, and this latest incident ushered in more.

In April, Grealish was pictured asleep at a Manchester rooftop bar surrounded by drinks. It was a scene that is certainly not against the law but was at best unwise, especially with ever-present phone cameras around and the fact he was in rehabilitation from injury.
In March 2020, he was fined by his club Aston Villa and apologised publicly after breaking lockdown guidelines during the pandemic after leaving his house to visit a friend.
In November 2020, he admitted two counts of careless driving relating to two incidents in which a Citroen van and a Mercedes were damaged.

And yet, speak to most people in football - certainly at Everton - and the character references are unfailingly glowing about his outgoing personality and kind-hearted gestures, making his breach of discipline even more painful for his many admirers.
But after this latest setback, Grealish is running out of time and opportunities to justify that continued support.

raw.title: Ρωσία: Έκλεισε η ανεξάρτητη εφημερίδα Novaya Gazeta λόγων των πιέσεων των αρχών
raw.summary: Η εφημερίδα Novaya Gazeta, ιστορικό προπύργιο του ανεξάρτητου Τύπου στη Ρωσία, ανακοίνωσε σήμερα ότι κλείνει λόγω των πιέσεων των ρωσικών αρχών.Περισσότερα...
paragraphs: Ρωσία: Έκλεισε η ανεξάρτητη εφημερίδα Novaya Gazeta λόγων των πιέσεων των αρχών
Η εφημερίδα Novaya Gazeta, ιστορικό προπύργιο του ανεξάρτητου Τύπου στη Ρωσία, ανακοίνωσε σήμερα ότι κλείνει λόγω των πιέσεων των ρωσικών αρχών.

«Στις 9 Νοεμβρίου θα κλείσουμε τα φώτα στο σπίτι μας όπου ζούσαμε για 30 χρόνια, θα κλείσουμε τους σέρβερ και θα φύγουμε. Η ‘Novaya Gazeta΄ δεν υπάρχει πια. Οι ρωσικές αρχές, οι ρωσικές ειδικές υπηρεσίες ανάγκασαν τη συντακτική ομάδα να τερματίσει το έργο της», ανέφερε ο διευθυντής της εφημερίδας Σεργκέι Σακαλόφ σε βίντεο που αναρτήθηκε στο YouTube.

Σε ξεχωριστή ανακοίνωση η συντακτική ομάδα της εφημερίδας ανέφερε ότι εκδόθηκε εντολή έξωσης, με αποτέλεσμα η Novaya Gazeta να είναι αναγκασμένη από σήμερα να εγκαταλείψει την ιστορική έδρα της στη Μόσχα. Παράλληλα απενεργοποιήθηκε το σύστημα μέσω του οποίου λάμβανε δωρεές από τους αναγνώστες της.

Η εφημερίδα Novaya Gazeta, που ιδρύθηκε το 1993, είναι γνωστή για τις έρευνες της για την διαφθορά και τα επικριτικά της άρθρα για Ρώσους πολιτικούς. Νωρίτερα φέτος το υπουργείο Δικαιοσύνης της Ρωσίας είχε χαρακτηρίσει την εφημερίδα «ξένο πράκτορα», ένα μέτρο που λαμβάνουν οι ρωσικές αρχές προκειμένου να φιμώσουν κάθε φωνή διαφωνίας.
«Περισσότερα από 30 χρόνια κοινής ζωής με τη χώρα και τους πολίτες θα καταλήξουν με εμάς στον δρόμο, χωρίς να έχουμε μέσα διαβίωσης, υπό τη συνεχή απειλή της καταστολής», πρόσθεσε η συντακτική ομάδα.

Στις 9 Απριλίου οι ρωσικές αρχές πραγματοποίησαν έρευνα στα γραφεία της Novaya Gazeta μετά την άσκηση ποινικών διώξεων εις βάρος του δημοσιογράφου της εφημερίδας Όλεγκ Ρολντουγκίν. Την ίδια ημέρα συνέλαβαν και ανέκριναν τον Ρολντουγκίν , ο οποίος τώρα βρίσκεται σε κατ’ οίκον περιορισμό εν αναμονή της δίκης του. Στα μέσα Οκτωβρίου συνελήφθη και ανακρίθηκε ο Σακαλόφ στο πλαίσιο της υπόθεσης αυτής.

Η Ρωσία έχει εντείνει την καταστολή των ανεξάρτητων μέσων ενημέρωσης μετά την εισβολή στην Ουκρανία, ενώ παράλληλα έχει θεσπίσει ένα αυστηρό σύστημα λογοκρισίας, αναγκάζοντας πολλούς ανεξάρτητους δημοσιογράφους να εγκαταλείψουν τη χώρα.

Το 2022 οι ρωσικές αρχές είχαν ανακαλέσει την άδεια της Novaya Gazeta, η οποία είχε ταχθεί ανοικτά κατά της στρατιωτικής επιχείρησης στην Ουκρανία. Η εφημερίδα είχε διακόψει την έντυπη έκδοσή της, αλλά είχε συνεχίσει να δημοσιεύει περιεχόμενο στο διαδίκτυο.
Ένας από τους συνιδρυτές της και πρώην αρχισυντάκτης της, ο Ντμίτρι Μουράτοφ, τιμήθηκε το 2021 με Νόμπελ Ειρήνης για «τις προσπάθειές του να προστατεύσει την ελευθερία της έκφρασης».

paragraphs: Η ΔΕΗ Συναντά την Τέχνη Vol. 2: Άνοιξε στο κοινό η έκθεση με 55 έργα στον Ιστορικό ΑΗΣ Νέου Φαλήρου
Έργα εμπνευσμένα από την 75χρονη διαδρομή και τη βιομηχανική κληρονομιά της ΔΕΗ. Πέντε νικητές και χρηματικά βραβεία συνολικού ύψους €20.000. Ελεύθερη είσοδος για το κοινό έως τις 10 Ιανουαρίου 2027.

Με 55 έργα σύγχρονης καλλιτεχνικής δημιουργίας και την ανάδειξη των πέντε νικητών του ομώνυμου ανοιχτού καλλιτεχνικού διαγωνισμού, εγκαινιάστηκε η έκθεση «Η ΔΕΗ Συναντά την Τέχνη Vol. 2» στις Ιστορικές Εγκαταστάσεις του Ατμοηλεκτρικού Σταθμού της ΔΕΗ στο Νέο Φάληρο. Η έκθεση ανοίγει στο κοινό με ελεύθερη είσοδο και θα διαρκέσει έως τις 10 Ιανουαρίου 2027, ενώ στους πέντε δημιουργούς που διακρίθηκαν απονεμήθηκαν χρηματικά βραβεία συνολικού ύψους 20.000€.

Η έκθεση, σε επιμέλεια του Χριστόφορου Μαρίνου, Ιστορικού Τέχνης, συγκεντρώνει τα έργα που διακρίθηκαν ανάμεσα σε περισσότερες από χίλιες συμμετοχές που υποβλήθηκαν στον δεύτερο ανοιχτό καλλιτεχνικό διαγωνισμό της ΔΕΗ. Ζωγραφική, γλυπτική, χαρακτική, design, κινούμενη εικόνα, ηχητικές δημιουργίες, εγκαταστάσεις και performance συνθέτουν μια πολυσυλλεκτική έκθεση σύγχρονης τέχνης, μέσα σε έναν χώρο άρρηκτα συνδεδεμένο με τη βιομηχανική κληρονομιά της χώρας.

Οι δημιουργοί προσέγγισαν την ιστορία και τη βιομηχανική κληρονομιά της ΔΕΗ μέσα από διαφορετικά μέσα και σύγχρονες καλλιτεχνικές γλώσσες, αξιοποιώντας παράλληλα υλικό από τις συλλογές του Ιστορικού Αρχείου ΔΕΗ. Τα έργα φωτίζουν έτσι διαφορετικές πτυχές της διαδρομής της ΔΕΗ για περισσότερα από 75 χρόνια και της σχέσης της με την ελληνική κοινωνία, μέσα σε έναν χώρο που αποτελεί ουσιαστικό μέρος αυτής της ιστορίας.

Στα εγκαίνια της έκθεσης και την τελετή βράβευσης στελέχη της εταιρείας, καλλιτέχνες, εκπρόσωποι από τον χώρο του πολιτισμού και προσκεκλημένοι, περιηγήθηκαν στα 55 έργα που παρουσιάζονται στον Ιστορικό Ατμοηλεκτρικό Σταθμό Νέου Φαλήρου της ΔΕΗ.

Πέντε από τα 55 έργα της έκθεσης απέσπασαν τα χρηματικά βραβεία του διαγωνισμού, συνολικού ύψους 20.000€. Συγκεκριμένα, το 1ο βραβείο (8.000€) απονεμήθηκε στον Ορέστη Μαυρουδή, το 2ο βραβείο (5.000€) στον Διονύση Χριστοφιλογιάννη και το 3ο βραβείο (3.000€) στη Σοφία Ντώνα. Το 4ο και το 5ο βραβείο, ύψους 2.000€ το καθένα, απονεμήθηκαν στους VASKOS (Βασίλης Νούλας και Κώστας Τζημούλης) και τη Βιργινία Μαστρογιαννάκη αντίστοιχα.

Τα πέντε έργα που βραβεύτηκαν στον διαγωνισμό επέλεξε η επταμελής κριτική επιτροπή, με μέλη τις/τους Κατερίνα Γρέγου, Γιώργο Κουμεντάκη, Χριστόφορο Μαρίνο, Μαρία Μαυροειδή, Έλενα Μαυρομιχάλη, Θούλη Μισιρλόγλου και Γιώργο Τζιρτζιλάκη.

Η έκθεση παρουσιάζεται στις Ιστορικές Εγκαταστάσεις του Ατμοηλεκτρικού Σταθμού της ΔΕΗ στο Νέο Φάληρο (Σολωμού 1 & Δημητρίου Φαληρέως,15847 Πειραιάς) και θα είναι ανοιχτή στο κοινό έως και την Κυριακή 10 Ιανουαρίου 2027.
Κατά τις επίσημες αργίες, η έκθεση θα παραμένει κλειστή
Ιστορικός Ατμοηλεκτρικός Σταθμός Ν. Φαλήρου της ΔΕΗ
(Σολωμού 1 & Δημητρίου Φαληρέως, 18547 Πειραιάς)

raw.title: Swedish academic says he has been barred from UK over event with Palestine Action founder
raw.summary: Andreas Malm was due to appear on a panel alongside a co-founder of the proscribed group next week.
paragraphs: Academic says he has been barred from UK over event with Palestine Action founder
A Swedish climate academic says he has been barred from entering the UK because he was due to speak on a panel with a co-founder of Palestine Action.

Andreas Malm told BBC Radio 4's Today programme that he had received a letter from the Home Office notifying him that his presence was "not conducive to the public good", with no further details given.
He said he could not "see any other explanation" for being denied entry than his scheduled appearance with Huda Ammori, a founder of the group, which is a proscribed terrorist organisation in the UK.
The Home Office said it did not comment on individual cases.

Malm is a senior lecturer in human ecology at Sweden's Lund University, whose work includes the 2021 book How to Blow up a Pipeline and 2025's The Destruction of Palestine is the Destruction of the Earth.

He said he had asked the Home Office to explain its decision, but could not see a reason beyond the upcoming talk in London with Ammori organised by the left-wing magazine Tribune - calling the move a "severe restriction on the free exchange of ideas".
Malm said he was not a member of Palestine Action, had never publicly endorsed it, nor had he given it any financial support.
"The only link to Palestine Action is her as a person," he said, criticising the UK government for ascribing "guilt by association".

The academic acknowledged that he had previously described the Hamas-led 7 October 2023 attacks on Israel - in which about 1,200 people were killed and another 251 taken hostage - as "fundamentally an act of liberation".

Malm said it was possible that these remarks, during a December 2023 talk in which he also condemned the "deplorable" killing of civilians in the cross-border attack, had been the reason for the Home Office's decision.
But he argued that these views had been in the public realm for a long time, including when he was last allowed into the UK to deliver a talk in May.

"I don't expect the British state to agree with me on Palestine or climate or anything. What I expect the British state to do is to continue to let me enter the country and to discuss with colleagues, with people who disagree with me - as I have done for years."
- Sally Rooney books withdrawn in UK over Palestine Action support
The UK Supreme Court is due to review Palestine Action's controversial ban under terrorism legislation. The Home Office has said that it will robustly defend against the appeal.

More than 3,700 people are believed to have been arrested in the UK over alleged support of the group. About 2,500 have been charged, though none have gone to trial as the legal challenge to the proscription continues.
The government has broad discretion to bar foreign nationals from entering the UK if their presence is deemed to pose a risk to society.
In April, 11 people described by then-Prime Minister Sir Keir Starmer as "far-right agitators" were banned from entering the UK ahead of a rally led by Tommy Robinson.

Kanye West was also denied entry that same month after backlash to his planned set at London's Wireless Festival, following a string of antisemitic, racist and pro-Nazi comments. He had previously apologised for the remarks and said his bipolar disorder had caused him to lose "touch with reality".
Left-wing political commentators Hasan Piker and Cenk Uygur claimed in June that their visas had been revoked ahead of planned appearances in London and Oxford, allegedly "for criticising Israel".

raw.title: What we know about Binance's $6.3bn hack
raw.summary: Cyber correspondent Joe Tidy explains more about what is suspected to be the biggest hack in history.
paragraphs: Binance, the world's biggest crypto exchange, has been hit by a $6.3bn (£4.7bn) hack - thought to be the biggest in history.
Half of the assets have been frozen but many remain in the hands of the hackers, the cryptocurrency giant said. It later added that it has "begun recovering" some funds.

Two analytics firms have attributed the incident to a North Korean hacking unit, though no one has claimed responsibility. Binance did not directly respond to questions about the incident's potential links to North Korea.
BBC cyber correspondent Joe Tidy explains more about the hack and what to do if you are affected.

raw.title: China denies allegations of spy operation targeting Nvidia CEO
raw.summary: US intelligence officials believe a Chinese businesswoman was gathering information for Beijing on the US chip-making giant, The New York Times reports.
paragraphs: China denies allegations of spy operation targeting Nvidia CEO
China has rejected allegations of a Chinese espionage operation targeting Nvidia's chief executive, Jensen Huang, describing the claims as "groundless speculation".

US intelligence officials believe that Alice Huang, a Chinese businesswoman linked to Singapore-based data centre firm Megaspeed, was gathering information for Beijing on the US chip-making giant, according to a report by The New York Times, external.

The report said Alice Huang, who is of no relation to Jensen Huang, was under investigation over the possible diversion of advanced Nvidia AI chips to China and had developed a close relationship with Jensen.
Nvidia said their interactions were routine business engagements, while Beijing accused Washington of attempting to smear China. Alice Huang did not respond to the paper's request for comment.
The BBC has contacted Megaspeed and the White House for comment.
US intelligence agencies had been monitoring Alice Huang and concluded that she was acting on behalf of the Chinese government, according to unnamed sources cited by The New York Times.
Surveillance reportedly revealed communications between Alice Huang and an American citizen, who was subsequently identified as Jensen Huang through a process known as "unmasking".
It remains unclear what information Alice Huang - who is also known as Huang Le - allegedly passed to Beijing, how valuable it was, or when she is believed to have begun gathering intelligence.
At a regular briefing on Friday, Chinese foreign ministry spokesman Guo Jiakun said: "The report in question is based on groundless speculation and is nothing more than an attempt to smear China."
The paper's report comes amid longstanding US concerns about China's access to advanced computing technology, which is considered crucial to developing artificial intelligence systems.
Jensen Huang has argued that allowing Nvidia to sell more of its products to China is important for maintaining US competitiveness in the global AI industry.

But Washington has restricted exports of the most advanced Nvidia chips to China since 2022, citing national security concerns and the risk that the technology could strengthen China's military operations. There have however been some loosening of restrictions during Trump's administration.

US officials said they had caught several firms illegally trafficking the chips across the Chinese border. They have also investigated whether companies operating through third countries are helping Chinese businesses access the restricted technology.
Nvidia has said it complies with applicable export laws and that there is no evidence its chips have been smuggled into China.
In response to the allegations made by the Times, John Rizzo, a spokesman for Nvidia, said: "Jensen's interactions with Ms Huang are not unusual or unexpected".
He said customers like Megaspeed "receive ordinary business information - not sensitive Nvidia trade secrets - and zero information relevant to national security."
He added that allegations the Singaporean company was smuggling chips to China "were thoroughly investigated and debunked last year".

Megaspeed told the paper its current leadership took the allegations seriously and had appointed external legal advisers to conduct an internal investigation. The company also said it had informed the US government that it was willing to cooperate.
It is unclear how closely Alice Huang remains involved with Megaspeed.

raw.title: Who could be behind the Binance hack and what we know so far
raw.summary: Binance has been hit by what could be the biggest crypto hack ever - here's what we know so far
paragraphs: Who could be behind the Binance hack and what we know so far
Binance, the world's largest crypto exchange, has been hit by what is believed to be the largest crypto hack ever at $6.3bn (£4.7bn).
Crypto is a type of digital asset which does not exist physically like cash or coins. Instead, people use digital wallets on their smartphones or computers to access and manage it.
Richard Teng, Binance's co-chief executive officer, said it is working with the authorities to work out what has happened and it will cover all losses.
Binance is the world's largest cryptocurrency exchange by trading volume, where people can buy, sell and trade digital currencies, like Bitcoin, as well as deposit and withdraw them.
It was founded in China in 2017 and has hundreds of millions of registered users worldwide.
The exchange has come under scrutiny over the past few years - notably in 2023, when its then-chief executive, Changpeng Zhao, resigned after pleading guilty to money laundering violations.
Last year, a lawsuit in the US accused the company of helping send millions of dollars to US-designated terrorist organisations.
In 2024, the company said it has more than $160bn in assets.
- From Bitcoin to blockchain: Key cryptocurrency terms and what they mean
The hack happened to Binance's global centralised exchange, Binance.com.
Binance.us, which provides trading services specifically for US residents, said it has not been affected by the issue.
In an initial announcement, Teng said: "Our initial investigation suggests this security incident may have started with a compromised DevOps engineer's laptop.
"That gave an attacker access to a service container, where they submitted unauthorised withdrawal transactions."
He said the hack "was not a simple 'one-click' action" but a "more complex attack process".

Raghu Nandakumara, vice president of industry strategy at cybersecurity platform Illumio, said this could mean an engineer was "talked into taking a test" and malware - malicious software – "landed on their laptop while they did it".
Because the laptop already had sufficient security privileges, Nandakumara said early reports suggest it became "the attacker's route straight into production, and from there to the wallets".
Teng has since said the hack was "not carried out by one person" and the hackers used sophisticated methods to hide their tracks, such as a "self-destruct mechanism".

"You can build a vault with mathematical firewalls, but if the individual holding the keys can be duped, the vault is opened," said Dr Clive Summerfield, head of FARx, a biometrics in AI security company.
It is not yet known who is behind the attack, but some analytics firms have pointed to North Korea - though this has not been confirmed.

AI-powered investigations company TRM Labs said in a report several elements of the Binance attack resembled earlier incidents linked to the territory, including a $1.5bn (£1.1bn) hack on the ByBit exchange in 2025.
These previous attacks have been linked to a cluster of cyber-criminals accused of working directly for the regime called the Lazarus Group - also known as TraderTraitor.
North Korean foreign policy expert Dr Edward Howell, from the University of Oxford, has told the BBC that Pyongyang "has a long history of using cyber warfare to extract cash".
Howell said North Korea "basically has a state-run cyber warfare agency", which it uses "to fund its weapons of mass destruction programmes" and as a "slush fund" for its leader Kim Jong Un's regime.
Howell added that as of the current day "about 40 – 50% of North Korea's weapons of mass destruction programmes are funded by cyber and crypto-currency warfare".
North Korea has always denied any involvement in these attacks; Binance has not directly responded to BBC queries about the incident's potential links to the area.
In his earlier statement, Teng said Binance users' funds are safe and, as a precaution, all deposits and withdrawals had been temporarily suspended.
He said the firm would cover all losses from its emergency reserve set up for such situations, and make up the rest with company funds.
Binance said it had been working with partners to freeze the affected assets, with around $3bn reportedly located so far.

Teng said concerned users can check funds on their Binance accounts. Experts suggest doing so through the official app and website, and to reach out to the company's customer service with any questions.
Users from other crypto platforms have also been warned to be wary of hackers seeking to exploit the situation.

Marijus Briedis, NordVPN's chief technology officer, said people should be on the lookout for things such as "an email claiming your funds are at risk", "a fake support account offering help" or "a message urging you to move your cryptocurrency to a 'safe' wallet".
"Check updates through the Binance app or a website address you already trust," he said.
"Avoid links in unsolicited messages, and never give anyone your password, verification codes or wallet recovery phrase."
What does this mean for cryptocurrency and the wider financial system?
Jennifer Craven, an international commercial fraud expert at the law firm Pinsent Masons, said the repercussions of the hack could "extend well beyond Binance".
"More broadly, the incident exposes the fragility of parts of the crypto ecosystem," she said.
"If a platform as sophisticated as Binance can suffer a serious attack, regulators will inevitably ask what that means for smaller, less mature platforms and currencies."
She said the attack would likely accelerate scrutiny of how the sector protects both its infrastructure and its customers.

Although there is no evidence yet that AI was used in this attack, it fits into a much wider concern in the financial industry of whether AI agents could potentially identify weaknesses in software and work out how to exploit them much faster than human hackers.
The Bank of England has warned, external this could leave institutions struggling to fix vulnerabilities before attackers take advantage of them.
Crypto has become an increasingly popular way of investing and transferring money online, partly because, unlike traditional currencies, it is not controlled by central banks or governments.
This makes it popular for people who think decentralisation can bring financial freedom.
But it also makes it extremely volatile, with it rising and falling in value at the whim of buyers and sellers.
According to Solcard, a crypto-funded prepaid payment and virtual card platform, somewhere between 560 million and 741 million people own crypto worldwide in 2026.

raw.title: Google value plunges by $500bn as its own AI search hits ad sales
raw.summary: Google spooked investors so badly that its stock hit a six-month low, after it revealed its AI own search summaries were affecting ad revenue.
paragraphs: Google value plunges by $500bn as AI fears rattle Wall Street
Google parent Alphabet lost just over $500bn (£374bn) in value on Thursday after it rattled Wall Street with its last update of the year on its business operations.
Google spooked investors so badly that its stock hit a six-month low, after it revealed its artificial intelligence (AI) summaries on search were affecting ad revenue.
Microsoft and Amazon also updated investors this week, and joined Google in plans to keep spending astronomical sums of cash in an ongoing AI race.
But investors appeared dismayed at the impacts these plans are having on the ability of each to keep growing their core lines of business.
Google AI is eating its core business - search
At first glance, the quarterly results of Alphabet, the parent company of Google, were not at all bad.
Total revenue grew 25% compared to last year, hitting $127.6bn. It was buoyed by the ongoing success of Google Cloud, where revenue grew by 103% to almost $31bn.

However, profits at the company fell by a considerable 25% during the quarter. And for the second time in its history as a public company, it showed negative free cash flow, this time in excess of $9bn. That's almost twice the loss of cash Alphabet showed just three months ago.

Cash flow represents the money a company retains after paying for operations and investments, meaning Alphabet is now spending more money than it is bringing in. That new level of spending is almost entirely dedicated to Google's AI investments.
By the end of Thursday, the company's total stock market value had fallen to $3.46 trillion from $3.97 trillion the day before.
Google's omnipresent search engine now defaults to AI summaries of a person's query, and that hit the number of advertisements it was able to sell during the quarter.
The sale of ads that appear alongside Google Search results is the vast majority of Alphabet's business.

Tracy Woo, a principal analyst at Forrester, said Alphabet's disappointing search business results "highlights the challenge of funding massive AI investments while maintaining the strength of established businesses."

Although Phillip Schindler, Google's chief business officer, said on Wednesday that he felt "very good about our trajectory" with an AI-focused version of the search engine, the company's stock fell by almost 13% on Thursday, its second lowest showing this year.
Investors not buying Amazon's trillion-dollar business hopes
Amazon's stock also took a hit on Thursday after it shared results that disappointed investors. Shares of the company fell 6% in after hours stock trading.
Alongside quarterly sales growth of 11%, hitting $201bn, the company shared a staggering cash flow figure of negative $42bn.
That number shows that Amazon is not only spending more money than it makes, but that spending has increased six-fold over the span of three months.
Chief executive Andy Jassy claimed the business was spending in part because it had the chance at, not one, but two businesses that could end up bringing in $1 trillion for Amazon the future.

Jassy did not specify what two Amazon businesses those may be. But during a call with financial analysts he repeatedly mentioned the financial opportunity presented by Amazon making and selling its own computer chips, as well as its AI developer platform Bedrock, which offers paying users access to most major AI models and tools.

"One of the lessons we've learned over 20-plus years is that there is not one tool to rule the world," Jassy said. "People always assume whatever is in the lead early on will be the only thing that people use - it's never true."
As Jassy was asked several times to explain the company's spending, he admitted it "would be more convenient" if it were spread over the next 25 years. "That's not the world we live in," he added.
"We can fund this plan, and I think it will forever change the size, the revenue, the free cash flow of Amazon."
Microsoft begs the question of AI's real value
Wall Street reacted less enthusiastically to Microsoft's update, with shares falling by less than 1% on Thursday.

The company, which is also one of OpenAI's largest investors, spent around $5bn less on investments dedicated to AI. It also revealed earlier this week plans to cut thousands of workers, which will further reduce the company's costs.
Meanwhile, its revenue grew 19% from a year earlier, hitting $92.3bn for the quarter. Its crucial cloud business grew by 30% to $63bn.
Chief executive Satya Nadella said the use of Copilot, Microsoft's AI chatbot and tool, has seen "automated tasks nearly double since July" as daily users grew by 500% from a year ago.
Usually lower spending and growing sales earns a positive reaction from investors.
But Woo said Wall Street is trying to look farther into the future when it comes to which businesses will truly make good on their big promises around AI.

"Microsoft's results reinforce that enterprise demand for AI remains strong, but they also highlight a much bigger question facing the technology industry, where AI value will ultimately be captured," Woo said.

raw.title: Democrats in the US have an identity crisis - it won't be an easy fix
raw.summary: Whatever the result of the midterm elections, the party is facing tough questions over what they stand for and who should represent them.
paragraphs: James Stevens calls himself a democratic socialist. The 24-year-old film student is the type of Democrat who recalls watching the provocative left-wing internet commentator Hasan Piker six years ago, "before he became relevant in politics". Last year, James flew up from his home in Georgia to New York City to canvass for Zohran Mamdani's mayoral campaign.

His mother, Tamara, 56, is a loyal Democrat too. But of a different ilk. She grew up Republican then switched to the Democratic Party after seeing Barack Obama on Oprah. These days, she's a loyal party woman, championing reproductive rights, attending campaign rallies and donating to local candidates.
Both mother and son want Democrats to win control of Congress at Tuesday's midterm elections, but they don't entirely agree on what they want their Democratic Party to be.

"I'm very sick of how compromising Democrats are to Republican policies that don't benefit a large group of people," James told me, as his mother looked on. "There needs to be a bold vision for the Democrats," he says, arguing that the party should adopt policies affiliated with the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA), a left-wing splinter group. In his view, that means anti-Zionism, getting corporate money out of politics, and government-run free healthcare.
The conventional wisdom in Washington is that Democrats are well-positioned to take control of the House, and possibly even the Senate, after the vote next week.

Underlying conditions are in Democrats' favour – Republican US President Donald Trump's approval rating is at a record low for a president heading into a midterm, comparable to George W Bush in his final term in 2006; the Iran war still isn't over and it's proving unpopular with American voters; and this has led to higher gas prices, which are frustrating an electorate that is already worried about the cost of living. Traditionally, the midterms are a referendum on a sitting president. In 18 of the last 20 US midterm elections, the party in power has lost seats in the House.

And yet despite those circumstances, the Democratic Party is also unpopular nationwide. The Real Clear Politics polling average shows the American public sees the Democrats as only marginally better than the Republicans. Recent polls show the Democratic Party still has a net unfavourability rating among Americans. Political analysts say that if the Republicans manage to buck the trend and survive these midterms, one key reason is that the Democratic Party (or the Democratic brand) is disliked by a majority of American voters too.

Behind the headlines of which party or which candidates win this Tuesday, there's also a story this election season about Democratic identity. This is a fight between institutionalists and reformists, of people who want incremental change and those who demand root-and-branch transformation. The question is, who will win out in the long run?

I've covered every national US election in the past dozen years and this is an unusual one. When I was out interviewing voters ahead of the 2018 midterms during Donald Trump's first term, I was struck by how united many Democratic voters were in their opposition to the president. This time, I've noticed that under the facade of unity, there's a brewing fight.

There are persistent questions about what the Democratic Party stands for, and these divides erupted during the primaries this midterm cycle. "The identity of the party is pretty cloudy," said Ruy Teixeira, a senior fellow at the American Enterprise Institute, a centre-right think tank. "It's all centred on reaction to the Trump administration and taking advantage of what is a thermostatic reaction against the administration... Beyond that, there's all these different factions in the party."

Part of the reason for this Democratic infighting is that the party never had a chance to have this fight during the 2024 presidential race, with the sudden departure of Joe Biden months before the election and nomination of Kamala Harris.

Analysts agree that if Democrats make big wins on election night, it still won't answer deeper, unresolved questions as they try to keep their big tent together to corral votes in Congress or eye the 2028 presidency.

In simplistic terms, the divide is between the centrist, more moderate wing of the party and its left flank. But operatives and analysts say it's also a divide between institutionalists and those who want to completely upend the existing institution. Both feel they have a better read on what voters genuinely want.

Usamah Andrabi, of the Justice Democrats, a prominent left-wing group, blames the Democratic establishment for ushering in a Republican Congress and president. "And so I think the people who led us into this mess are simply not gonna be the ones who lead us out of it," he told me.

"The affordability crisis… is a massive one, and it's not going to be resolved by tinkering at the margins," he added. Instead, he insists, it'll be solved through policies like universal healthcare and childcare, and redistributing money by cutting the Pentagon's budget to stop "endless wars". His organisation sprang up in 2017 to recruit and support the congressional members who became known as "the Squad", the furthest-left faction in the House, which includes members such as Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez and Ilhan Omar.

Healthcare will be one of the main arenas in which this fight is likely to play out, says Carrie Dann, managing editor of the Cook Political Report, a nonpartisan newsletter that forecasts the competitiveness of races.

"There is a lot of appetite for, at the very least, more transparency, more understanding of why healthcare costs are so high," said Dann. " Take a bad step, break your leg, and a huge swathe of Americans would see their worlds turned upside down by that because of the healthcare system as it is."

Several Democratic candidates this election cycle have outlined ideas to lower "out-of-pocket" costs for those who already have health insurance - being hit with additional costs on top of regular insurance payments is a common feature of the American healthcare system. But there's another flank of the party that is fed up with incremental changes and wants a national healthcare system that is free at the point of use - Medicare for All.
Recent polling suggests a majority of Democrats favour this kind of healthcare system, but a majority of Republicans oppose it.
But some Democrats say there's nuance in the issue.

"People want to have universal healthcare, and they also want to be able to keep their health insurance," says Neera Tanden, Joe Biden's former domestic policy adviser, now CEO of the Center for American Progress, a liberal think tank.

Mainstream establishment Democrats acknowledge that many people see healthcare as a right, but they insist that others strongly oppose a fully government-run programme, fearing lower standards of care, and insist on having the option of keeping their private health insurance.

Healthcare costs have gone up across the board - health insurance and out-of-pocket healthcare expenses, hospital expenses and prescription drug costs have all surged in recent years, rising faster than the rate of inflation. As medical expenses have increased, polls suggest the idea of universal healthcare isn't as outlandish as it once seemed, and this campaign cycle has shown that it's far less taboo for politicians to openly call for it.
Back in Georgia, it's an issue on which Tamara and James agree - they want universal healthcare.
But their most fundamental disagreement is over Israel. Tamara calls herself a Zionist. "My kids get mad at me for saying that," she said.
And they're hardly the only Democrats having this debate.

Dann, from the Cook Political Report, says one of the biggest lessons from this election cycle is that Democratic voters weren't just looking for candidates willing to fight Trump, but candidates willing to take on the establishment. Dann points to the key swing state of Michigan, where in the primary, Abdul El-Sayed - a fierce critic of Israel and its actions in Gaza - came out on top over the objections of the Democratic establishment.

"I think one reason for that was that he was not only talking about taking on Donald Trump, but taking on the Democratic establishment… the establishment in Washington writ large," she said. And part of that anti-establishment attitude is about US support for Israel.
Some who left the party in 2024 because they believe Biden was too supportive of Israel's actions in Gaza are now returning, energised by El-Sayed's tough tone.
"My red line has been Gaza," said Samraa Luqman, an Arab-American activist in Michigan who voted for Trump in the last presidential election, feeling betrayed by Democrats that year.

"2023 and 2024 have really taught this community a lesson that we are no longer going to be wishy-washy about the issue. It's Gaza or bust," she told me. "If you're not good on Gaza, on Israel, on Palestine, then we don't need you. We don't need you in office, and we don't need to vote for you, no matter what your party affiliation is."

But as El-Sayed has energised voters, he's also alienated others, particularly some who see support for Israel as connected to Jewish safety in the US and feel that antisemitism in their party has grown after the deadly Hamas attacks of October 7.
Zach Nessel is one of those Democrats. And he's increasingly worried about becoming politically homeless.

"We have people who don't think Zionists should have a place in our party, that they should be removed from the party," Nessel told me. "And as a proud Zionist, I don't want to be removed from the Democratic coalition just over this one issue in the Middle East."

Support for Israel became a litmus test in some Democratic primaries this season, leading to mounting resistance to the American Israel Public Affairs Committee, the longtime influential lobbying group.
But Dann tells me that it's not just Israel that's a litmus test, it's El-Sayed's race itself.

"Abdul El-Sayed's theory of the case is that he can run as an unabashed progressive in a purple state [a state that swings between the 'red' Republican party and 'blue' Democrats] and win because progressive ideas are not only popular if they're communicated correctly, but also activate voters who are not necessarily a normal part of the political process, particularly young people," she said.

If he wins, left-wing candidates will see it as a model, she adds. And if he loses, Democrats in the more centrist wing of the party will see it as evidence that left-wing ideas are out of touch with mainstream voters.

But there are others, like Jim Kessler with Third Way, a centrist think tank, who think Michigan shouldn't be the focus. He pointed out that if Democrats take control of the Senate it'll be because of more centrist candidates: Roy Cooper in North Carolina, Mary Peltola in Alaska, James Talarico in Texas, Josh Turek in Iowa, Adam Hamilton in Kansas. They, he said, are the ones expanding Democrats' odds this cycle. " So the bigger the Democratic victory, the more it seems like the centrist Democrats came through, not the DSA candidates," he said.
DSA-endorsed candidates made gains during the primaries this election cycle, but their ideas are still controversial to many.

" I don't think… the vast majority of working-class people in America are kind of mini socialists," Tanden told me, pointing to reporting that suggests the majority of people who support the DSA are college-educated voters.
" Working-class people are pretty moderate on issues like crime and immigration," she added.
Nonetheless, if Democrats gain the majority, their congressional leaders will have to navigate a group of Democrats in which there will likely be an increase in the loudest and most left-wing voices.

" The Democrats' biggest challenge is to figure out how to actually deliver on running the economy better and making things more affordable, because they've said over and over again and very loudly that's what they're going to do," said Teixeira.
In all likelihood, people will start thinking seriously about the next presidential candidate the day after the midterms.
So, who actually has the momentum: the left flank or the centre?

"I think after the election we'll see a lot of fighting between the factions to claim credit," Teixeira said. " And that will of course feed into the jostling for the presidential nomination for 2028."
Back in Georgia, Tamara and James may disagree on some things, but they both want Democrats to win big on Tuesday.
"I'm a very pragmatic person when it comes to progressive politics," James said. He wants to make it clear he doesn't agree with everything DSA members espouse.
So much of this midterm cycle has also come down to candidate quality - not just the message but the messenger. So I asked both mother and son who their "ideal" Democrat is.
Tamara instantly answered Jon Ossoff, the Democratic senator running for re-election in Georgia.
It's a point of agreement. They both really like their Georgia senator.

Ossoff is seen by many as a rising star of his party. The seat he is contesting is characterised by the Cook Political Report as "likely Democratic" - considered by analysts to be an impressive achievement in a swing state that voted for Trump in 2024.
"He knows how to speak to moderate Republicans, moderate Democrats, and members of the DSA," Tamara said. "He's not afraid to pull any punches… I appreciate how much he talks about corruption."
On Wednesday night, she joined thousands of people just outside Atlanta for a rally to cheer on the senator as former President Barack Obama campaigned for Democrats.
And when Ossoff took the mic, he spoke at length about what he sees as "corruption" in the Trump administration and in American politics, healthcare and corporate money.
And I heard this concern from voters in Georgia this past week, not just at the campaign rally, but at early voting sites in both Republican and Democratic counties.

"We have a corruption crisis," said Richard Schosky as he walked out of the voting booth in north Atlanta, after casting his ballot early. It's an issue that seems to be resonating deeply with voters, although the White House has repeatedly denied any allegations of wrongdoing.
In fact, Dann with the Cook Political Report says "corruption has become one of the central issues of this election".
Still, she added, "Democrats would be foolish to believe that a very good night for them in November is a mandate for the Democratic Party," said Dann.
"They are as almost as unpopular as Republicans and the president."

raw.title: Patrick Stewart, ‘Star Trek’ Captain and ‘X-Men’ Superhero, Dies at 86
paragraphs: Patrick Stewart, the sophisticated actor who brought a Shakespearean touch to Star Trek and X-Men as he made an otherworldly transformation from British stage veteran to sci-fi icon, has died. He was 86.
Stewart died Wednesday at his home in Los Angeles following “a brief and poignant journey with Alzheimer’s disease and Lewy body dementia,” longtime spokesperson Kelly Bush Novak announced.

“He has been held in the warm embrace of family and friends, surrounded by live music, prayer, tears, laughter and the kind of profound emotion that only he could inspire after a lifetime of devotion to us all,” Bush Novak wrote. “We will forever cherish the peaceful ease and reflection on his face, an enduring reminder of his invincible grace.”
In the late 1980s, Stewart had decades of classical theater work in England under his belt but was unfamiliar in America when he was given command of the U.S.S. Enterprise.

Star Trek: The Next Generation producer Robert Justman happened upon a UCLA lecture featuring Stewart and witnessed him reading from Shakespeare in his trademark patrician style. Justman called the actor in for an audition against the wishes of Star Trek creator Gene Roddenberry, who didn’t think a bald Brit could be the face of the new series.

After a contentious casting process, Stewart won over the famously persnickety Roddenberry and signed a long-term contract to play Capt. Jean-Luc Picard, thinking there was no way the show would last beyond one season.

“Every single person I spoke to — agents, directors, screenwriters, other actors — said, ‘Oh, don’t worry about six years. You’ll be lucky to make it through the first year,’ ” Stewart recalled in 2010. “Everybody felt it was madness to try to revive an iconic series like William Shatner and Leonard Nimoy‘s Star Trek. So, on the basis of that advice, I signed the six-year contract.”

The Los Angeles Times referred to him as an “unknown British Shakespearean actor” in a story announcing his casting. Brent Spiner, who played the android Data on the show, fashioned a sign to go above Stewart’s dressing room that read in bright red, “WARNING: Unknown British Shakespearean Actor.”

Next Generation premiered in September 1987, two months after Stewart’s 47th birthday, and initially struggled to catch on with Star Trek fans, many of whom considered the new cast to be pretenders to the throne. But after ups and downs, the series soared to new heights in 1990 with the season-three finale, “Best of Both Worlds.”

That episode featured the first cliffhanger in Star Trek history and saw Picard abducted and assimilated by an alien race known as The Borg. It was a genuinely shocking moment pulled off decades before such twists became common on the small screen.

Stewart also was at the center of several episodes considered among history’s finest hours of sci-fi television, including the alternate timeline-focused “Yesterday’s Enterprise” in 1990 and 1992’s “The Inner Light,” which had Picard live an entire lifetime, all in the blink of an eye.

Stewart and his cast of Americans became known as one of the closest in television, but in the early years, the theater veteran had trouble accepting the jokes that accompanied a typical 14-hour day on the set.
“Those guys taught me that you can do good work and have a good time at the same time,” he said in 2013. “Before that, I had always thought the two were unconnected completely.”

Next Generation ended in 1994 after seven seasons, going out with an Emmy nomination for outstanding drama series and spawning four films: Star Trek: Generations (1994), co-starring Shatner; Star Trek: First Contact (1996); Star Trek: Insurrection (1998); and Star Trek: Nemesis (2002), which saw Stewart face off against a then-unknown Tom Hardy as a younger clone of Picard.

Stewart acknowledged that Star Trek saw him fall victim to typecasting, so when he was offered the role of Prof. Charles Xavier in X-Men (2000) in the final years of Next Generation‘s movie run, he was hesitant.

An adaptation of the Marvel comic books, X-Men was a pioneering film and helped launch a new age of superhero cinema. Stewart worked opposite longtime friend Ian McKellen, who played the villain Magneto, and appeared as Xavier in seven more films, starring in X2: X-Men United (2003), X-Men: The Last Stand (2006), X-Men: Days of Future Past (2014) and Logan (2017) and having cameos in X-Men Origins: Wolverine (2009), The Wolverine (2013) and Avengers: Doomsday (2026).
Portraying Picard and Xavier for many years allowed him to explore layers upon layers with his characters, an opportunity few actors ever get.

“Both of them … I immensely admired for their morality, for their kindness, for their sensitivity, for their compassion,” Stewart told THR‘s Stephen Galloway in 2017. “Even for their intellectual capacities. Playing Jean-Luc for all those years had a real impact on me.”
After 17 years away, he returned to a familiar world to star in the CBS All Access series Star Trek: Picard, which debuted in January 2020.

Stewart was born on July 13, 1940, in Mirfield, Yorkshire, England, to Alfred and Gladys Stewart. His father worked as a semi-skilled laborer and was a veteran of World War II, among the last men evacuated from Dunkirk.

A heavy drinker, Alfred was physically abusive toward his wife, but not his three sons. It was only decades later that Stewart learned his dad’s violent behavior likely stemmed from undiagnosed post-traumatic stress disorder.

The youngest in the family, Stewart found himself terrified at home and often tasked with getting between his father’s fists and his mother. Growing up under those circumstances led him to advocate for veterans as well as domestic abuse victims later in life.

“I managed to find my own refuge in acting. The stage was a far safer place for me than anything I had to live through at home — it offered escape. I could be someone else, in another place, in another time,” he wrote in 2009.

At 15, he got a job at the local newspaper, The Dewsbury Reporter, where he was tasked with interviewing bereaved family members when someone would die in the town. Journalism turned out not to be his passion, and he spent much of his free time with drama groups. His editor finally told him he had to choose between acting and journalism — and he quit on the spot.

To support himself, Stewart got a sales job at a furniture store, but by 18 he had won a scholarship to Bristol Old Vic Theatre School. At 26, he became a member of the Royal Shakespeare Company, spending much of the 1960s with the group as well as with the National Theatre.

After a series of roles in British film and television, he made his U.S. debut in John Boorman’s King Arthur film Excalibur (1981), then appeared as the minstrel Gurney Halleck in David Lynch‘s cult sci-fi classic Dune (1984).
Stewart received Emmy and Golden Globe nominations for playing Captain Ahab in the 1998 miniseries Moby Dick and for his work as King Henry II in 2003’s The Lion in Winter.

A humorous guest spot on the HBO comedy Extras, in which he portrayed a lecherous version of himself obsessed with seeing women naked, earned him another Emmy nom in 2006, and he was nominated yet again in 2010, for playing King Claudius in the Royal Shakespeare Company’s Hamlet.

In 2015-16, he starred as cantankerous British talk show host Walter Blunt on Starz’s Blunt Talk, which earned him a third Golden Globe nom. He also had a long-running gig as the voice of Avery Bullock on American Dad!
He portrayed Bosley in Elizabeth Banks’ reboot of Charlie’s Angels (2019) and this year had a voice role in The Sheep Detectives.

On the 2001 New Year Honours list, Queen Elizabeth II appointed him an Officer of the Order of the British Empire, and he was knighted by her in 2010. “I never imagined anything like that could possibly happen to me, and in fact, it is still a significant unreality to me,” he said.

Stewart was married three times. He wed theater choreographer Sheila Falconer in 1966, and the pair remained together until 1990. They had two children, Daniel — who appeared in Blunt Talk — and Sophia. He was married to Star Trek producer Wendy Neuss from 2000-03 before wedding jazz musician Sunny Ozell in a 2013 ceremony officiated by McKellen.

“Like me, Jean-Luc has lived an unusual life that has taken him far beyond the bounds of normal human experience,” he wrote in his 2023 memoir, Making It So. “But he is also someone who has remained true to his earthbound roots, for they are what gave him his identity. In the end, he feels the call of home, as do I.”

raw.title: Emerging Arab Directors Given a Pathway Toward Filmmaking Careers by Expanded Pitching Platform at Sharjah Film Festival
raw.summary: The 13th edition of the UAE’s Sharjah Intl. Film Festival for Children and Youth is expanding its pitching platform for its second iteration. Six projects were selected this year, up from the three that took part during its inaugural program.
paragraphs: The 13th edition of the UAE’s Sharjah Intl. Film Festival for Children and Youth is expanding its pitching platform for its second iteration. Six projects were selected this year, up from the three that took part during its inaugural program.

The expansion is part of SIFF’s effort to build a pathway for emerging filmmakers beyond training and exhibition. As festival director Sheikha Jawaher bint Abdullah Al Qasimi told Variety ahead of this year’s edition, learning how to make a film is only part of the equation, “getting that film produced and seen is a completely different challenge.” This year’s projects bring together filmmakers from across the Arab world and diaspora, with the principal goal of finding financing and production partners from Sharjah and beyond.
Here are the six short film projects presented at this year’s pitching sessions:
(Mike Mo Elsherif, U.S. Produced by JohnBen Lacy)

Palestinian-American filmmaker Mike Mo Elsherif’s “The Black Hole” follows a Gazan refugee living in the U.S. who develops a mysterious illness as he searches for answers about his family in Gaza. El Sherif describes the film as a “visceral exploration of the complex ways in which our bodies store and process trauma throughout our lives, highlighting the deep connection between physical sensations and emotional experiences.”

The film is part of a trilogy of shorts. The first installment, “Maqluba,” screens in the Arabic short films competition at SIFF following stops at Woodstock, BlackStar and El Gouna, while “Goodbye Habibi,” now in post-production, was financed by FilmLab Palestine, the Islamic Scholarship Fund, the Doha Film Institute and the Kentucky Arts Council.

Currently in the financing stage, the project was developed through screenwriting lab The Front Porch Lab, under Louisville-based nonprofit 502 film, as well as The New Harmony Project, a writing organization.

Partially privately financed, “The Black Hole” is seeking further funding in Sharjah ahead of a winter 2027 shoot in Louisville, Kentucky. Elsherif describes the project as “a psychological study of a Palestinian grappling with the heartbreak and dehumanization he witnesses every day,” and a search for healing amid the devastation of his homeland.

“Kot Kot Kot” follows a young girl grappling with the loss of her mother. Her father gives her a chick that she raises into a hen with which she grows deeply attached, only for it to suddenly disappear one day.

The film grew from a story Boukhari’s mother told him as a child, which he had largely forgotten until his young nephew recounted it years later at a family gathering. “The emotion and wonder in his voice made me realize that this was a story worth telling again,” Boukhari tells Variety.

Currently in production, the independently-produced UAE project has been self-financed and is seeking funding to complete post-production, particularly in music, sound design, sound effects and sound recording. Boukhari has also signed Tunisian co-producer Alaeddin Abou Taleb of Key Production Films, whose credits include the Tanit d’Or-winning stop-motion short “Diaspora” at the Carthage Film Festival. Completion is planned by the end of 2026.

Illustrator Nadia Zilanova, whose international work includes commissions for the New York Times and publishing houses, recently joined the project to create and color the film’s backgrounds “in a distinctive visual style.”

UAE-based filmmaker Saleh Mohammed’s “The Last Call” begins with an unexpected phone call from a number connected to a forgotten memory, sending its protagonist on an emotional journey through the past, unresolved feelings and unanswered questions. Mohammed says the film explores “the things we leave unsaid and the moments we fail to appreciate until they are gone.”

The director described the visual approach of his film as “restrained,” allowing the film to reflect “on how a single moment can change a life and how we sometimes recognize the value of someone’s presence only after they are gone.”
The screenplay is complete and the project is in pre-production, with location scouting underway and casting and crew assembly next.
Mohammed is seeking financing and sponsorship, as well as potential co-producers and industry partners to help move the film into production.

“In a world where communication is constant, genuine connection can sometimes be the thing we overlook most,” Mohammed says. He is also using SIFF to build relationships with festivals and distributors ahead of the film’s eventual release.
Mohammed, who began his career as a theater actor and director, also co-stars in Khalid Al Mahmood’s “The Mangrove House,” the opening film of this year’s festival.
(Salah Al Hadhrami, Oman. Screenwriter Dalila Al-Dar’iya)

Omani filmmaker Salah Al Hadhrami’s “Lucky Shot” centers on Amjad, a boy from a working-class neighborhood whose passion for football fuels dreams of a life beyond his modest circumstances. An unexpected turn of events forces him to choose between those ambitions and temptation that could change his future.

Written by Omani filmmaker, writer and actor Dalila Al-Dar’iya, the 12-15 minute narrative short is in development, with initial approaches made to potential cast members. The independent project has yet to secure production financing and is seeking backers and co-producers in Sharjah and elsewhere in the region, with a tentative 2027 shoot dependent on funding.

“I believe that simple stories can carry the profoundest human messages,” Al Hadhrami says. For the director, the film is less about football itself than the moment when an unexpected opportunity becomes “a true test.”

The goal, above all, Al Hadhrami shares, is “to tell an authentic story that transcends geographical and cultural boundaries, one that resonates with the audience’s emotions. We hope to find partners who believe in this message and will help bring the film to the screen.”
(Aljouri Abdelaziz Alzarooni, UAE. Creative Producer Shahad Al Ali)

Emirati writer-director Aljouri Abdelaziz Alzarooni’s “My Uncle Saman” follows three young men on their way to their uncle’s long-awaited wedding. The groom, who is close enough in age to feel more like a cousin, sends them on a quick errand that turns into a string of misadventures, leaving the trio at risk of missing the wedding altogether.

The comedy short is in development and has yet to secure financing or attach a production company. Alzarooni is seeking financing and production partners at SIFF, along with collaborators in areas including cinematography, sound and post-production. She says the pitch has already generated interest from potential partners, with discussions now underway. The young director says potential partners expressed strong enthusiasm for the project’s “fresh and distinctive approach to Emirati storytelling.”

“‘My Uncle Saman’ is rooted in the natural humour, relationships, and everyday experiences of Emirati families, and I want to bring that authenticity to the screen in a way that audiences everywhere can connect with,” Alzarooni says.
Alzarooni is also eyeing eventual support from potential distributors, broadcasters, streaming platforms and industry mentors as her search to secure financing continues.
(Thoraya Farzaneh, UAE. Produced by Sayed Mousavi)

UAE-based filmmaker Thoraya Farzaneh makes her directing debut with “Tomato Merchant,” about an elderly man who spends his day selling tomatoes in a quiet neighborhood and refuses to leave until they are all sold. As repeated attempts are made to persuade him to go home, the reason for the insistence gradually becomes clear.

Farzaneh, who has spent the past several years working as an assistant director and writing scripts, says she waited until she felt ready to direct a story of her own. “I feel this is the right moment to take that step and share one of my stories with the world.”

The independent short has received funding from the RAK Art Fund, supported by the Sharjah-based Al Qasimi Foundation, while FANN – Media Discovery Platform, the parent organization of the festival, will provide post-production support following its SIFF pitch.

Now in pre-production, “Tomato Merchant” is set to shoot in the UAE in early November, with completion targeted for January. Farzaneh is using SIFF to explore festival and distribution opportunities for the finished film.
Producer Sayed Mousavi says, “This film reminds us that kindness often begins with the simple choice to be patient.”

raw.title: Prominent Russian newspaper shuts down under pressure from authorities
raw.summary: Novaya Gazeta has been one of the most high-profile independent news outlets in Russia over the last three decades.
paragraphs: Prominent Russian newspaper shuts down under pressure from authorities
For the last three decades, Novaya Gazeta has been one of the most high-profile independent news outlets in Russia.
Now it's shutting down - and it has accused the Russian authorities of the "murder" of a newspaper.
"They've killed us," reads a statement on the Novaya Gazeta website.
"The newspaper is no more. The Russian authorities and Russian special services have forced the paper to stop its work."
Novaya Gazeta has received an eviction order. Crucially, at the same time, the system that had allowed the paper to receive donations from readers was disabled.

Novaya Gazeta had developed a reputation for fearless investigative reporting on subjects such as corruption, human rights violations and abuse of power by officials and bureaucrats - dangerous topics in Russia.

The paper said that over time six journalists connected with the paper were killed for "fulfilling their professional and civic duty." Those reporters include Anna Politkovskaya, who was shot dead in the stairwell of her apartment block 20 years ago this month. Among the subjects she had reported on were the wars in Chechnya.

In the statement announcing its closure, Novaya Gazeta launched a stinging attack on the Russian authorities, claiming the newspaper was the victim of a "coordinated act" and blaming "the repressive state apparatus".
"Human rights and freedoms have been eliminated in the country and their protection has been equated to a crime," the statement said.
"The courts have been destroyed along with the law. Having personal convictions is now state treason."
Since Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, the pressure on independent journalism and independent Russian journalists has been growing.

Soon after the start of what the Kremlin calls the so-called "special military operation", new laws were adopted in Russia. Their aim: to punish dissent and silence criticism of the war and of those in power.
Novaya Gazeta itself and its staff had been facing a multitude of problems.

The authorities had already revoked the newspaper's licence and blocked access to its website. Several of its journalists and contributors had been designated "foreign agents", a label often used by the Russian authorities to punish critics.
Earlier this year there was a police search of the editorial office. A veteran investigative journalist, Oleg Roldugin, was arrested and charged with "unlawful access to computerised information".
In connection with the case, the newspaper's editor-in-chief, Sergei Sokolov, was recently taken in for police questioning and his home was searched.
Despite increasing pressure, Novaya Gazeta had managed to continue operating, albeit in a reduced form.
Loyal readers used virtual private networks to circumvent official blocking of the website and access content. But the loss of its licence and other restrictions dealt a major blow.

One of the founders of Novaya Gazeta in the 1990s - and for many years its chief editor - was journalist Dmitry Muratov, external. In 2021, Muratov was awarded the Nobel Peace Prize for efforts "to safeguard freedom of expression, which is a precondition for democracy and lasting peace".
The award didn't stop the authorities from declaring him a "foreign agent" in 2023.
At the offices of Novaya Gazeta, they've already started packing.
The end of this newspaper is very much the end of an era.
In an increasingly authoritarian Russia, it's also a sign of the times.

raw.title: Streeting denies 'kicking can down the road' in defence spending row
raw.summary: The government is under pressure to set out a path to greater defence spending, as ministers unveil plans to boost UK firms.
paragraphs: Streeting denies 'kicking can down the road' in defence spending row
Defence Secretary Wes Streeting has denied "kicking the can down the road" over how much the UK spends on defence.
The government has faced criticism for not setting out a pathway at Wednesday's Budget to hit its target of spending 3% of GDP on defence by 2030.
Streeting is at odds with MPs on the Commons defence committee over the issue.
It comes as Chancellor John Healey and Streeting announce that foreign firms which are awarded defence contracts of more than £50m will need to invest an equal value back into the UK.
Under the new investment rules, described as an "offset strategy", these companies will need to spend an equivalent amount on British factories, jobs and training.

The Ministry of Defence will apply the rules on a "case-by-case" basis from April 2027, the government said. Healey and Streeting will unveil the policy on a visit to UK defence contractor BAE's shipbuilding site in Glasgow later.
Countries including Poland, Norway and the Netherlands have mandated similar rules to "boost the economic benefit from defence procurement", the government said.
While ministers hope the rules increase investment in Britain's defence industry, they appear designed to do so in a politically palatable way rather than committing to spending cuts.

Tan Dhesi, Labour chair of the cross-party Commons defence committee, said on Wednesday that decisions had been "kicked into the long grass" to next year's government spending review, rather than announced in the Budget.
He warned that without building capabilities now, "we risk leaving ourselves seriously vulnerable in the event of a major conflict".
Streeting hit back at these comments as "unfair" and "unfounded".
Speaking on Thursday, Dhesi said the committee stands by its criticism.
"We had hoped to see that the chancellor would set out a precise pathway to spend 3% of GDP on defence by 2030," Dhesi told BBC Radio 4's Today programme.
"But instead some of those key decisions on defence have lamentably been delayed until next year's spending review."
He praised the government for plugging a £4.7bn hole in the Defence Investment Plan in the Budget, through asking government departments to cut their capital budgets by 1%.
Responding on Thursday, Streeting told Today: "I like Tan very much, he's a friend and I respect him, but I strongly disagree with him.
"And I don't think the charge he makes of delaying or kicking the can down the road stacks up against the extra money that is already going into defence and the capability we're funding right now."

Streeting told BBC Breakfast the new rules, aiming to create "bang for the British buck", would help achieve this target given increasing defence spending "does come at a cost to the country and other things we'd like to spend money on".
He said waiting for the spending review, which does not have a fixed date and could come in the second half of 2027, was "the right thing to do" so ministers can look at "spending in the round".
He added that the UK was ready to deal with hostile threats, but "we're not where we'd want to be".
"There's no sugarcoating the fact that our Armed Forces were under-invested in for more than a decade," he told Breakfast.
Defence analysts have questioned the government's ability to deliver on its 2030 target and the Nato-wide target of 3.5% by 2035. UK defence spending is at an estimated 2.6% of GDP this year.
Some estimates have suggested the government will need to spend an additional £10bn annually to reach its targets.
Tory leader Kemi Badenoch said on Wednesday that Healey "failed his own test" by not setting out a "plan for 3%".
Healey resigned as then-Prime Minister Sir Keir Starmer's defence secretary in June over not spending enough on defence.

In the Budget, Healey said the UK was negotiating with Finland, Poland and the Netherlands to set up an international bank - the Multilateral Defence Mechanism - to boost defence investment and joint procurement.
But Conservative shadow defence secretary James Cartlidge said this amounted to "turning to borrowing at a time when the national debt is over £3 trillion".
"The answer is not more borrowing – it's to cut welfare to fund defence," he said.

raw.title: 3 industrials stocks with warning signs
raw.summary: Whether you see them or not, industrials businesses play a crucial part in our daily activities. But they are at the whim of volatile macroeconomic factors that influence capital spending (like interest rates), and the market seems convinced that demand will slow. Due to this bearish outlook, the industry has tumbled by 8.9% over the past six months. This drop is a stark contrast from the S&P 500’s 7.5% gain.
paragraphs: Whether you see them or not, industrials businesses play a crucial part in our daily activities. But they are at the whim of volatile macroeconomic factors that influence capital spending (like interest rates), and the market seems convinced that demand will slow. Due to this bearish outlook, the industry has tumbled by 8.9% over the past six months. This drop is a stark contrast from the S&P 500's 7.5% gain.

A cautious approach is imperative when dabbling in these companies as the losers can be left for dead when the cycle naturally turns and the winners consolidate. Taking that into account, here are three industrials stocks we would avoid.
