raw.title: Anderson 'shocked' by Lancs exit and unsure if he will continue
raw.summary: Speaking for the first time since his Lancashire exit, James Anderson says the decision made him question whether is "something fundamentally wrong with me as a person".
paragraphs: Anderson 'shocked' by Lancs exit and unsure if he will continue
England legend James Anderson says he is "sad" and "shocked" by his release by Lancashire and has not decided whether to continue his career at another county.

Speaking at length on the Tailenders podcast for the first time since being told he will not have his Lancashire contract renewed, the 44-year-old said the decision made him question whether there is "something fundamentally wrong with me as a person".

Anderson, England's leading wicket-taker and a Lancashire legend, took 50 wickets in the County Championship and served as captain last season but he was told by Lancashire's new hierarchy they want to build an attack for the future.
"I went in for what I thought was a conversation about how the team moves forward," Anderson said.
"It wasn't a great year for the team. Being captain I thought it was chat about that.
"A couple of minutes in I realised it wasn't a conversation. I was being told they thought the best way for the team to move forward was without me.
Lancashire's decision was made by their incoming director of cricket Paul Farbrace, who held a meeting with Anderson and Lancashire's new chief executive Richard Kenyon.
Despite Anderson's wickets, the club finished second bottom in Division Two of the County Championship.
In 2024, England also chose to move on from their record wicket-taker in similar circumstances as they attempted to refresh and build an attack for the 2025-26 Ashes in Australia.
"All of the way through the season myself and the head coach were like 'is it something we are doing? Could we be doing more to help the team?'" Anderson said.
"I finished the season thinking 'was it something I did? Was I doing something wrong?' - and then I get this news.
"I am thinking 'this is happening again. Is there something fundamentally wrong with me as a person?' Your head just sort of races.
"I don't know if my career is done, we will have to wait and see, but it would be nice at some point if someone would let me retire."
'I wouldn't have thought so' - Anderson on Yorkshire move

The decision has angered Lancashire members and was criticised for being "pretty disrespectful" by Anderson's former England bowling partner Stuart Broad, who said it showed a lack of leadership given the veteran was not given a farewell.
Anderson first played List A cricket in 2000 as a 17-year-old for the Lancashire Cricket Board against Suffolk.

In addition to his 911 international wickets - an England record and a record for all pace bowlers - Anderson claimed 443 first-class scalps for Lancashire, along with 83 in List A cricket and a further 50 in T20s.
It is understood other counties are interested in signing the bowler, who turns 45 next summer.

He joked he "wouldn't have thought" he could play for Lancashire's historic rivals Yorkshire, but on his future added: "I am still trying to process everything and weigh up the best way forward for me.
"I am starting to get excited about the future, whether it is something different or playing cricket again. It is exciting.
"There are exciting challenges ahead. I have to attack it like that and not dwell too much on how or why it finished at Lancs."
He added: "I am sad the way it ended with the club I supported as a kid but now I have thought about it I am quite excited for the future.
"I was born there, grew up watching them, had some of my most memorable days out with dad watching them, got to play for them and captain the club, which is something most people dream about.
"I feel like I have a special connection with the club and will always support them."

raw.title: Student-backed election winners demand sweeping resignations in Serbia
raw.summary: Days after ousting Aleksandar Vučić's party from power, Student List MPs call for top figures to stand down.
paragraphs: Student-backed election winners demand sweeping resignations in Serbia
Serbia's victorious student-led movement has called for top figures in the police, intelligence and judiciary to stand down, days after ousting ex-president Aleksandar Vučić's party from power.

Standing in Pioneers' Park opposite parliament, newly elected MPs on the Student List demanded the immediate dismissal of all police officers who had broken the law, singling out the heads of the police, the BIA security agency and anti-terror unit.

It is not often a European country votes to fully reset its political system overnight, and Serbians have voted to hand the task to a group of novice politicians, made up of intellectuals, professors, artists, athletes and as many as 12 medical doctors and surgeons.
But the handover of power will take weeks, and the students' movement is concerned that evidence of possible wrongdoing could be destroyed in that time.
Just a few days ago, the park they were standing in on Thursday was a tent camp, filled with Vučić loyalists outside his office.
Within hours of him admitting defeat on Sunday night, the camp was dismantled, and a team of volunteers moved in on Monday morning to clean up the mess.
"This is just the first wave of spring cleaning, the new ones are coming now - we are very excited but ready to do it too," said Marija Milovanović, 25, as she scrubbed a park bench.
The student movement emerged from protests following the fatal collapse of a railway station canopy that killed 16 people in November 2024, in Serbia's second largest town Novi Sad.
Their desire was to bring those responsible to justice, and investigate widespread corruption claims blamed for one of the most tragic events in Serbia's modern history.
- How a movement of students brought down Serbia's Vučić
Under their Student Plan, they promise to "halt the plunder, return stolen goods to the state budget, and invest directly in education and the economy".
The purge of Vučić loyalists has already begun at Serbia's state broadcaster RTS, where director Manja Grčić has stepped down.
Newly elected MP Mirjana Nikolić said Serbian citizens had the right to truthful information and RTS had served the interests of the government for years.
The new MPs have also set their sights on replacing the head of Telekom Srbija, Vladimir Lučić.

Vučić loyalist Ana Brnabić, who is currently Serbia's acting president, has accused her opponents of choosing "revolutionary justice, not rule of law," and of aiming to shut down "all of the media they dislike".
But one of the next government's best-known MPs, Dejan Šoškić, argues that key reforms need to be in place fast.

"In the first six months, I would like to see the media scene liberated, fighting against corruption on the way, the institutions operating as prescribed by laws and a lustration law introduced," said Šoškić, an economist who served as governor of the central bank between 2010 and 2012.
By lustration, he means banning from public office members of the Vučić government or party apparatus who are found to have violated the rights of Serbians.
That kind of purge will take time, as all of Serbia's main pillars of authority have been held by Vučić and his party for so long, warns Strahinja Subotić of Belgrade-based European Policy Centre.
Ultimately, he believes the new administration will have to "build bridges to the segments that have been operating well in the past".

All 141 successful candidates were chosen by students from universities across Serbia through a lengthy, secretive and carefully crafted process, and tasked with implementing the movement's plan for a complete rebuild of the country.

That political agenda took months for a highly diverse group of students to agree to. Now it is up to the equally disparate team of successful candidates to put the plan into practice, rather than the students themselves.
Another prominent figure on the Student List, is Radomir Saičić, a professor of organic chemistry at the University of Belgrade.
"While the practical mechanisms will be developed on the go, the new MPs will stick to the students' 1200-page long and detailed plan," he told the BBC.
"Parliament is making decisions, but since this change was led by students' efforts, we would highly value their opinion and work closely with them," he promised.

Not only are they newcomers to politics, but Serbia's election winners have no obvious leader and are faced with a series of complex challenges, including taking on the country's highly complex balancing act on the international stage.

Serbia is both a candidate to join the European Union and maintains close relations with Russia. Its bid to join the bloc has long been on the back-burner, while its Western Balkan neighbours press ahead.
The EU was quick to welcome the Student List victory and has promised to back their push for reforms to the rule of law, media freedom and fight against corruption.
But EU integration occupies a strikingly minor place in the students' election manifesto, which describes the bloc merely as Serbia's "most important economic partner".

For years, Belgrade has balanced its foreign policy between the EU and its eastern partners, Russia and China. Belgrade has managed to stand out in Europe by not imposing sanctions on Moscow since the start of its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.
In return, Serbia has been rewarded with preferential gas prices that have helped maintain domestic stability, and Vladimir Putin publicly endorsed Vučić's bid to remain in power.
That does not mean that the students have any plans to change course, and changing Serbia's foreign policy may not be high on their list.

"Serbia had it own experience with sanctions in the 1990s and we know that they mostly harm ordinary people and do not affect policies of a state," said Dejan Šoškić, referring to UN sanctions imposed during the wars in former Yugoslavia.

The new government's initial focus will most likely be on domestic reform, and the clock is already ticking before the next election campaign, with presidential elections due to take place in December.

Aleksandar Vučić is legally barred from running for a third term as president, but he has promised that his defeated Serbian Progressive Party will fight back: "We will beat them much faster than they can even imagine."

raw.summary: Big Tech is dragging the Nasdaq toward its worst open in weeks while Dow components post earnings beats and barely budge. Whether the damage stays contained or spreads to the broader market depends on what happens the moment the opening bell rings.
paragraphs: Stock Market Today: Nasdaq Futures Plunge 2% as Big Tech Sells Off

Big Tech is dragging the Nasdaq toward its worst open in weeks while Dow components post earnings beats and barely budge. Whether the damage stays contained or spreads to the broader market depends on what happens the moment the opening…

Big Tech is pulling Wall Street toward a lower open on Friday, while a lot of earnings reports from energy, healthcare and utility companies keeps blue chips steady. Before the open, a fund tracking the S&P 500 was down 1% in premarket trading. The Nasdaq-100 proxy was off more than 2%. Those S&P 500 losses are concentrated in tech, and Barron’s lists Intel and Amazon among the stocks driving the morning.
Diesel Profits Keep Chevron Ahead of the Market
Chevron (NYSE:CVX | CVX Price Prediction) posted adjusted EPS of $5.28, ahead of the $4.83 estimate. The beat came from refining.

U.S. downstream earnings jumped to $3.58B from $638M on record refinery throughput, and CNBC tied the surge to high diesel fuel prices. Chevron is a Dow component, and its shares gained about 1% premarket, which helps hold that index near flat.
AbbVie Raises Its Outlook While Cameco Stumbles

AbbVie (NYSE:ABBV) earned $3.82 per share against a $3.78 estimate. It also lifted full-year EPS guidance to $13.95-$13.99. Its chief executive said the company is “once again increasing AbbVie’s full-year guidance and raising our quarterly dividend.” The stock still slid about 1%, because a narrow beat was not enough to excite buyers.
Cameco (NYSE:CCJ) delivered the morning’s worst miss. Adjusted EPS came in at $0.00 against expectations of $0.27.
A long maintenance shutdown at the Key Lake mill cut output to 1.1M lbs from 2.2M lbs. Shares fell about 9%, a hit to sentiment across nuclear stocks.
Data Center Power Demand Lifts Utility Outlooks

Exelon (NASDAQ:EXC) beat with $0.87 per share and pointed to about 11 GW of high-probability data center load. Dominion Energy (NYSE:D) now expects 2026 earnings in the top half of its range. Falling yields help too: the 10-year Treasury slid to nearly 5%. The utilities feeding the AI expansion are exactly the kind of non-chip suppliers we profiled in a free report on seven stocks powering the AI boom.
The exchange operator that runs the VIX franchise raised its organic revenue outlook to the “high teens” after record trading in same-day options.
What a Tech Sell-Off With a Flat Dow Tells You

The early split points to a rotation. As money leaves highly valued tech for companies with clear earnings support, the Dow and Russell 2000 are holding up better than the Nasdaq-100. A VIX near 17 shows traders are cautious but calm. A sharp jump today would signal the sell-off is spreading beyond tech.
Once trading starts, check whether tech losses stay in the Nasdaq or spread to the broader market. Dominion faces a Virginia hearing on its proposed merger starting November 17.

paragraphs: How Kenyans got caught in $130m US ghost student scam
In May 2024, Francis Mogambi arrived in the United States after winning the Diversity Visa lottery, a programme that gives people from around the world a chance to become permanent residents.
Just over two years later, the Kenyan national found himself at the centre of a US investigation into an alleged nationwide scheme to defraud the federal student aid system.
On 19 October 2026, a grand jury in Nebraska indicted Mogambi on five counts of theft of government money and five counts of aggravated identity theft.

Prosecutors allege that, between November 2025 and May 2026, he worked with associates in Kenya to steal the identities of US citizens and use them to fraudulently enroll fictitious students in American colleges.
Once the fake students were enrolled, Mogambi allegedly diverted their financial aid payments to himself, keeping 30% and sending the remainder to his associates in Kenya.
The intended loss in his case was $20,000 (£15,000), according to prosecutors.

Court documents say Mogambi received $2,000 a week and attempted to recruit another person into the scheme. He allegedly told the individual he needed a business that would allow him to cash larger cheques without paying taxes.
Mogambi was arrested shortly after the indictment was returned and is being held in custody pending trial. He has not yet commented on the allegations against him.

His case forms part of a wider US investigation, dubbed Operation Ghostbusters, into the alleged use of stolen identities to enrol fictitious students at colleges and claim federal financial aid that resulted in a loss of $130m in taxpayers funds.

US authorities say the investigation has so far resulted in five indictments that involved Kenyan nationals, while a further 40 investigations remain open. Hundreds of people have been affected after fraudsters allegedly stole their personally identifiable information (PII) and used it to access federal student aid.
The stolen personal information was sometimes sold online for between $4 and $8, with fraudsters targeting low-income Americans who had never had the opportunity to attend college.

At a news conference on 29 October announcing the first charges in the investigation, Assistant Attorney General Colin M McDonald, who heads the Justice Department's National Fraud Enforcement Division, vowed to pursue those involved.
"If you steal taxpayers' dollars, if you exploit a programme meant to help students, we are resolved to find you and prosecute you," he said.

The Justice Department says those behind the fraud use what is described as "super intelligence" to place fake students in classrooms and complete coursework, creating the impression that they are attending college and allowing financial aid payments to continue.
"The goal is to keep the ghost student in school as long as possible. Semester after semester after semester stealing money from the taxpayers," McDonald said.
But the consequences extend beyond the financial losses suffered by the US government.
People whose identities are stolen can find themselves facing unexpected student loan debts, even if they have never enrolled in college.
"His identity was stolen, his credit is now at risk, and his name is on the bill," McDonald said, describing the impact on one victim.
He also said that nearly a third of community college applicants in California in 2024 had been identified as fraudulent.
The scale of the suspected fraud is significant.

Investigators identified 830,840 potentially fraudulent Federal Student Aid identification numbers associated with nearly $130m in September and October 2026. They recommended that the Department of Education disable them.
The figure represents financial aid associated with potentially fraudulent accounts, not confirmed losses.
"In a flash, the money vanishes, often overseas in places like Kenya," McDonald said.
The investigation has also exposed alleged financial links between the US and Kenya.
In September, US officials travelled to Kenya to work with local law enforcement on extraditions, prosecutions and the recovery of money allegedly stolen from American taxpayers.

With the help of Kenyan investigators, US authorities seized more than $750,000 from a cryptocurrency account belonging to a Kenyan national connected to the wider scheme. The Justice Department described it as the first international seizure of its kind in Kenya.
The seizure was not connected to Mogambi's individual case.

In a separate case in Virginia, prosecutors allege that a Kenyan national received more than 700 fraudulent student-aid refunds totalling approximately $1.44m. At least $1.3m was subsequently transferred through thousands of transactions to accounts in the US and Kenya.
Meanwhile, in New Jersey, three people have been charged with allegedly acting as money mules in a scheme to obtain more than $1m in federal student aid.
Prosecutors say they received the funds through US bank accounts, kept a portion for themselves and transferred the remainder to alleged co-conspirators in Kenya linked to a purported safari company.
If convicted, Mogambi faces a mandatory prison term of at least 10 years, according to the Justice Department.
Authorities say those convicted will also face appropriate orders for forfeiture of assets and restitution to victims, in addition to any prison sentences.

raw.title: Record number of purges as Xi emphasises 'party discipline' at China political gathering
raw.summary: Xi's anti-corruption campaign has become "an effort to consolidate and maintain authority", observers say.
paragraphs: Record number of purges as Xi emphasises 'party discipline' at China political gathering
A record 33 members have been expelled from China's Communist Party as it concluded a major annual political gathering, which had the most empty seats ever seen.
The fifth plenum was attended by 279 Central Committee members, compared to 315 at the fourth plenum in October 2025 and 364 at the third one in July 2024.
While recent plenums focused on economic reforms or social and development issues, party discipline took centre stage at this week's gathering.
Xi Jinping has made the fight against corruption a central pillar of his rule since he took the reins in 2012, calling it the "biggest threat" to the party.
Sixteen of the 33 members expelled are from the military, according to a communique issued on Thursday, which marked the end of the four-day closed-door gathering held at a hotel in Beijing.
It's unclear what specific charges these members face beyond "serious disciplinary and legal violations". Such broad allegations have become routine under Xi's anti-corruption campaign.
It has now become "an effort to consolidate and maintain authority", says Chong Ja Ian, a non-resident scholar with Carnegie China.
"In this case, the campaign will continue and expand depending on how secure Xi feels rather than any real issue with corruption."

In its statement, the party said it has "squarely confronted the grim reality that party leadership had at times weakened or hollowed out" and that it will continue to "enforce strict party self-governance, including turning the knife inwards to... curb disorder".
The latest expulsions bring the total number of members removed under Xi's third term to a record 51, up from 35 and five in his first and second terms respectively.
Beyond the plenum, China's top anti-corruption watchdog reported that 680,000 people across the party apparatus have been disciplined in the first nine months of this year.
This is also the first time in Xi's 14 years of leadership that plenum attendance fell below 300. The current Central Committee started its term in 2022 with more than 370 members.
Observers argue that Xi views corruption not just as graft but also ideological impurity and, crucially, disloyalty.
In January, he warned against "two-faced cadres" who profess political loyalty but defy orders and act in their self-interest.

Among the high-ranking officials expelled are former Xinjiang party chief Ma Xingrui, and ex-top generals Zhang Youxia and Liu Zhenli. Official statements announcing their removal this year said they "seriously violating [the party's] discipline and rules", which is widely read as a euphemism for corruption.

The culling of the military's top brass has been particularly significant, with Neil Thomas, Lobsang Tsering and Shengyu Wang from the Asia Society Policy Institute describing it as "in a category of its own".
"It raises serious questions about organisational leadership and combat readiness, even as China continues to unveil formidable new military hardware," they wrote.

Zhang was also vice-chairman of the Central Military Commission, which controls the armed forces. The seven-member commission has since been whittled down to just two members: Xi as chairman and Zhang Shengmin vice-chairman.
Ma and Zhang Youxia were former Politburo members. Their removal, along with former general He Weidong in 2025, meant the powerful 24-man Politburo was at one point left with 21 members.
Zhang Shengmin was promoted to the top decision-making body at the fifth plenum, bringing the number to 22.
Former prominent diplomat Liu Jianchao, who disappeared from public view in July last year, was also named among those who have been purged.
"Xi has few qualms about removing people he promoted," Chong says. "That he does so at will with little opposition underscores how unassailable his position is at the moment."
Analysts believe one reason for the increased empahsis on discipline – which many interpret as loyalty – is next year's Party Congress, when the CCP will vote again for its next leader.

A leadership reshuffle is due in 2027 and many analysts expect Xi to hold on to the top job for a fourth term and beyond. No leader has served that long except Mao Zedong, the founder Communist China.
Xi has reason to "scrutinise the next cohort more closely" given the fall of so many officials from the current committee, Thomas says.

"Today's rising stars tend to be relatively young, boast technocratic backgrounds, and have connections to Xi's political network," he says, adding that "provincial leadership ranks are a promising place to look".
Observers say that ultimately, Xi is expected to dominate personnel selection at the 21st Party Congress, which will further cement his grip on the party and the country.

"Xi's focus is further consolidating power around himself... The readout from the plenum suggests he intends to be at the centre of China and the Communist Party for the foreseeable future," Chong says.
"However, further down the road, such concentration of power may pave the way for a more serious power vacuum when Xi ages and slows down."

raw.title: Three dead after two helicopters collide midair near Oregon airport
raw.summary: The collision involving a Robinson R22 and an Airbus helicopter occurred on Thursday afternoon, with both aircraft crashing in a field adjacent to a highway.
paragraphs: Three dead after two helicopters collide midair near Oregon airport
Three people have died after two helicopters collided midair near a small airport in Oregon, officials said.

The collision involving a Robinson R22 and an Airbus helicopter occurred near McMinnville Municipal Airport on Thursday afternoon. Both aircraft crashed in a field adjacent to a highway, the sheriff's office said.

Authorities identified the victims as a 22-year-old flight instructor from Texas and a student pilot from the United Kingdom, who were aboard one of the helicopters. The sole occupant of the other aircraft was also killed.
It was not immediately clear what caused the crash.
The Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) and the National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB) responded to the scene and are leading the ongoing investigation.

The flight instructor on the Robinson R22 was identified Maddie Aasbo. The student pilot from the UK has not yet been publicly identified, as authorities work with the consulate and the FBI to notify the next of kin.
The sole occupant of the Airbus was identified as Tyler Delane Sturdevant, 38, of Newberg, Oregon.
One of the aircraft was operated by Jerry Trimble Helicopters, a flight training school based at the McMinnville Municipal Airport, according to a statement from the company.

"Jerry Trimble Helicopters is deeply saddened to confirm that one of our aircraft was involved in an aviation incident this afternoon," the company said, adding that they were fully cooperating with investigators.
Authorities asked the public to avoid the area as they responded to the incident.

raw.title: Human rights lawyer couple sentenced to 10 years' prison in Pakistan
raw.summary: Imaan Mazari and Hadi Ali Chattha were charged over an incident in 2024, when England's cricket team was touring Pakistan.
paragraphs: Human rights lawyer couple sentenced to 10 years' prison in Pakistan
A Pakistani anti-terrorism court has sentenced human rights lawyer Imaan Mazari and her husband Hadi Ali Chattha to 10 years in prison, over an alleged security breach during a cricket tour in 2024.
The couple were accused of removing road barriers and obstructing police officers in Islamabad - charges that both have denied.
Mazari and Chattha were previously sentenced to up to 17 years in prison for social media posts criticising the military.

Pakistan's Supreme Court had suspended those sentences in August, but police re-arrested the couple before they could be released. They have been imprisoned in Rawalpindi's Adiala Jail for the past several months.
This latest case concerns an incident on 25 October 2024, when England's cricket team was touring Pakistan.

Prosecutors accused Mazari and Chattha of removing barriers from a road designated for the team's security convoy and obstructing police officers at Zero Point, a major cloverleaf road junction in Islamabad.

They were each sentenced to 10 years in prison under the Anti-Terrorism Act, as well as additional one-year and two-year terms for obstructing and using force against public servants. All sentences will run concurrently.
The court also fined each of them 200,000 Pakistani Rupees (£541:$723).
In statements recorded during the trial, the couple described themselves as "prisoners of conscience" who had faced state persecution.
"I am being punished for not only supporting my wife's work and activism, but for choosing this path of resisting injustice as our life journey together," Chatta said in his statement to Dawn News.
The couple had earlier said that they were "being made an example to further cement the chilling effect against those who stand (or want to stand) against tyranny, oppression, and injustice".
Amnesty International has criticised the proceedings, saying the couple were denied an open and fair trial.
"These convictions are an indictment of Pakistan's justice system." said Yasmine Ahmed, Amnesty International's Senior Director for Regional Human Rights Impact.
"Imaan and Hadi are being targeted solely because of their refusal to stop their fearless human rights work and for exercising their right to freedom of expression and peaceful assembly."
The organisation also raised concerns that the trial had been moved inside the prison, where Mazari and Chattha were kept behind a cage-like structure during hearings.
The couple have faced several criminal cases in recent months.

They have been in custody since 23 January, when they were arrested in a separate case involving an alleged altercation outside the Islamabad High Court. A day later, they were sentenced to up to 17 years in prison under Pakistan's Prevention of Electronic Crimes Act over social media posts critical of the military.

Pakistan's Supreme Court suspended those sentences and granted them bail on 17 September - but they were arrested again the same day in connection with a separate case over a protest in March 2025, in which they were accused of chanting "anti-government slogans" and "blocking roads".
Mazari and Chattha are prominent human rights lawyers who have represented activists, journalists and marginalised communities subjected to enforced disappearances.
Mazari's mother, Shireen Mazari, is a former human rights minister who served in the government of former Pakistan prime minister Imran Khan.
The couple's convictions have long drawn criticism from international human rights organisations, which have raised concerns about the treatment of lawyers and activists in Pakistan.

raw.title: How video game remakes tap the power of nostalgia
raw.summary: Video games are good at triggering nostalgia, a key reason why classic games keep getting remade.
paragraphs: How video game remakes tap the power of nostalgia
The moment she saw footage from the remake of The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time, Kacey Doran picked up her phone. She had to tell her sister.
"Have you seen this?" messaged Doran, excitedly.

Nearly 30 years ago, a 10-year-old Doran had sat in front of her family's TV, reading out the dialogue on screen to her sister, a year younger, as they inched their way through the original Nintendo 64 game's sprawling, puzzle-filled dungeons. Ocarina's fantasy-like story, and beautiful music, enthralled them both.
It was also the first game Doran ever completed. Now, countless memories rushed back to her as she devoured clips of the fully redesigned version, due to arrive on the Switch 2 later this year.
Doran's sister messaged back: "I'm not tearing up… YOU'RE tearing up."

This is the power of nostalgia – and a perfect example of how video games can trigger it. Doran now teaches an esports course at Rowan University in New Jersey. She says the original Ocarina of Time, released in 1998, had a "magical" quality that she hopes to rediscover, and also share with her sister's children.

The video games industry has long leaned on remakes. From Mario Kart to the Final Fantasy series, or even Pac-Man, some games just keep coming back in updated forms, as new generations of gamers emerge and as computer hardware improves, enabling more detailed graphics and increasingly expansive game worlds.

While the emotional hook may be the most significant draw, putting out a remake can be a double-edged sword. Some gamers are very protective of their favourite titles and new versions don't always meet certain fans' astronomically high expectations.

Nostalgia is an important but mixed emotion, says Tim Wulf, at the Centre for Advanced Internet Studies in Bochum, Germany. It has positive aspects but also a kind of sadness, too. Happiness in remembering things that were important to us, and also an awareness that that time is now gone.
"It's a social emotion because memories that induce nostalgia for us are connected to other people," he explains, adding that nostalgia can boost our self-esteem while highlighting key social bonds.

Video games, says Wulf, are notoriously good at triggering nostalgia because gamers can "jump into the same environment". In other words, games are like time machines for our emotions, and returning to fondly remembered places can feel stabilising or reassuring in an ever-changing world.

Doran, for one, notes that when you return to a favourite old game, there's something satisfying about deploying previously learned skills. You know what to do here, you're winning again. Just like the old days.
Putting out remasters and remakes has been a "really successful" strategy for the games industry, says Piers Harding-Rolls, head of games research at Ampere Analysis.

"Tying in with established audiences and building on existing content is quite a safe route for a lot of companies," he adds. In many cases, it is cheaper to update an existing game rather than create a new title from scratch.
Among other remakes that have found big audiences recently are those of Resident Evil 4 and Assassin's Creed Black Flag.

But Ocarina of Time perhaps stands out because, ever since its original release, it has been considered by many as one of the greatest games ever made. "The interest from all the Gen Zs that I work with is really high," says Harding-Rolls. The legend of The Legend of Zelda, as it were.
Clearly, nostalgia is not the only driver of interest in the remake, and today's audiences will expect a game that plays to today's standards.

Games companies must keep innovating when linking contemporary audiences to the past, says Wulf, in order satisfy their desire for fresh experiences. And although Wulf himself was a big fan of the original, he has no personal interest in the Ocarina of Time remake. "I want a new game – I don't want to play an old game," he says. Nostalgia isn't always enough for some.

Plus, critics often highlight a tension between originals and remakes. Which is the definitive version? In 2021, Square Enix released the bizarrely titled Nier Replicant ver.1.22474487139... – a remaster of a game first published in 2010. One reviewer wrote, external, "What we're left with is two nearly identical Niers each vying to be the true Nier."
Fans may react badly should a remaster or remake fail to do justice to the source material. And, in the gaming world, angry fan reactions can be serious.
"There's always going to be that fan base or group of people that are going to nit-pick," says Stephanie Ijoma, chief executive and founder of NNESAGA, a consultancy and creative agency.

Ultimately, games developers working on remakes have to "find the right balance" between appealing to fans and allowing themselves to be creative with the material, she adds. "You can't make art in fear, you can't create in fear."
Ijoma gives the example of Final Fantasy VII. First released in 1997, it got a highly anticipated remake in 2020.
This was a game Ijoma played back in the late 1990s and she was thrilled to be able to share it with younger players today.
Remakes enable this sharing of experiences because getting old computer hardware or video games consoles to work, while a pastime loved by some, is not possible for everyone.

"I've tried multiple times to play Silent Hill 2 because I'm interested in older games but it's such a difficult game to come into nowadays," says Niklas Hallin, a solo indie game developer who runs the studio Neckbolt. "They made a remake and it's so smooth, it just works. It works on your modern hardware."

Hallin did not play many games as a child so he says nostalgia isn't much of a motivator for him. However, in his own games, he likes to include subtle stylistic references to classic games because he knows that this appeals to gamers.

Indie developers often lean on retro games aesthetics not just because people respond well to them – but also because they are easier to achieve. "You can't compete with billion dollar budgets, super high-fidelity, Triple A graphics," he says.

One question remains. The visual difference, today, between games released years apart is, arguably, negligible. So will there be any point in remaking a game from 2026 in, say, 2038? Will technology have moved on so much by then that it's actually worth it?
Harding-Rolls predicts that games companies will still seek to connect new audiences with classic titles by offering updates.
Remakes might become less about graphical improvements and more about editorial adjustments. "Reinterpretations," he says. "Or versions with additional content."
